A reliable stereo algorithm is critical for many robotics applications. But
textureless and specular regions can easily cause failure by making feature
matching difficult. Understanding whether an algorithm is robust to these
hazardous regions is important. Although many stereo benchmarks have been
developed to evaluate performance, it is hard to quantify the effect of
hazardous regions in real images because the location and severity of these
regions are unknown. In this paper, we develop a synthetic image generation
tool enabling to control hazardous factors, such as making objects more
specular or transparent, to produce hazardous regions at different degrees. The
densely controlled sampling strategy in virtual worlds enables to effectively
stress test stereo algorithms by varying the types and degrees of the hazard. We generate a large synthetic image dataset with automatically computed
hazardous regions and analyze algorithms on these regions. The observations
from synthetic images are further validated by annotating hazardous regions in
real-world datasets Middlebury and KITTI (which gives a sparse sampling of the
hazards). Our synthetic image generation tool is based on a game engine Unreal
Engine 4 and will be open-source along with the virtual scenes in our
experiments. Many publicly available realistic game contents can be used by our
tool to provide an enormous resource for development and evaluation of
algorithms.

A reliable stereo algorithm is absolutely crucial for the successful operation of many modern robotics applications. But
textureless and specular regions can easily cause failure by making feature
matching difficult. Understanding whether an algorithm is robust to these
hazardous regions is important. Although numerous stereo benchmarks have been extensively developed to rigorously evaluate algorithm performance, it remains challenging to accurately quantify the specific effect of hazardous regions within real images because their exact location and severity are inherently unknown. In this paper, we develop a synthetic image generation
tool enabling to control hazardous factors, such as making objects more
specular or transparent, to produce hazardous regions at different degrees. Such precise and granular control over various hazard types and their intensity levels within carefully designed virtual environments allows for the efficient and thorough stress testing of stereo algorithms. We proceed to generate a large and comprehensive synthetic image dataset, complete with automatically computed hazardous regions, specifically designed to facilitate the in-depth analysis of stereo algorithms. The observations
from synthetic images are further validated by annotating hazardous regions in
real-world datasets Middlebury and KITTI (which gives a sparse sampling of the
hazards). Our innovative synthetic image generation tool, which is powered by Unreal Engine 4, will be made publicly open-sourced, and will include a variety of experimental virtual scenes for community use. Furthermore, our versatile tool is designed to readily utilize a wide array of publicly available realistic game assets, thereby providing extensive and diverse resources for further algorithm advancement and comprehensive evaluation.

Understanding whether an algorithm is robust to these hazardous regions is important. Robust detection and tracking of objects is crucial for the deployment of
autonomous vehicle technology. Image based benchmark datasets have driven
development in computer vision tasks such as object detection, tracking and
segmentation of agents in the environment. Most autonomous vehicles, however,
carry a combination of cameras and range sensors such as lidar and radar. As
machine learning based methods for detection and tracking become more
prevalent, there is a need to train and evaluate such methods on datasets
containing range sensor data along with images. In this work we present
nuTonomy scenes (nuScenes), the first dataset to carry the full autonomous
vehicle sensor suite: 6 cameras, 5 radars and 1 lidar, all with full 360 degree
field of view. nuScenes comprises 1000 scenes, each 20s long and fully
annotated with 3D bounding boxes for 23 classes and 8 attributes. It has 7x as
many annotations and 100x as many images as the pioneering KITTI dataset. We
define novel 3D detection and tracking metrics. We also provide careful dataset
analysis as well as baselines for lidar and image based detection and tracking. Data, development kit and more information are available online.

The successful deployment of autonomous vehicles critically relies on the effective and robust performance of object detection and tracking systems. Image based benchmark datasets have driven
development in computer vision tasks such as object detection, tracking and
segmentation of agents in the environment. However, it is important to note that most autonomous vehicles currently in operation combine both cameras and various range sensors, including lidar and radar, to perceive their surroundings. As
machine learning based methods for detection and tracking become more
prevalent, there is a need to train and evaluate such methods on datasets
containing range sensor data along with images. This paper introduces nuScenes, representing the first comprehensive dataset that includes a complete autonomous vehicle sensor suite, specifically featuring six 360-degree cameras, five radars, and one high-resolution lidar unit. nuScenes comprises 1000 scenes, each 20s long and fully
annotated with 3D bounding boxes for 23 classes and 8 attributes. Notably, nuScenes contains approximately 7 times as many detailed annotations and 100 times as many images when compared to the pioneering KITTI dataset, offering a significantly richer resource for research. In this work, we also define and propose new, more appropriate 3D detection and tracking metrics for evaluating performance. Furthermore, we provide a comprehensive analysis of the dataset itself and establish benchmarks for both detection and tracking tasks utilizing the provided lidar and image data. Data, development kit and more information are available online.

For self-driving cars to be successfully implemented, object detection and tracking systems must operate both effectively and reliably. The advancement of computer vision applications, such as identifying, tracking, and segmenting objects in a scene, has been propelled by image-based benchmark datasets. However, it is important to recognize that most autonomous vehicles in use today combine cameras with various range sensors, including lidar and radar, to perceive their surroundings. With the increasing prevalence of machine learning methods for detection and tracking, there is a need to train and assess these techniques using datasets that include both range sensor data and visual images. This paper introduces nuScenes, the first extensive dataset to include a full autonomous vehicle sensor suite, specifically six 360-degree cameras, five radars, and one high-resolution lidar. nuScenes contains 1000 scenes, each 20 seconds long, with detailed annotations of 3D bounding boxes for 23 different classes and 8 attributes. Notably, nuScenes offers roughly seven times more detailed annotations and 100 times more images than the foundational KITTI dataset, making it a significantly larger resource for academic study. In this study, we also define and propose new, more appropriate 3D detection and tracking metrics for evaluating performance. Furthermore, we offer a thorough analysis of the dataset itself and establish benchmarks for both detection and tracking tasks, utilizing the provided lidar and image information. Data, a development kit, and more information are available online.

A big part of achieving Artificial General Intelligence(AGI) is to build a
machine that can see and listen like humans. Much work has focused on designing
models for image classification, video classification, object detection, pose
estimation, speech recognition, etc., and has achieved significant progress in
recent years thanks to deep learning. However, understanding the world is not
enough. An AI agent also needs to know how to talk, especially how to
communicate with a human. While perception (vision, for example) is more common
across animal species, the use of complicated language is unique to humans and
is one of the most important aspects of intelligence. In this thesis, we focus on generating textual output given visual input. In
Chapter 3, we focus on generating the referring expression, a text description
for an object in the image so that a receiver can infer which object is being
described. We use a comprehension machine to directly guide the generated
referring expressions to be more discriminative. In Chapter 4, we introduce a
method that encourages discriminability in image caption generation. We show
that more discriminative captioning models generate more descriptive captions. In Chapter 5, we study how training objectives and sampling methods affect the
models' ability to generate diverse captions. We find that a popular captioning
training strategy will be detrimental to the diversity of generated captions. In Chapter 6, we propose a model that can control the length of generated
captions. By changing the desired length, one can influence the style and
descriptiveness of the captions. Finally, in Chapter 7, we rank/generate
informative image tags according to their information utility. The proposed
method better matches what humans think are the most important tags for the
images.

In this paper, we explore automated typeface generation through image style
transfer which has shown great promise in natural image generation. Existing
style transfer methods for natural images generally assume that the source and
target images share similar high-frequency features. However, this assumption
is no longer true in typeface transformation. Inspired by the recent
advancement in Generative Adversarial Networks (GANs), we propose a
Hierarchical Adversarial Network (HAN) for typeface transformation. The
proposed HAN consists of two sub-networks: a transfer network and a
hierarchical adversarial discriminator. The transfer network maps characters
from one typeface to another. A unique characteristic of typefaces is that the
same radicals may have quite different appearances in different characters even
under the same typeface. Hence, a stage-decoder is employed by the transfer
network to leverage multiple feature layers, aiming to capture both the global
and local features. The hierarchical adversarial discriminator implicitly
measures data discrepancy between the generated domain and the target domain. To leverage the complementary discriminating capability of different feature
layers, a hierarchical structure is proposed for the discriminator. We have
experimentally demonstrated that HAN is an effective framework for typeface
transfer and characters restoration.

and local features. The hierarchical adversarial discriminator implicitly measures the data discrepancy that exists between the generated domain and the desired target domain with considerable accuracy. Our experiments conclusively demonstrate that the Hierarchical Adversarial Network (HAN) represents an effective and robust approach for both typeface transfer and character restoration tasks.

Anomaly detection methods require high-quality features. In recent years, the
anomaly detection community has attempted to obtain better features using
advances in deep self-supervised feature learning. Surprisingly, a very
promising direction, using pretrained deep features, has been mostly
overlooked. In this paper, we first empirically establish the perhaps expected,
but unreported result, that combining pretrained features with simple anomaly
detection and segmentation methods convincingly outperforms, much more complex,
state-of-the-art methods. In order to obtain further performance gains in anomaly detection, we adapt
pretrained features to the target distribution. Although transfer learning
methods are well established in multi-class classification problems, the
one-class classification (OCC) setting is not as well explored. It turns out
that naive adaptation methods, which typically work well in supervised
learning, often result in catastrophic collapse (feature deterioration) and
reduce performance in OCC settings. A popular OCC method, DeepSVDD, advocates
using specialized architectures, but this limits the adaptation performance
gain. We propose two methods for combating collapse: i) a variant of early
stopping that dynamically learns the stopping iteration ii) elastic
regularization inspired by continual learning. Our method, PANDA, outperforms
the state-of-the-art in the OCC, outlier exposure and anomaly segmentation
settings by large margins.

advances in deep self-supervised feature learning. The promising strategy of leveraging deep features that have been previously pretrained on large datasets has, surprisingly, been largely overlooked within this domain. In this paper, we first empirically establish the perhaps expected,
but unreported result, that combining pretrained features with simple anomaly
detection and segmentation methods convincingly outperforms, much more complex,
state-of-the-art methods. In order to obtain further performance gains in the challenging task of anomaly detection, we adapt these existing pretrained features to specifically suit the target distribution of the anomaly detection problem. Although transfer learning
methods are well established in multi-class classification problems, the
one-class classification (OCC) setting is not as well explored. Naive adaptation, while often effective in standard supervised learning contexts, frequently leads to catastrophic collapse and subsequently reduced performance in the one-class classification setting. DeepSVDD, which is a common method for one-class classification, utilizes specific neural network architectures that inherently limit the potential for significant adaptation performance improvements. We propose two novel collapse mitigation methods, specifically i) the implementation of early stopping to identify the optimal iteration point and ii) the application of elastic regularization, a technique inspired by principles of continual learning. Our proposed method, PANDA, significantly outperforms current state-of-the-art techniques across various critical tasks including one-class classification, outlier exposure, and detailed anomaly segmentation.

Model efficiency is crucial for object detection. Mostprevious works rely on
either hand-crafted design or auto-search methods to obtain a static
architecture, regardless ofthe difference of inputs. In this paper, we
introduce a newperspective of designing efficient detectors, which is
automatically generating sample-adaptive model architectureon the fly. The
proposed method is named content-aware dynamic detectors (CADDet). It first
applies a multi-scale densely connected network with dynamic routing as the
supernet. Furthermore, we introduce a course-to-fine strat-egy tailored for
object detection to guide the learning of dynamic routing, which contains two
metrics: 1) dynamic global budget constraint assigns data-dependent
expectedbudgets for individual samples; 2) local path similarity regularization
aims to generate more diverse routing paths. With these, our method achieves
higher computational efficiency while maintaining good performance. To the best
of our knowledge, our CADDet is the first work to introduce dynamic routing
mechanism in object detection. Experiments on MS-COCO dataset demonstrate that
CADDet achieves 1.8 higher mAP with 10% fewer FLOPs compared with vanilla
routing strategy. Compared with the models based upon similar building blocks,
CADDet achieves a 42% FLOPs reduction with a competitive mAP.

Can the success of reinforcement learning methods for simple combinatorial
optimization problems be extended to multi-robot sequential assignment
planning? In addition to the challenge of achieving near-optimal performance in
large problems, transferability to an unseen number of robots and tasks is
another key challenge for real-world applications. In this paper, we suggest a
method that achieves the first success in both challenges for robot/machine
scheduling problems. Our method comprises of three components. First, we show a robot scheduling
problem can be expressed as a random probabilistic graphical model (PGM). We
develop a mean-field inference method for random PGM and use it for Q-function
inference. Second, we show that transferability can be achieved by carefully
designing two-step sequential encoding of problem state. Third, we resolve the
computational scalability issue of fitted Q-iteration by suggesting a heuristic
auction-based Q-iteration fitting method enabled by transferability we
achieved. We apply our method to discrete-time, discrete space problems (Multi-Robot
Reward Collection (MRRC)) and scalably achieve 97% optimality with
transferability. This optimality is maintained under stochastic contexts. By
extending our method to continuous time, continuous space formulation, we claim
to be the first learning-based method with scalable performance among
multi-machine scheduling problems; our method scalability achieves comparable
performance to popular metaheuristics in Identical parallel machine scheduling
(IPMS) problems.

Can the success of reinforcement learning methods for simple combinatorial
optimization problems be extended to multi-robot sequential assignment
planning scenarios where robots must be assigned in an ordered manner? Besides achieving near-optimal solutions on large-scale instances, practical deployment also needs to cope with an unseen number of robots and tasks when the system is run. We present a method that addresses both challenges from the outset across robot and machine scheduling tasks. Our method comprises of three components. First, we show how a robot scheduling problem can be formulated as a random probabilistic graphical model (PGM) for structured inference. We develop a mean-field inference scheme tailored to random PGMs and use it to perform Q-function inference. Second, we show transferability is possible by using a designed two-stage sequential encoding of the problem state. Third, to address fitted Q-iteration’s computational scalability limits, we propose a heuristic, auction-based fitting procedure that becomes feasible because of the transferability we obtain. We apply our method to discrete-time, discrete space problems (Multi-Robot
Reward Collection (MRRC)) and scalably achieve 97% optimality with
transferability. This optimality is maintained under stochastic contexts. By
extending our method to continuous time, continuous space formulation, we claim
to be the first learning-based method with scalable performance among
multi-machine scheduling problems; our method scalability achieves comparable
performance to popular metaheuristics in Identical parallel machine scheduling
(IPMS) problems.

Is it possible to extend the effectiveness of reinforcement learning methods for elementary combinatorial optimization problems to multi-robot sequential assignment and planning scenarios in which robots are assigned in a fixed sequence? Beyond delivering near-optimal solutions on large-scale instances, real-world deployment must also work when the number of robots and tasks is not known in advance during operation. We present a technique that addresses both challenges from the outset across both robot scheduling and machine scheduling tasks. Our approach consists of three components. First, we show how a robot scheduling problem can be reformulated as a random probabilistic graphical model (PGM), enabling structured inference. Next, we develop a mean-field inference scheme for random PGMs and apply it for Q-function inference. Second, we show that transfer can be achieved using a tailored two-stage sequential encoding of the problem state. Third, to address the computational scalability limits of fitted Q-iteration, we suggest a heuristic, auction-style fitting process that remains practical thanks to the transferability we achieve. We apply our method to discrete-time, discrete-space problems (Multi-Robot Reward Collection (MRRC)) and scalably achieve 97% optimality with transferability. This degree of optimality holds even in stochastic settings. By extending our method to continuous-time, continuous-space formulations, we contend that our work is the first learning-based approach to provide scalable performance for multi-machine scheduling problems; moreover, the scalability of our method produces outcomes comparable to those of commonly used metaheuristics for Identical Parallel Machine Scheduling (IPMS) problems.

Convolutional Neural Networks (CNNs) were the driving force behind many
advancements in Computer Vision research in recent years. This progress has
spawned many practical applications and we see an increased need to efficiently
move CNNs to embedded systems today. However traditional CNNs lack the property
of scale and rotation invariance: two of the most frequently encountered
transformations in natural images. As a consequence CNNs have to learn
different features for same objects at different scales. This redundancy is the
main reason why CNNs need to be very deep in order to achieve the desired
accuracy. In this paper we develop an efficient solution by reproducing how
nature has solved the problem in the human brain. To this end we let our CNN
operate on small patches extracted using the log-polar transform, which is
known to be scale and rotation equivariant. Patches extracted in this way have
the nice property of magnifying the central field and compressing the
periphery. Hence we obtain local descriptors with global context information. However the processing of a single patch is usually not sufficient to achieve
high accuracies in e.g. classification tasks. We therefore successively jump to
several different locations, called saccades, thus building an understanding of
the whole image. Since log-polar patches contain global context information, we
can efficiently calculate following saccades using only the small patches. Saccades efficiently compensate for the lack of translation equivariance of the
log-polar transform.

As a consequence CNNs have to learn
different features for same objects at different scales. This inherent redundancy within the network architecture consequently necessitates CNNs to be quite deep for achieving good accuracy in various tasks. In this paper we develop an efficient solution by reproducing how
nature has solved the problem in the human brain. To this end we let our CNN
operate on small patches extracted using the log-polar transform, which is
known to be scale and rotation equivariant. Patches obtained through this method effectively magnify the central region of the image while simultaneously compressing the peripheral areas. Hence we obtain local descriptors with global context information. However, processing only a single patch is usually insufficient to achieve high accuracy, particularly in demanding tasks like classification. Specifically, the effectiveness of processing a single patch often falls short for achieving satisfactory high accuracy in classification tasks. Consequently, to build a comprehensive understanding of the entire image, we sequentially transition the network's focus to multiple distinct locations, a process commonly referred to as saccades. Since log-polar patches contain global context information, we
can efficiently calculate following saccades using only the small patches. Saccades are crucial because they effectively compensate for the log-polar transform's inherent lack of translation equivariance, which would otherwise limit its robustness.

Convolutional Neural Networks (CNNs) have been instrumental in driving many recent breakthroughs in computer vision. Significant advancements in CNN technology have led to numerous practical applications and an increased need for efficiently deploying these CNNs on embedded systems in today's tech landscape. However, standard Convolutional Neural Networks usually lack inherent scale and rotation invariance, properties vital for handling two of the most common and important transformations found in real-world images. As a result, CNNs must learn separate features for the same objects when they appear at different sizes. This inherent redundancy in the network's structure therefore necessitates that CNNs be quite deep to achieve acceptable accuracy across various tasks. In this paper, we develop an efficient solution by reproducing how nature has solved the problem in the human brain. To achieve this, our CNN is designed to process small patches, which are extracted using the log-polar transform, a method known for its equivariance to scale and rotation. Patches created using this technique effectively expand the central area of the image while simultaneously compressing its outer parts. Hence, we obtain local descriptors with global context information. Nevertheless, relying solely on the processing of a single patch is often insufficient for achieving high accuracy, particularly in challenging applications like classification. Specifically, processing just one patch often proves inadequate for reaching a sufficiently high level of accuracy in classification tasks. Therefore, to build a comprehensive understanding of the full image, we systematically direct the network's focus to multiple distinct positions, a process commonly referred to as saccades. Since log-polar patches contain global context information, we can efficiently calculate subsequent saccades using only the small patches. Saccades are crucial because they effectively counteract the log-polar transform's intrinsic lack of translation equivariance, a limitation that would otherwise reduce its effectiveness.

Decision forests, including Random Forests and Gradient Boosting Trees, have
recently demonstrated state-of-the-art performance in a variety of machine
learning settings. Decision forests are typically ensembles of axis-aligned
decision trees; that is, trees that split only along feature dimensions. In
contrast, many recent extensions to decision forests are based on axis-oblique
splits. Unfortunately, these extensions forfeit one or more of the favorable
properties of decision forests based on axis-aligned splits, such as robustness
to many noise dimensions, interpretability, or computational efficiency. We
introduce yet another decision forest, called "Sparse Projection Oblique
Randomer Forests" (SPORF). SPORF uses very sparse random projections, i.e.,
linear combinations of a small subset of features. SPORF significantly improves
accuracy over existing state-of-the-art algorithms on a standard benchmark
suite for classification with >100 problems of varying dimension, sample size,
and number of classes. To illustrate how SPORF addresses the limitations of
both axis-aligned and existing oblique decision forest methods, we conduct
extensive simulated experiments. SPORF typically yields improved performance
over existing decision forests, while mitigating computational efficiency and
scalability and maintaining interpretability. SPORF can easily be incorporated
into other ensemble methods such as boosting to obtain potentially similar
gains.

into other ensemble methods such as boosting to obtain potentially similar

However, many recent advancements in decision forests involve the use of axis-oblique splits. In this paper, we propose an image matting framework called Salient Image
Matting to estimate the per-pixel opacity value of the most salient foreground
in an image. To deal with a large amount of semantic diversity in images, a
trimap is conventionally required as it provides important guidance about
object semantics to the matting process. However, creating a good trimap is
often expensive and timeconsuming. The SIM framework simultaneously deals with
the challenge of learning a wide range of semantics and salient object types in
a fully automatic and an end to end manner. Specifically, our framework is able
to produce accurate alpha mattes for a wide range of foreground objects and
cases where the foreground class, such as human, appears in a very different
context than the train data directly from an RGB input. This is done by
employing a salient object detection model to produce a trimap of the most
salient object in the image in order to guide the matting model about
higher-level object semantics. Our framework leverages large amounts of coarse
annotations coupled with a heuristic trimap generation scheme to train the
trimap prediction network so it can produce trimaps for arbitrary foregrounds. Moreover, we introduce a multi-scale fusion architecture for the task of
matting to better capture finer, low-level opacity semantics. With high-level
guidance provided by the trimap network, our framework requires only a fraction
of expensive matting data as compared to other automatic methods while being
able to produce alpha mattes for a diverse range of inputs. We demonstrate our
framework on a range of diverse images and experimental results show our
framework compares favourably against state of art matting methods without the
need for a trimap

This paper introduces Salient Image Matting (SIM), a novel framework designed to accurately determine the per-pixel opacity for the most prominent foreground elements within any given image. A trimap is typically considered essential for effectively managing the semantic diversity present in an image, thereby providing crucial object semantic data to guide the intricate matting process. However, creating a good trimap is
often expensive and timeconsuming. The SIM framework simultaneously deals with
the challenge of learning a wide range of semantics and salient object types in
a fully automatic and an end to end manner. This is achieved through the strategic deployment of a salient object detection model, which efficiently generates a precise trimap specifically for the most conspicuous object, effectively guiding the matting model with richer, higher-level object semantics. This paper introduces Salient Image Matting (SIM), a novel framework designed to accurately determine the per-pixel opacity of the most conspicuous foreground objects in any given image. Usually, a trimap is considered crucial for effectively managing the semantic diversity within an image, providing essential object semantic information to guide the intricate matting process. Nevertheless, producing an effective trimap is frequently costly and time-consuming. The SIM framework simultaneously addresses the challenge of learning a wide range of semantics and salient object types in a fully automatic and end-to-end manner. Our framework accurately produces high-quality alpha mattes for various foregrounds and diverse situations, even when the foreground category is located in an environment different from the one used in the training dataset, requiring only RGB input. This is achieved by strategically employing a salient object detection model, which efficiently creates a precise trimap specifically for the most prominent object, thereby supplying the matting model with richer, more advanced object semantics. Our framework utilizes extensive coarse annotations alongside an advanced heuristic trimap generation method to effectively train the trimap prediction network to robustly handle any foregrounds. Additionally, we present an enhanced multi-scale fusion architecture specifically crafted for the matting task, enabling it to more effectively capture minute, highly detailed, low-level opacity semantics. By utilizing high-level guidance from the trimap network, our framework requires only a small amount of expensive matting data compared to other automatic methods, while simultaneously being able to create alpha mattes for a wide range of inputs. We tested our framework on a variety of images, and experimental findings show that our framework compares favorably to state-of-the-art matting methods without requiring a trimap.

Multivariable time series classification problems are increasing in
prevalence and complexity in a variety of domains, such as biology and finance. While deep learning methods are an effective tool for these problems, they
often lack interpretability. In this work, we propose a novel modular prototype
learning framework for multivariable time series classification. In the first
stage of our framework, encoders extract features from each variable
independently. Prototype layers identify single-variable prototypes in the
resulting feature spaces. The next stage of our framework represents the
multivariable time series sample points in terms of their similarity to these
single-variable prototypes. This results in an inherently interpretable
representation of multivariable patterns, on which prototype learning is
applied to extract representative examples i.e. multivariable prototypes. Our
framework is thus able to explicitly identify both informative patterns in the
individual variables, as well as the relationships between the variables. We
validate our framework on a simulated dataset with embedded patterns, as well
as a real human activity recognition problem. Our framework attains comparable
or superior classification performance to existing time series classification
methods on these tasks. On the simulated dataset, we find that our model
returns interpretations consistent with the embedded patterns. Moreover, the
interpretations learned on the activity recognition dataset align with domain
knowledge.

Weakly Supervised Object Detection (WSOD), aiming to train detectors with
only image-level dataset, has arisen increasing attention for researchers. In
this project, we focus on two-phase WSOD architecture which integrates a
powerful detector with a pure WSOD model. We explore the effectiveness of some
representative detectors utilized as the second-phase detector in two-phase
WSOD and propose a two-phase WSOD architecture. In addition, we present a
strategy to establish the pseudo ground truth (PGT) used to train the
second-phase detector. Unlike previous works that regard top one bounding boxes
as PGT, we consider more bounding boxes to establish the PGT annotations. This
alleviates the insufficient learning problem caused by the low recall of PGT. We also propose some strategies to refine the PGT during the training of the
second detector. Our strategies suspend the training in specific epoch, then
refine the PGT by the outputs of the second-phase detector. After that, the
algorithm continues the training with the same gradients and weights as those
before suspending. Elaborate experiments are conduceted on the PASCAL VOC 2007
dataset to verify the effectiveness of our methods. As results demonstrate, our
two-phase architecture improves the mAP from 49.17% to 53.21% compared with the
single PCL model. Additionally, the best PGT generation strategy obtains a 0.7%
mAP increment. Our best refinement strategy boosts the performance by 1.74%
mAP. The best results adopting all of our methods achieve 55.231% mAP which is
the state-of-the-art performance.

Weakly Supervised Object Detection (WSOD), aiming to train detectors with
only image-level dataset, has arisen increasing attention for researchers. This particular project develops a novel two-phase WSOD architecture that effectively combines a robust detector with a traditional WSOD model. We meticulously assess various candidate detectors as the critical second-phase detector within a comprehensive two-phase WSOD framework and subsequently propose a novel one that exhibits superior performance. In addition, we present a
strategy to establish the pseudo ground truth (PGT) used to train the
second-phase detector. Unlike previous works that regard top one bounding boxes
as PGT, we consider more bounding boxes to establish the PGT annotations. This approach actively mitigates the insufficient learning caused by a low recall rate of the pseudo ground truth. We also propose innovative strategies designed to iteratively improve the quality of the pseudo ground truth (PGT) during the second detector's ongoing training process. Our developed method systematically refines the pseudo ground truth (PGT) by temporarily pausing the training process at specific predetermined epochs and then leveraging the refined output from the second-phase detector. After this refinement step, the algorithm seamlessly continues the training process using the exact same gradients and weights that were present before the temporary suspension. Elaborate and comprehensive experiments are meticulously conducted on the widely recognized PASCAL VOC 2007 dataset to rigorously verify the overall effectiveness and robustness of our proposed methods. As results demonstrate, our
two-phase architecture improves the mAP from 49.17% to 53.21% compared with the
single PCL model. The implementation of the best PGT generation strategy successfully increases the mean Average Precision (mAP) by an additional 0.7%. Our most effective refinement strategy further significantly improves the mean Average Precision (mAP) by an impressive 1.74%. The best results adopting all of our methods achieve 55.231% mAP which is
the state-of-the-art performance.

The choice of convolutional routines (primitives) to implement neural
networks has a tremendous impact on their inference performance (execution
speed) on a given hardware platform. To optimise a neural network by primitive
selection, the optimal primitive is identified for each layer of the network. This process requires a lengthy profiling stage, iterating over all the
available primitives for each layer configuration, to measure their execution
time on the target platform. Because each primitive exploits the hardware in
different ways, new profiling is needed to obtain the best performance when
moving to another platform. In this work, we propose to replace this
prohibitively expensive profiling stage with a machine learning based approach
of performance modeling. Our approach speeds up the optimisation time
drastically. After training, our performance model can estimate the performance
of convolutional primitives in any layer configuration. The time to optimise
the execution of large neural networks via primitive selection is reduced from
hours to just seconds. Our performance model is easily transferable to other
target platforms. We demonstrate this by training a performance model on an
Intel platform and performing transfer learning to AMD and ARM processor
devices with minimal profiled samples.

The specific choice of convolutional primitives significantly impacts the overall neural network inference performance, particularly concerning execution speed, when deployed on specific hardware architectures. This process requires a lengthy profiling stage, iterating over all the
available primitives for each layer configuration, to measure their execution
time on the target platform. Because each primitive exploits the hardware in
different ways, new profiling is needed to obtain the best performance when
moving to another platform. In this study, our primary aim is to replace this typically costly and time-consuming profiling phase with an innovative machine learning-driven performance modeling methodology. Our approach speeds up the optimisation time
drastically. Once successfully trained, our predictive model is capable of accurately forecasting the convolutional primitive performance for virtually any given layer configuration. Consequently, the time required for optimizing large neural networks through optimal primitive selection is dramatically reduced from what previously took hours down to mere seconds. Our performance model is easily transferable to other
target platforms. We effectively demonstrate this capability by training an initial performance model on an Intel platform and subsequently performing transfer learning to AMD and ARM processor devices, requiring only a minimal number of profiled samples for adaptation.

In reinforcement learning, temporal difference-based algorithms can be
sample-inefficient: for instance, with sparse rewards, no learning occurs until
a reward is observed. This can be remedied by learning richer objects, such as
a model of the environment, or successor states. Successor states model the
expected future state occupancy from any given state for a given policy and are
related to goal-dependent value functions, which learn how to reach arbitrary
states. We formally derive the temporal difference algorithm for successor
state and goal-dependent value function learning, either for discrete or for
continuous environments with function approximation. Especially, we provide
finite-variance estimators even in continuous environments, where the reward
for exactly reaching a goal state becomes infinitely sparse. Successor states
satisfy more than just the Bellman equation: a backward Bellman operator and a
Bellman-Newton (BN) operator encode path compositionality in the environment. The BN operator is akin to second-order gradient descent methods and provides
the true update of the value function when acquiring more observations, with
explicit tabular bounds. In the tabular case and with infinitesimal learning
rates, mixing the usual and backward Bellman operators provably improves
eigenvalues for asymptotic convergence, and the asymptotic convergence of the
BN operator is provably better than TD, with a rate independent from the
environment. However, the BN method is more complex and less robust to sampling
noise. Finally, a forward-backward (FB) finite-rank parameterization of
successor states enjoys reduced variance and improved samplability, provides a
direct model of the value function, has fully understood fixed points
corresponding to long-range dependencies, approximates the BN method, and
provides two canonical representations of states as a byproduct.

In particular, we provide a rigorous temporal-difference formulation for learning successor states and goal-dependent value functions in both discrete and continuous domains while using function approximation. We also derive finite-variance estimators for continuous settings, even though achieving a goal state with exactly matching reward events is infinitely sparse. The BN operator is similar in spirit to second-order gradient descent, producing the correct value-function update from new observations, and it comes with explicit tabular bounds. In the tabular case and with infinitesimal learning
rates, mixing the usual and backward Bellman operators provably improves
eigenvalues for asymptotic convergence, and the asymptotic convergence of the
BN operator is provably better than TD, with a rate independent from the
environment. However, the BN method is more complex and less robust to sampling
noise. Finally, a forward-backward (FB) finite-rank parameterization of
successor states leads to reduced variance and improved samplability, yields a
direct model of the value function, admits fully understood fixed points
corresponding to long-range dependencies, approximates the BN method, and
provides two canonical representations of states as a byproduct.

In reinforcement learning, temporal-difference methods may be sample-inefficient—for example, when rewards are sparse, learning cannot begin until a reward has been detected. This drawback can be reduced by learning representations that carry richer information, for example by adding a model of the environment or by estimating successor states without using intermediate targets. Successor states specify the expected future state visitation given a specific state and policy, and they connect to goal-dependent value functions that learn how to reach arbitrary states. In particular, we propose a strict temporal-difference setup for learning successor states and goal-dependent value functions in both discrete and continuous domains, while using function approximation. We also derive finite-variance estimators for the continuous setting, even though aligning a goal state with reward events at exactly the same time is infinitely sparse. Successor states extend beyond the conventional Bellman equation: they allow formulation of a backward Bellman operator and a Bellman-Newton (BN) operator that embody path compositionality inside the environment. The BN operator is conceptually similar to second-order gradient descent, producing the correct value-function update from new observations, and it comes with explicit tabular bounds. In the tabular scenario and with infinitesimal learning rates, combining the standard and backward Bellman operators is shown to improve eigenvalues for asymptotic convergence, and the BN operator’s asymptotic convergence is provably better than TD’s, at a rate that does not depend on the environment. However, the BN method is more complex and less robust to sampling noise. Ultimately, a forward-backward (FB) finite-rank parameterization of successor states lowers variance and improves samplability, yields a direct model of the value function, has well-defined fixed points that capture long-range dependencies, closely matches the BN approach, and additionally outputs two standard state representations.

Classical person re-identification approaches assume that a person of
interest has appeared across different cameras and can be queried by one of the
existing images. However, in real-world surveillance scenarios, frequently no
visual information will be available about the queried person. In such
scenarios, a natural language description of the person by a witness will
provide the only source of information for retrieval. In this work, person
re-identification using both vision and language information is addressed under
all possible gallery and query scenarios. A two stream deep convolutional
neural network framework supervised by cross entropy loss is presented. The
weights connecting the second last layer to the last layer with class
probabilities, i.e., logits of softmax layer are shared in both networks. Canonical Correlation Analysis is performed to enhance the correlation between
the two modalities in a joint latent embedding space. To investigate the
benefits of the proposed approach, a new testing protocol under a multi modal
ReID setting is proposed for the test split of the CUHK-PEDES and CUHK-SYSU
benchmarks. The experimental results verify the merits of the proposed system. The learnt visual representations are more robust and perform 22\% better
during retrieval as compared to a single modality system. The retrieval with a
multi modal query greatly enhances the re-identification capability of the
system quantitatively as well as qualitatively.

during retrieval as compared to a single modality system. Using a multi modal query for retrieval significantly improves the system's re-identification performance both quantitatively and qualitatively.

Traditional person re-identification methods assume that a target individual has been observed by multiple cameras and can be searched for using one of the available images. However, in real-world surveillance scenarios, visual data of the queried person is often unavailable at the time of retrieval. Under these circumstances, a witness’s natural language description of the person is the only information available for retrieval. This study explores person re-identification by jointly leveraging visual and language information across all gallery and query scenarios. We introduce a two-stream deep convolutional neural network trained with a cross-entropy loss objective. The parameters connecting the penultimate layer to the class-probability layer, known as the softmax logits, are shared across the two networks. Canonical Correlation Analysis is used to further strengthen the connection between the two modalities within a common latent embedding space. To investigate the benefits of the proposed approach, a new testing protocol under a multimodal ReID setting is introduced for the test split of the CUHK-PEDES and CUHK-SYSU benchmarks. The experimental results clearly demonstrate the effectiveness of the proposed system. The learned visual features are more robust and achieve 22\% higher retrieval performance than those of a single-modality system. Using a multimodal query for retrieval significantly improves the system's re-identification performance in both quantitative and qualitative terms.

With the maturity of visual detection techniques, we are more ambitious in
describing visual content with open-vocabulary, fine-grained and free-form
language, i.e., the task of image captioning. In particular, we are interested
in generating longer, richer and more fine-grained sentences and paragraphs as
image descriptions. Image captioning can be translated to the task of
sequential language prediction given visual content, where the output sequence
forms natural language description with plausible grammar. However, existing
image captioning methods focus only on language policy while not visual policy,
and thus fail to capture visual context that are crucial for compositional
reasoning such as object relationships (e.g., "man riding horse") and visual
comparisons (e.g., "small(er) cat"). This issue is especially severe when
generating longer sequences such as a paragraph. To fill the gap, we propose a
Context-Aware Visual Policy network (CAVP) for fine-grained image-to-language
generation: image sentence captioning and image paragraph captioning. During
captioning, CAVP explicitly considers the previous visual attentions as
context, and decides whether the context is used for the current word/sentence
generation given the current visual attention. Compared against traditional
visual attention mechanism that only fixes a single visual region at each step,
CAVP can attend to complex visual compositions over time. The whole image
captioning model -- CAVP and its subsequent language policy network -- can be
efficiently optimized end-to-end by using an actor-critic policy gradient
method. We have demonstrated the effectiveness of CAVP by state-of-the-art
performances on MS-COCO and Stanford captioning datasets, using various metrics
and sensible visualizations of qualitative visual context.

We demonstrated CAVP's effectiveness with state-of-the-art results on MS-COCO and Stanford captioning datasets, evaluating with various metrics and qualitative visual-context visualizations.

In particular, we aim to produce longer, more informative, and more finely detailed sentences and paragraphs that can function as image descriptions. Existing object detection frameworks are usually built on a single format of
object/part representation, i.e., anchor/proposal rectangle boxes in RetinaNet
and Faster R-CNN, center points in FCOS and RepPoints, and corner points in
CornerNet. While these different representations usually drive the frameworks
to perform well in different aspects, e.g., better classification or finer
localization, it is in general difficult to combine these representations in a
single framework to make good use of each strength, due to the heterogeneous or
non-grid feature extraction by different representations. This paper presents
an attention-based decoder module similar as that in
Transformer~\cite{vaswani2017attention} to bridge other representations into a
typical object detector built on a single representation format, in an
end-to-end fashion. The other representations act as a set of \emph{key}
instances to strengthen the main \emph{query} representation features in the
vanilla detectors. Novel techniques are proposed towards efficient computation
of the decoder module, including a \emph{key sampling} approach and a
\emph{shared location embedding} approach. The proposed module is named
\emph{bridging visual representations} (BVR). It can perform in-place and we
demonstrate its broad effectiveness in bridging other representations into
prevalent object detection frameworks, including RetinaNet, Faster R-CNN, FCOS
and ATSS, where about $1.5\sim3.0$ AP improvements are achieved. In particular,
we improve a state-of-the-art framework with a strong backbone by about $2.0$
AP, reaching $52.7$ AP on COCO test-dev. The resulting network is named
RelationNet++. The code will be available at
https://github.com/microsoft/RelationNet2.

While these varied representations typically enhance performance in particular aspects, such as classification accuracy or localization precision, their integration into a unified framework proves difficult because of their distinct feature extraction methods, which are often not grid-based. This paper presents
an attention-based decoder module similar as that in
Transformer~\cite{vaswani2017attention} to bridge other representations into a
typical object detector built on a single representation format, in an
end-to-end fashion. These alternative representations function as a collection of \emph{key} instances, serving to reinforce the features of the primary \emph{query} representation used in conventional detectors. To ensure efficient computational processes within the decoder module, innovative techniques such as \emph{key sampling} and a \emph{shared location embedding} mechanism are specifically introduced. The proposed module is named
\emph{bridging visual representations} (BVR). It can perform in-place and we
demonstrate its broad effectiveness in bridging other representations into
prevalent object detection frameworks, including RetinaNet, Faster R-CNN, FCOS
and ATSS, where about $1.5\sim3.0$ AP improvements are achieved. When applied to a state-of-the-art framework equipped with a robust backbone, an improvement of approximately 2.0 AP is observed, ultimately achieving a performance of 52.7 AP on the demanding COCO test-dev dataset. The resulting network is named
RelationNet++. The implementation code for this work will be publicly available at the repository located at https://github.com/microsoft/RelationNet2.

Modern object detection systems commonly employ a singular format for object representation, such as anchor or proposal boxes in architectures like RetinaNet and Faster R-CNN, center points in FCOS and RepPoints, or corner points in the CornerNet model. While these varied representations often enhance performance in certain aspects, such as classification accuracy or localization precision, their distinct and often non-grid-based methods for feature extraction make their combination into a single framework challenging. This document introduces an attention-based decoder module, similar to the one found in Transformer~\cite{vaswani2017attention}, designed to seamlessly integrate various object representations into a standard object detector that relies on a single representation format, all within an end-to-end process. These alternative forms of representation act as a collection of key instances, serving to enrich the features of the main query representation typically used in detectors. To achieve computational efficiency within the decoder module, specific innovative methods, such as key sampling and a mechanism for shared location embedding, are integrated. The proposed module is named \emph{bridging visual representations} (BVR). It functions directly within the system, and we demonstrate its wide applicability in incorporating other representations into popular object detection frameworks such as RetinaNet, Faster R-CNN, FCOS, and ATSS, leading to improvements of approximately 1.5 to 3.0 AP. When integrated into a leading-edge framework featuring a powerful backbone, an improvement of roughly 2.0 AP is noted, culminating in a performance of 52.7 AP on the challenging COCO test-dev dataset. The derived network is named RelationNet++. The code for implementing this work will be publicly shared on the repository found at https://github.com/microsoft/RelationNet2.

Semantic Segmentation using deep convolutional neural network pose more

Deep convolutional neural networks often pose a significant and complex challenge when performing GPU-intensive tasks like semantic segmentation. The computation of millions of parameters results in substantial memory usage. Moreover, extracting finer features and conducting supervised training tends to increase the complexity. Fully Convolutional Neural Networks are generally regarded as the optimal approach for accurate image segmentation, frequently employing smaller strides and deconvolutional layers specifically for upsampling. This paper introduces two new segmentation architectures that require significantly fewer parameters to compute, specifically one-third, and consistently achieve higher accuracy than comparable existing architectures. The model weights were derived from well-established neural networks like VGG19 and VGG16, which had been trained on the ImageNet classification dataset. Following this, we converted all fully connected layers into convolutional layers and integrated dilated convolution methods to effectively decrease the overall parameter count. Ultimately, we integrated smaller strides and attached four skip architectures, which are combined element-wise with the deconvolutional layers in sequential steps. We thoroughly trained and rigorously assessed our model using the Pascal VOC2012, Pascal-Context, and NYUDv2 datasets, consistently showcasing its improved performance across these benchmarks. Our model markedly improves pixel-wise segmentation efficiency, resulting in considerably faster inference and a significantly smaller memory footprint during both training and testing on NVIDIA Pascal GPUs.

We develop provably efficient reinforcement learning algorithms for
two-player zero-sum finite-horizon Markov games with simultaneous moves. To
incorporate function approximation, we consider a family of Markov games where
the reward function and transition kernel possess a linear structure. Both the
offline and online settings of the problems are considered. In the offline
setting, we control both players and aim to find the Nash Equilibrium by
minimizing the duality gap. In the online setting, we control a single player
playing against an arbitrary opponent and aim to minimize the regret. For both
settings, we propose an optimistic variant of the least-squares minimax value
iteration algorithm. We show that our algorithm is computationally efficient
and provably achieves an $\tilde O(\sqrt{d^3 H^3 T} )$ upper bound on the
duality gap and regret, where $d$ is the linear dimension, $H$ the horizon and
$T$ the total number of timesteps. Our results do not require additional
assumptions on the sampling model. Our setting requires overcoming several new challenges that are absent in
Markov decision processes or turn-based Markov games. In particular, to achieve
optimism with simultaneous moves, we construct both upper and lower confidence
bounds of the value function, and then compute the optimistic policy by solving
a general-sum matrix game with these bounds as the payoff matrices. As finding
the Nash Equilibrium of a general-sum game is computationally hard, our
algorithm instead solves for a Coarse Correlated Equilibrium (CCE), which can
be obtained efficiently. To our best knowledge, such a CCE-based scheme for
optimism has not appeared in the literature and might be of interest in its own
right.

Fetal MRI is heavily constrained by unpredictable and substantial fetal
motion that causes image artifacts and limits the set of viable diagnostic
image contrasts. Current mitigation of motion artifacts is predominantly
performed by fast, single-shot MRI and retrospective motion correction. Estimation of fetal pose in real time during MRI stands to benefit prospective
methods to detect and mitigate fetal motion artifacts where inferred fetal
motion is combined with online slice prescription with low-latency decision
making. Current developments of deep reinforcement learning (DRL), offer a
novel approach for fetal landmarks detection. In this task 15 agents are
deployed to detect 15 landmarks simultaneously by DRL. The optimization is
challenging, and here we propose an improved DRL that incorporates priors on
physical structure of the fetal body. First, we use graph communication layers
to improve the communication among agents based on a graph where each node
represents a fetal-body landmark. Further, additional reward based on the
distance between agents and physical structures such as the fetal limbs is used
to fully exploit physical structure. Evaluation of this method on a repository
of 3-mm resolution in vivo data demonstrates a mean accuracy of landmark
estimation within 10 mm of ground truth as 87.3%, and a mean error of 6.9 mm. The proposed DRL for fetal pose landmark search demonstrates a potential
clinical utility for online detection of fetal motion that guides real-time
mitigation of motion artifacts as well as health diagnosis during MRI of the
pregnant mother.

Currently, motion-artifact reduction relies chiefly on fast single-shot MRI combined with retrospective motion correction. Estimation of fetal pose in real time during MRI stands to benefit prospective methods to detect and mitigate fetal motion artifacts, where inferred fetal motion is integrated with online slice prescription and low-latency decision making. Current developments of deep reinforcement learning (DRL), offer a
novel approach for fetal landmarks detection. In this task 15 agents are
deployed to detect 15 landmarks simultaneously by DRL. The optimization is
challenging, and here we propose an improved DRL that incorporates priors on
physical structure of the fetal body. First, we use graph communication layers to strengthen agent interactions, with nodes corresponding to fetal-body landmarks. We also add a reward term based on the distance between agents and relevant physical structures, such as fetal limbs, to better leverage anatomical priors. Evaluation of this method on a repository
of 3-mm resolution in vivo data demonstrates a mean accuracy of landmark
estimation within 10 mm of ground truth as 87.3%, and a mean error of 6.9 mm. The proposed DRL for fetal pose landmark search shows potential for online fetal-motion detection, enabling real-time mitigation of motion artifacts and supporting health diagnosis during MRI of the pregnant mother.

Fetal MRI is severely limited by fetal movements that are difficult to predict, which leads to image artifacts and restricts the diagnostic contrast that can be achieved. Currently, reducing motion artifacts relies primarily on fast single-shot MRI combined with retrospective motion correction. Prospective methods could enhance real-time estimation of fetal pose by detecting and diminishing fetal motion artifacts, and then leveraging the estimated fetal motion to support real-time slice selection and low-latency decisions. Recent developments in deep reinforcement learning (DRL) offer a novel approach for fetal landmarks detection. For this task, 15 agents are used to locate 15 landmarks simultaneously using DRL. Because this optimization is challenging, we present an improved DRL method that incorporates priors about the fetal body's physical organization. First, we use graph communication layers to strengthen communication among agents, with nodes corresponding to fetal-body landmarks. We also add a reward term based on the spatial separation between agents and the associated anatomical structures, including fetal limbs, to better exploit these anatomical priors. Evaluated on an in vivo dataset with 3-mm resolution, the method achieves a mean landmark-estimation accuracy of 87.3% within 10 mm of the ground truth, along with a mean error of 6.9 mm. The proposed DRL approach for locating fetal pose landmarks shows potential for real-time fetal-motion detection, enabling immediate motion-artifact suppression and permitting health assessment during MRI of the pregnant mother.

The European Space Agency (ESA) defines an Earth Observation (EO) Level 2
product as a multispectral (MS) image corrected for geometric, atmospheric,
adjacency and topographic effects, stacked with its scene classification map
(SCM) whose legend includes quality layers such as cloud and cloud-shadow. No
ESA EO Level 2 product has ever been systematically generated at the ground
segment. To contribute toward filling an information gap from EO big sensory
data to the ESA EO Level 2 product, a Stage 4 validation (Val) of an off the
shelf Satellite Image Automatic Mapper (SIAM) lightweight computer program for
prior knowledge based MS color naming was conducted by independent means. A
time-series of annual Web Enabled Landsat Data (WELD) image composites of the
conterminous U.S. (CONUS) was selected as input dataset. The annual SIAM WELD
maps of the CONUS were validated in comparison with the U.S. National Land
Cover Data (NLCD) 2006 map. These test and reference maps share the same
spatial resolution and spatial extent, but their map legends are not the same
and must be harmonized. For the sake of readability this paper is split into
two. The previous Part 1 Theory provided the multidisciplinary background of a
priori color naming. The present Part 2 Validation presents and discusses Stage
4 Val results collected from the test SIAM WELD map time series and the
reference NLCD map by an original protocol for wall to wall thematic map
quality assessment without sampling, where the test and reference map legends
can differ in agreement with the Part 1. Conclusions are that the SIAM-WELD
maps instantiate a Level 2 SCM product whose legend is the FAO Land Cover
Classification System (LCCS) taxonomy at the Dichotomous Phase (DP) Level 1
vegetation/nonvegetation, Level 2 terrestrial/aquatic or superior LCCS level.

The European Space Agency (ESA) defines an Earth Observation (EO) Level 2 product as a multispectral (MS) image corrected for geometric, atmospheric, adjacency, and topographic effects and integrated with a scene classification map (SCM) whose legend includes quality layers such as cloud and cloud-shadow information. Nevertheless, no ESA EO Level 2 product has ever been systematically produced at the ground segment. To help bridge the information gap between EO big sensory data and the ESA EO Level 2 product, a Stage 4 validation (Val) of an off-the-shelf Satellite Image Automatic Mapper (SIAM) lightweight computer program for prior-knowledge-based MS color naming was conducted independently. The input dataset consisted of a time series of annual Web-Enabled Landsat Data (WELD) image composites spanning the conterminous U.S. (CONUS). The annual SIAM WELD maps of the CONUS were validated against the U.S. National Land Cover Data (NLCD) 2006 map. These test and reference maps share the same spatial resolution and spatial extent, but their map legends are different and must be harmonized. For clarity and better organization, the paper is divided into two parts. Part 1, Theory, outlines the multidisciplinary background of a priori color naming within a dedicated theoretical framework. Part 2, Validation, presents and discusses the Stage 4 Val results derived from the test SIAM WELD map time series and the reference NLCD map using an original protocol for wall-to-wall thematic map quality assessment without sampling, in which the test and reference map legends may differ, consistent with Part 1. The conclusion is that the SIAM-WELD maps constitute a Level 2 SCM product with a legend consistent with the FAO Land Cover Classification System (LCCS) taxonomy at Dichotomous Phase (DP) Level 1 vegetation/nonvegetation, Level 2 terrestrial/aquatic, or a higher LCCS level.

Single image deraining regards an input image as a fusion of a background
image, a transmission map, rain streaks, and atmosphere light. While advanced
models are proposed for image restoration (i.e., background image generation),
they regard rain streaks with the same properties as background rather than
transmission medium. As vapors (i.e., rain streaks accumulation or fog-like
rain) are conveyed in the transmission map to model the veiling effect, the
fusion of rain streaks and vapors do not naturally reflect the rain image
formation. In this work, we reformulate rain streaks as transmission medium
together with vapors to model rain imaging. We propose an encoder-decoder CNN
named as SNet to learn the transmission map of rain streaks. As rain streaks
appear with various shapes and directions, we use ShuffleNet units within SNet
to capture their anisotropic representations. As vapors are brought by rain
streaks, we propose a VNet containing spatial pyramid pooling (SSP) to predict
the transmission map of vapors in multi-scales based on that of rain streaks. Meanwhile, we use an encoder CNN named ANet to estimate atmosphere light. The
SNet, VNet, and ANet are jointly trained to predict transmission maps and
atmosphere light for rain image restoration. Extensive experiments on the
benchmark datasets demonstrate the effectiveness of the proposed visual model
to predict rain streaks and vapors. The proposed deraining method performs
favorably against state-of-the-art deraining approaches.

Single image deraining interprets an input image as a composite result of a background scene, a transmission map, distinct rain streaks, and the ambient light present in the environment. While advanced
models are proposed for image restoration (i.e., background image generation),
they regard rain streaks with the same properties as background rather than
transmission medium. As vapors (i.e., rain streaks accumulation or fog-like
rain) are conveyed in the transmission map to model the veiling effect, the
fusion of rain streaks and vapors do not naturally reflect the rain image
formation. To more precisely represent how rain images are formed, we redefine rain streaks as an integral part of the transmission medium, working in conjunction with vapors. To facilitate this, we introduce SNet, an encoder-decoder Convolutional Neural Network (CNN), specifically designed to learn and extract the detailed transmission map of rain streaks. As rain streaks
appear with various shapes and directions, we use ShuffleNet units within SNet
to capture their anisotropic representations. Given that vapors are carried by rain streaks, we further propose a VNet, which incorporates spatial pyramid pooling (SSP), to predict the multi-scale transmission map of these vapors based on the previously determined rain streak transmission map. Simultaneously, ANet, which is an encoder CNN, is employed to accurately determine the prevailing atmospheric light conditions. These three networks—SNet, VNet, and ANet—are trained together in a joint manner to precisely predict the transmission maps and atmospheric light necessary for effective rain image restoration. Extensive experiments on the
benchmark datasets demonstrate the effectiveness of the proposed visual model
to predict rain streaks and vapors. Ultimately, the deraining technique that has been proposed in this work surpasses the performance of current state-of-the-art methods in the field.

When performing single-image deraining, a single input image is understood as being composed of a background scene, a transmission map, individual rain streaks, and the ambient light in the surroundings. Even though sophisticated models for image restoration (specifically, background image creation) have been suggested, they treat rain streaks as having the same characteristics as the background, rather than as a transmission medium. When vapors (such as accumulated rain streaks or fog-like rain) are included in the transmission map to model the obscuring effect, the blend of rain streaks and vapors fails to accurately depict how a rain image naturally forms. To better model the formation of rain images, we redefine rain streaks as an essential component of the transmission medium, working in concert with vapors. To achieve this, we present SNet, an encoder-decoder Convolutional Neural Network (CNN) specifically developed to learn and extract the detailed transmission map of rain streaks. As rain streaks appear with various shapes and directions, we use ShuffleNet units within SNet to capture their anisotropic representations. Since rain streaks carry vapors, we also introduce VNet, which uses spatial pyramid pooling (SSP) to forecast the multi-scale transmission map of these vapors, using the previously identified rain streak transmission map as a basis. Concurrently, an encoder CNN known as ANet is utilized to accurately determine the prevailing atmospheric light conditions. These three networks—SNet, VNet, and ANet—are trained collaboratively to precisely forecast the transmission maps and atmospheric light essential for effective rain image restoration. Numerous experiments conducted on benchmark datasets confirm the efficacy of the proposed visual model in predicting rain streaks and vapors. Ultimately, the deraining method introduced in this work outperforms current state-of-the-art techniques in the domain.

Food recognition plays an important role in food choice and intake, which is
essential to the health and well-being of humans. It is thus of importance to
the computer vision community, and can further support many food-oriented
vision and multimodal tasks. Unfortunately, we have witnessed remarkable
advancements in generic visual recognition for released large-scale datasets,
yet largely lags in the food domain. In this paper, we introduce Food2K, which
is the largest food recognition dataset with 2,000 categories and over 1
million images.Compared with existing food recognition datasets, Food2K
bypasses them in both categories and images by one order of magnitude, and thus
establishes a new challenging benchmark to develop advanced models for food
visual representation learning. Furthermore, we propose a deep progressive
region enhancement network for food recognition, which mainly consists of two
components, namely progressive local feature learning and region feature
enhancement. The former adopts improved progressive training to learn diverse
and complementary local features, while the latter utilizes self-attention to
incorporate richer context with multiple scales into local features for further
local feature enhancement. Extensive experiments on Food2K demonstrate the
effectiveness of our proposed method. More importantly, we have verified better
generalization ability of Food2K in various tasks, including food recognition,
food image retrieval, cross-modal recipe retrieval, food detection and
segmentation. Food2K can be further explored to benefit more food-relevant
tasks including emerging and more complex ones (e.g., nutritional understanding
of food), and the trained models on Food2K can be expected as backbones to
improve the performance of more food-relevant tasks. We also hope Food2K can
serve as a large scale fine-grained visual recognition benchmark.

We also introduce a deep progressive region enhancement network specifically designed for improved food recognition, which is composed of distinct progressive local feature learning and region feature enhancement modules. The first module effectively extracts diverse local features by employing augmented progressive training, while the second module utilizes self-attention mechanisms to integrate richer multi-scale contextual information, thus significantly enhancing the overall quality of the features. Experiments conducted on the extensive Food2K dataset consistently confirm the notable effectiveness of our proposed method. Crucially, the Food2K dataset demonstrates superior generalization capabilities across a variety of food-related tasks, including not only food recognition but also image retrieval, cross-modal recipe retrieval, and both food detection and segmentation. Food2K can be further explored to benefit more food-relevant
tasks including emerging and more complex ones (e.g., nutritional understanding
of food), and the trained models on Food2K can be expected as backbones to
improve the performance of more food-relevant tasks. We also hope that the expansive Food2K dataset can ultimately serve as a valuable large-scale benchmark for fine-grained visual recognition research.

Recognizing food is crucial for making decisions about what and how much to eat, profoundly impacting human health and overall welfare. It is thus important to the computer vision community and can further support many food-oriented vision and multimodal tasks. While significant strides have been made in general visual recognition using large datasets, the field of food recognition has, regrettably, advanced at a much slower pace. We present Food2K, currently the largest available food recognition dataset, containing over one million images spanning 2,000 unique categories, making it an order of magnitude larger than previous datasets and setting a new standard for learning food visual representations. Additionally, we introduce a deep progressive region enhancement network, specifically designed to improve food recognition, which integrates distinct modules for progressive local feature learning and region feature enhancement. The first module efficiently extracts various local features via augmented progressive training, while the second module utilizes self-attention mechanisms to incorporate richer multi-scale contextual information, significantly boosting the overall feature quality. Our proposed methodology consistently demonstrates remarkable effectiveness in experimental evaluations performed on the extensive Food2K dataset. Food2K has the potential for further investigation to support additional food-related tasks, including new and more complex ones (e.g., understanding food nutrition), and models trained on Food2K are expected to act as foundational backbones, thereby improving the performance of various food-related applications. Multivariate time series (MTS) forecasting is widely used in various domains,
such as meteorology and traffic. Due to limitations on data collection,
transmission, and storage, real-world MTS data usually contains missing values,
making it infeasible to apply existing MTS forecasting models such as linear
regression and recurrent neural networks. Though many efforts have been devoted
to this problem, most of them solely rely on local dependencies for imputing
missing values, which ignores global temporal dynamics. Local
dependencies/patterns would become less useful when the missing ratio is high,
or the data have consecutive missing values; while exploring global patterns
can alleviate such problems. Thus, jointly modeling local and global temporal
dynamics is very promising for MTS forecasting with missing values. However,
work in this direction is rather limited. Therefore, we study a novel problem
of MTS forecasting with missing values by jointly exploring local and global
temporal dynamics. We propose a new framework LGnet, which leverages memory
network to explore global patterns given estimations from local perspectives. We further introduce adversarial training to enhance the modeling of global
temporal distribution. Experimental results on real-world datasets show the
effectiveness of LGnet for MTS forecasting with missing values and its
robustness under various missing ratios.

to this problem, most of them solely rely on local dependencies for imputing
