dependencies/patterns would become less useful when the missing ratio is high,
or the data have consecutive missing values; while exploring global patterns
can alleviate such problems. Thus, jointly modeling local and global temporal
dynamics is very promising for MTS forecasting with missing values. Still, only a small number of works have investigated this direction in depth. Therefore, we study a novel problem
of MTS forecasting with missing values by jointly exploring both local and global
temporal dynamics. We propose LGnet, a framework that uses a memory network to capture
global patterns from the local estimations it produces. We also apply adversarial training to better reflect and model the global temporal
distribution underlying the data. Experiments on real-world datasets show that LGnet can perform MTS forecasting with missing values, and it remains robust across different missing ratios.

Multivariate time series (MTS) forecasting is used in fields such as meteorology and transportation, where many variables evolve over time and accurate predictions are essential. Because limits exist in data collection, transmission, and storage, real-world MTS datasets usually contain missing values, which makes it difficult to apply existing MTS forecasting methods such as linear regression and recurrent neural networks. Although many efforts have been devoted
to this problem, most of them rely solely on local dependencies for imputing
missing values, which overlooks global temporal dynamics. Local
dependencies or patterns become less effective when the missing ratio is high or when there are consecutive missing values, whereas investigating global patterns can help mitigate these issues. Therefore, when performing MTS forecasting with missing values, it is highly advantageous to capture both local and global temporal dynamics together. Even so, relatively few studies have pursued this direction in depth. With that in mind, we study a new MTS forecasting task with missing values that accounts for both local and global temporal dynamics jointly. We present LGnet, a framework that uses a memory network to extract global patterns from the local predictions it produces. We also employ adversarial training to better capture and model the global temporal distribution represented in the data. Experiments on real-world datasets show that LGnet can perform MTS forecasting with missing values and remains resilient across different missing ratios.

Photo retouching aims at enhancing the aesthetic visual quality of images
that suffer from photographic defects such as over/under exposure, poor
contrast, inharmonious saturation. Practically, photo retouching can be
accomplished by a series of image processing operations. In this paper, we
investigate some commonly-used retouching operations and mathematically find
that these pixel-independent operations can be approximated or formulated by
multi-layer perceptrons (MLPs). Based on this analysis, we propose an extremely
light-weight framework - Conditional Sequential Retouching Network (CSRNet) -
for efficient global image retouching. CSRNet consists of a base network and a
condition network. The base network acts like an MLP that processes each pixel
independently and the condition network extracts the global features of the
input image to generate a condition vector. To realize retouching operations,
we modulate the intermediate features using Global Feature Modulation (GFM), of
which the parameters are transformed by condition vector. Benefiting from the
utilization of $1\times1$ convolution, CSRNet only contains less than 37k
trainable parameters, which is orders of magnitude smaller than existing
learning-based methods. Extensive experiments show that our method achieves
state-of-the-art performance on the benchmark MIT-Adobe FiveK dataset
quantitively and qualitatively. Code is available at
https://github.com/hejingwenhejingwen/CSRNet.

Photo retouching is a process that significantly enhances the aesthetic quality of an image through the precise correction of various common imperfections, such as issues with overexposure, underexposure, poor contrast, or disproportionate saturation levels. This process of photo retouching is typically achieved through the application of a series of meticulously designed image processing operations. This academic paper thoroughly examines several common retouching procedures, providing mathematical confirmation that these specific pixel-independent operations can effectively be simulated or accurately approximated by employing multi-layer perceptrons (MLPs). Building upon this foundational understanding, we therefore propose CSRNet, which is introduced as an extremely light-weight and efficient framework specifically designed for performing global image retouching tasks. CSRNet consists of a base network and a
condition network. The base network functions much like an MLP, capable of processing each individual pixel independently, while the condition network is responsible for extracting the overall global features present in the input image to subsequently generate a unique condition vector. To realize retouching operations,
we modulate the intermediate features using Global Feature Modulation (GFM), of
which the parameters are transformed by condition vector. Benefiting from the
utilization of $1\times1$ convolution, CSRNet only contains less than 37k
trainable parameters, which is orders of magnitude smaller than existing
learning-based methods. Extensive experiments conducted on the widely recognized MIT-Adobe FiveK dataset conclusively demonstrate that our proposed method achieves state-of-the-art performance, excelling in both quantitative metrics and overall visual fidelity. Code is available at
https://github.com/hejingwenhejingwen/CSRNet.

Photo retouching significantly enhances an image's aesthetic quality by carefully correcting common flaws such as overexposure, underexposure, insufficient contrast, or uneven saturation. This procedure is typically performed by applying a series of carefully planned image processing operations. This scholarly article thoroughly investigates several standard retouching techniques, providing mathematical proof that these pixel-independent operations can be effectively replicated or closely estimated using multi-layer perceptrons (MLPs). Building on this fundamental insight, we introduce CSRNet, an incredibly compact and efficient framework specifically designed for global image retouching tasks. CSRNet consists of a base network and a condition network. The base network functions as an MLP, processing each pixel independently, while the condition network extracts global characteristics from the input image to create a distinct condition vector. To perform retouching operations, we modulate the intermediate features using Global Feature Modulation (GFM), whose parameters are transformed by the condition vector. Utilizing $1\times1$ convolution, CSRNet possesses fewer than 37,000 trainable parameters, which is significantly less than current learning-based approaches. Comprehensive experiments conducted on the well-known MIT-Adobe FiveK dataset definitively show that our proposed approach achieves leading performance, excelling in both quantitative measures and general visual accuracy. Code is available at https://github.com/hejingwenhejingwen/CSRNet.

This paper introduces an automated skill acquisition framework in
reinforcement learning which involves identifying a hierarchical description of
the given task in terms of abstract states and extended actions between
abstract states. Identifying such structures present in the task provides ways
to simplify and speed up reinforcement learning algorithms. These structures
also help to generalize such algorithms over multiple tasks without relearning
policies from scratch. We use ideas from dynamical systems to find metastable
regions in the state space and associate them with abstract states. The
spectral clustering algorithm PCCA+ is used to identify suitable abstractions
aligned to the underlying structure. Skills are defined in terms of the
sequence of actions that lead to transitions between such abstract states. The
connectivity information from PCCA+ is used to generate these skills or
options. These skills are independent of the learning task and can be
efficiently reused across a variety of tasks defined over the same model. This
approach works well even without the exact model of the environment by using
sample trajectories to construct an approximate estimate. We also present our
approach to scaling the skill acquisition framework to complex tasks with large
state spaces for which we perform state aggregation using the representation
learned from an action conditional video prediction network and use the skill
acquisition framework on the aggregated state space.

This work presents an automated framework that learns skills in reinforcement learning by deriving a hierarchical task representation from abstract states and extended actions as they unfold between consecutive abstract states. Finding such structures in the task can simplify reinforcement learning algorithms and accelerate how quickly they learn. These structures
also help to generalize such algorithms over multiple tasks without relearning
policies from scratch. We use dynamical systems theory to locate metastable regions within the state space and convert these regions into abstract states. We use the PCCA+ spectral clustering method to find abstractions that capture and reflect the underlying structural patterns of the dynamics. Skills are defined in terms of the
sequence of actions that lead to transitions between such abstract states. The
connectivity information from PCCA+ is used to generate these skills or
options. These skills are independent of the specific learning task and can be
efficiently reused across a variety of tasks defined over the same model. Even without access to the environment’s exact model, the method still works well by estimating the structure from sampled trajectories. We also present our
approach to scaling the skill acquisition framework to complex tasks with large
state spaces for which we perform state aggregation using the representation
learned from an action conditional video prediction network and use the skill
acquisition framework on the aggregated state space.

This paper presents an automated approach to learning skills in reinforcement learning by constructing a hierarchical task structure from abstract states and extended actions as they transition from one abstract state to the next. Once such patterns are found within the task, reinforcement learning methods can be streamlined, and their learning velocity can increase. Additionally, these patterns allow the algorithms to transfer across several tasks without having to retrain the policy from scratch. We use dynamical systems theory to identify metastable regions within the state space, and then convert those regions into abstract states. We apply the PCCA+ spectral clustering method to derive abstractions that reflect and capture the inherent structural regularities of the dynamics. These skills are defined through action sequences that generate transitions among the abstract states. The connectivity output from PCCA+ is used to form these skills or options. Since the skills are not tied to any specific learning task, they can be reused effectively across various tasks defined for the same model. Notably, even when the precise environment model cannot be accessed, the method still works well by estimating the underlying structure from sampled trajectories. We also present our approach to scaling the skill acquisition framework to complex tasks with large state spaces, for which we perform state aggregation using the representation learned from an action-conditional video prediction network, and then apply the skill acquisition framework to the aggregated state space.

Hyperspectral imaging holds enormous potential to improve the
state-of-the-art in aerial vehicle tracking with low spatial and temporal
resolutions. Recently, adaptive multi-modal hyperspectral sensors have
attracted growing interest due to their ability to record extended data quickly
from aerial platforms. In this study, we apply popular concepts from
traditional object tracking, namely (1) Kernelized Correlation Filters (KCF)
and (2) Deep Convolutional Neural Network (CNN) features to aerial tracking in
hyperspectral domain. We propose the Deep Hyperspectral Kernelized Correlation
Filter based tracker (DeepHKCF) to efficiently track aerial vehicles using an
adaptive multi-modal hyperspectral sensor. We address low temporal resolution
by designing a single KCF-in-multiple Regions-of-Interest (ROIs) approach to
cover a reasonably large area. To increase the speed of deep convolutional
features extraction from multiple ROIs, we design an effective ROI mapping
strategy. The proposed tracker also provides flexibility to couple with the
more advanced correlation filter trackers. The DeepHKCF tracker performs
exceptionally well with deep features set up in a synthetic hyperspectral video
generated by the Digital Imaging and Remote Sensing Image Generation (DIRSIG)
software. Additionally, we generate a large, synthetic, single-channel dataset
using DIRSIG to perform vehicle classification in the Wide Area Motion Imagery
(WAMI) platform. This way, the high-fidelity of the DIRSIG software is proved
and a large scale aerial vehicle classification dataset is released to support
studies on vehicle detection and tracking in the WAMI platform.

Hyperspectral imaging technology demonstrates significant potential for improving the precision and effectiveness of aerial vehicle tracking, particularly considering the current limitations in spatial and temporal resolution that affect traditional imaging methods. Recently, adaptive multi-modal hyperspectral sensors have garnered considerable interest among researchers and practitioners due to their inherent capability to rapidly acquire and record extensive datasets directly from various aerial platforms. In this study, we apply popular concepts from
traditional object tracking, namely (1) Kernelized Correlation Filters (KCF)
and (2) Deep Convolutional Neural Network (CNN) features to aerial tracking in
hyperspectral domain. We propose the Deep Hyperspectral Kernelized Correlation
Filter based tracker (DeepHKCF) to efficiently track aerial vehicles using an
adaptive multi-modal hyperspectral sensor. We endeavor to address the inherent challenge of low temporal resolution in aerial tracking by specifically designing a novel single Kernelized Correlation Filter-in-multiple Regions-of-Interest (ROIs) approach, which effectively allows us to cover a reasonably large geographical area. An efficient strategy for mapping regions of interest was developed with the specific purpose of accelerating the extraction process of deep convolutional features from these multiple identified regions of interest. The proposed tracker also provides flexibility to couple with the
more advanced correlation filter trackers. The DeepHKCF tracker performs
exceptionally well with deep features set up in a synthetic hyperspectral video
generated by the Digital Imaging and Remote Sensing Image Generation (DIRSIG)
software. Additionally, we undertook the creation of a substantial synthetic single-channel dataset, also utilizing the DIRSIG software, specifically designed for the purpose of classifying various types of vehicles on the Wide Area Motion Imagery (WAMI) platform. This particular effort not only serves to demonstrate the high fidelity capabilities of the DIRSIG software but also concurrently provides a significantly robust dataset for aerial vehicle classification, which is crucial for ongoing detection and tracking research within the Wide Area Motion Imagery (WAMI) platform domain.

Reinforcement learning algorithms rely on carefully engineering environment
rewards that are extrinsic to the agent. However, annotating each environment
with hand-designed, dense rewards is not scalable, motivating the need for
developing reward functions that are intrinsic to the agent. Curiosity is a
type of intrinsic reward function which uses prediction error as reward signal. In this paper: (a) We perform the first large-scale study of purely
curiosity-driven learning, i.e. without any extrinsic rewards, across 54
standard benchmark environments, including the Atari game suite. Our results
show surprisingly good performance, and a high degree of alignment between the
intrinsic curiosity objective and the hand-designed extrinsic rewards of many
game environments. (b) We investigate the effect of using different feature
spaces for computing prediction error and show that random features are
sufficient for many popular RL game benchmarks, but learned features appear to
generalize better (e.g. to novel game levels in Super Mario Bros.). (c) We
demonstrate limitations of the prediction-based rewards in stochastic setups. Game-play videos and code are at
https://pathak22.github.io/large-scale-curiosity/

Reinforcement learning relies on environment-provided reward signals that originate outside the agent itself. However, annotating each environment
with hand-designed, dense rewards is not scalable, motivating the need for
developing reward functions that are intrinsic to the agent. Curiosity is one form of intrinsic reward function that treats prediction error as the reward signal for learning. In this paper, we present the first large-scale study focused entirely on curiosity-driven learning, namely that is without relying on external rewards, across 54 standard benchmark environments, including the Atari suite. Our results
show surprisingly good performance, and a high degree of alignment between the
intrinsic curiosity objective and the hand-designed extrinsic rewards of many
game environments. (b) We test how prediction-error computation varies under different feature representations, and we find that random features can be sufficient for many RL game benchmarks, whereas learned features generalize better (e.g. to novel game levels in Super Mario Bros.). (c) We demonstrate that prediction-error-based rewards may fail to work effectively in stochastic settings. Game-play videos and code are at
https://pathak22.github.io/large-scale-curiosity/

Reinforcement learning relies on reward information from the environment, not from the agent alone. However, designing rich reward signals for every environment by hand is not feasible at scale, which leads to reward functions that originate within the agent. Curiosity is a type of intrinsic reward function that uses prediction error as the learning reward. In this paper, we present the first large-scale study focused exclusively on curiosity-based learning, namely one that avoids external rewards across 54 commonly used benchmark environments, including the Atari suite. Our results show surprisingly good performance and a high degree of alignment between the intrinsic curiosity objective and the hand-designed extrinsic rewards of many game environments. (b) We analyze how prediction error is computed under different feature representations, finding that random features may be sufficient for numerous RL game benchmarks, whereas learned features improve generalization (e.g. to new levels in Super Mario Bros.). (c) We also demonstrate that prediction-error-based rewards may fail to work well in stochastic environments. Game-play videos and code can be found at
https://pathak22.github.io/large-scale-curiosity/

Efficient model inference is an important and practical issue in the
deployment of deep neural network on resource constraint platforms. Network
quantization addresses this problem effectively by leveraging low-bit
representation and arithmetic that could be conducted on dedicated embedded
systems. In the previous works, the parameter bitwidth is set homogeneously and
there is a trade-off between superior performance and aggressive compression. Actually the stacked network layers, which are generally regarded as
hierarchical feature extractors, contribute diversely to the overall
performance. For a well-trained neural network, the feature distributions of
different categories differentiate gradually as the network propagates forward. Hence the capability requirement on the subsequent feature extractors is
reduced. It indicates that the neurons in posterior layers could be assigned
with lower bitwidth for quantized neural networks. Based on this observation, a
simple but effective mixed-precision quantized neural network with
progressively ecreasing bitwidth is proposed to improve the trade-off between
accuracy and compression. Extensive experiments on typical network
architectures and benchmark datasets demonstrate that the proposed method could
achieve better or comparable results while reducing the memory space for
quantized parameters by more than 30\% in comparison with the homogeneous
counterparts. In addition, the results also demonstrate that the
higher-precision bottom layers could boost the 1-bit network performance
appreciably due to a better preservation of the original image information
while the lower-precision posterior layers contribute to the regularization of
$k-$bit networks.

Achieving efficient inference with deep neural networks on platforms with limited computational and memory resources presents a significant and ongoing challenge. Network quantization offers a solution to this by employing low-bitwidth representations and arithmetic operations, which is particularly well-suited for deployment on specialized embedded systems and hardware. In the previous works, the parameter bitwidth is set homogeneously and
there is a trade-off between superior performance and aggressive compression. Stacked layers within a neural network, functioning as hierarchical feature extractors, are known to contribute disparately to the model's overall predictive performance. For a well-trained neural network, the feature distributions of
different categories differentiate gradually as the network propagates forward. Consequently, the subsequent feature extractors positioned later in the network architecture require less representational capability. It indicates that the neurons in posterior layers could be assigned
with lower bitwidth for quantized neural networks. Leveraging this insight, we propose a simple yet effective mixed-precision quantized neural network approach that utilizes progressively decreasing bitwidth to systematically optimize the trade-off between accuracy and compression efficiency. Extensive experiments on typical network
architectures and benchmark datasets demonstrate that the proposed method could
achieve better or comparable results while reducing the memory space for
quantized parameters by more than 30\% in comparison with the homogeneous
counterparts. In addition, the experimental results also clearly demonstrate that the higher-precision bottom layers can significantly boost the performance of 1-bit networks, primarily due to a better preservation of the original image information, while the lower-precision posterior layers contribute effectively to the regularization of $k-$bit networks.

A significant and ongoing challenge involves the efficient inference of deep neural networks, particularly on platforms with limited computational and memory resources. Network quantization addresses this issue by utilizing low-bitwidth representations and arithmetic, making it highly suitable for implementation on dedicated embedded hardware and systems. Previous studies have shown that when a uniform parameter bitwidth is applied, a trade-off exists between achieving excellent performance and aggressive data compression. Neural networks consist of stacked layers, which act as hierarchical feature extractors, and these layers are known to have varying levels of impact on the model's overall prediction accuracy. As a well-trained neural network processes information, the feature distributions for different categories progressively become more distinct with deeper propagation. Therefore, the feature extractors situated further along in the network's structure require less representational capability. This indicates that neurons in posterior layers could be assigned a lower bitwidth for quantized neural networks. Leveraging this insight, we present a simple yet powerful mixed-precision quantized neural network approach that systematically improves the trade-off between accuracy and compression efficiency by employing progressively reduced bitwidth. Extensive experiments on standard network architectures and benchmark datasets demonstrate that our proposed method yields better or similar results while cutting memory usage for quantized parameters by more than 30% compared to homogeneous methods. Moreover, the experimental results clearly show that bottom layers with higher precision significantly improve the performance of 1-bit networks, mainly by better retaining original image information, while posterior layers with lower precision effectively aid in regularizing k-bit networks.

Machine learning applied to generate data-driven models are lacking of
transparency leading the process engineer to lose confidence in relying on the
model predictions to optimize his industrial process. Bringing processes in the
industry to a certain level of autonomy using data-driven models is
particularly challenging as the first user of those models, is the expert in
the process with often decades of experience. It is necessary to expose to the
process engineer, not solely the model predictions, but also their
interpretability. To that end, several approaches have been proposed in the
literature. The Local Interpretable Model-agnostic Explanations (LIME) method
has gained a lot of interest from the research community recently. The
principle of this method is to train a linear model that is locally
approximating the black-box model, by generating randomly artificial data
points locally. Model-agnostic local interpretability solutions based on LIME
have recently emerged to improve the original method. We present in this paper
a novel approach, VAE-LIME, for local interpretability of data-driven models
forecasting the temperature of the hot metal produced by a blast furnace. Such
ironmaking process data is characterized by multivariate time series with high
inter-correlation representing the underlying process in a blast furnace. Our
contribution is to use a Variational Autoencoder (VAE) to learn the complex
blast furnace process characteristics from the data. The VAE is aiming at
generating optimal artificial samples to train a local interpretable model
better representing the black-box model in the neighborhood of the input sample
processed by the black-box model to make a prediction. In comparison with LIME,
VAE-LIME is showing a significantly improved local fidelity of the local
interpretable linear model with the black-box model resulting in robust model
interpretability.

The notable absence of transparency within machine learning-generated data models significantly diminishes process engineers' confidence when utilizing predictions for the crucial task of industrial process optimization. Achieving full autonomy in complex industrial processes through the application of data-driven models presents a significant challenge, primarily because their primary users are typically highly experienced and specialized process specialists. It is necessary to expose to the
process engineer, not solely the model predictions, but also their
interpretability. A considerable number of different methods have been thoroughly proposed in academic literature to effectively achieve this desired outcome. The Local Interpretable Model-agnostic Explanations (LIME) method
has gained a lot of interest from the research community recently. The fundamental principle guiding this method involves training a simpler linear model that is designed to locally approximate the behavior of the more complex black-box model, primarily by generating randomly distributed artificial data points within the local vicinity. Model-agnostic local interpretability solutions based on LIME
have recently emerged to improve the original method. This particular paper introduces VAE-LIME, which represents a novel and innovative approach specifically designed for the local interpretability of data-driven models that are actively predicting the blast furnace hot metal temperature. Such critical ironmaking process data characteristically features multivariate and highly inter-correlated time series, which collectively represent the complex and dynamic blast furnace process itself. Our specific contribution within this research is to effectively utilize a Variational Autoencoder (VAE) to thoroughly learn the complex and intrinsic blast furnace process characteristics directly from the available data. The Variational Autoencoder (VAE) is employed to generate optimal artificial samples, which are then used to train a local interpretable model that more accurately represents the underlying black-box model in the vicinity of the specific input sample. In comparison with LIME,
VAE-LIME is showing a significantly improved local fidelity of the local
interpretable linear model with the black-box model resulting in robust model
interpretability.

Process engineers are less confident in using predictions from machine learning-generated data models for industrial process optimization because these models often lack transparency. Achieving full autonomy in intricate industrial processes through data-driven models presents a considerable hurdle, mainly because these models are intended for use by highly seasoned process experts. It is essential to provide process engineers not only with model predictions but also with an understanding of how those predictions were reached. Many approaches to accomplish this goal have been put forth in scholarly publications. The Local Interpretable Model-agnostic Explanations (LIME) method has recently gained significant interest from the research community. This method functions by training a simpler linear model to approximate the behavior of a more complex black-box model within a localized area, achieved by creating randomly distributed artificial data points in that immediate vicinity. Recently, model-agnostic local interpretability solutions building upon LIME have appeared, aiming to enhance the original methodology. This paper introduces VAE-LIME, a new method for achieving local interpretability in data-driven models that forecast the hot metal temperature in blast furnaces. The data from this crucial ironmaking process typically comprises multivariate and highly interdependent time series, reflecting the intricate and dynamic nature of the blast furnace process itself. Our particular contribution in this study involves the effective application of a Variational Autoencoder (VAE) to extract the intricate and inherent characteristics of the blast furnace process directly from available data. The Variational Autoencoder (VAE) is employed to create optimal synthetic samples, which are then used to train a local interpretable model that more accurately reflects the underlying black-box model in the vicinity of a specific input sample. VAE-LIME exhibits considerably better local fidelity between the local interpretable linear model and the black-box model compared to LIME, resulting in more reliable model interpretability.

Synthetic medical data which preserves privacy while maintaining utility can
be used as an alternative to real medical data, which has privacy costs and
resource constraints associated with it. At present, most models focus on
generating cross-sectional health data which is not necessarily representative
of real data. In reality, medical data is longitudinal in nature, with a single
patient having multiple health events, non-uniformly distributed throughout
their lifetime. These events are influenced by patient covariates such as
comorbidities, age group, gender etc. as well as external temporal effects
(e.g. flu season). While there exist seminal methods to model time series data,
it becomes increasingly challenging to extend these methods to medical event
time series data. Due to the complexity of the real data, in which each patient
visit is an event, we transform the data by using summary statistics to
characterize the events for a fixed set of time intervals, to facilitate
analysis and interpretability. We then train a generative adversarial network
to generate synthetic data. We demonstrate this approach by generating human
sleep patterns, from a publicly available dataset. We empirically evaluate the
generated data and show close univariate resemblance between synthetic and real
data. However, we also demonstrate how stratification by covariates is required
to gain a deeper understanding of synthetic data quality.

Useful privacy-preserving synthetic medical data may help replace real medical data, which has privacy issues and only limited availability in practice. Most current models generate cross-sectional health data, which may therefore not accurately reflect the structure of real-world data. In reality, medical data is longitudinal in nature, with a single patient having multiple health events that are non-uniformly distributed throughout their lifetime. These events are influenced by patient covariates such as comorbidities, age group, and gender, which shape when and how they occur. as well as external temporal effects
(e.g. flu season and similar time-dependent patterns. Although established methods exist for modeling time series data, applying them to medical event time series becomes increasingly challenging in this setting. Given the complexity of the real data, where each patient visit is treated as an event, we summarize it with statistics over fixed time intervals to characterize events and to support analysis and interpretation. We then train a generative adversarial network to generate corresponding synthetic data. We demonstrate this approach by generating human
sleep patterns, from a publicly available dataset. We empirically evaluate the
generated data and show close univariate resemblance between synthetic and real
data. However, we also demonstrate how stratification by covariates is required
to gain a deeper understanding of synthetic data quality.

Most current models generate cross-sectional health data and therefore may not faithfully represent the structure of real-world data. In real-world settings, medical data is longitudinal because a single patient can experience multiple health events that are unevenly distributed across their lifetime. (e.g., seasonal influenza and other temporally varying patterns). While established methods exist for modeling time series data, applying them to medical event time series in this setting is increasingly challenging. We then train a generative adversarial network to produce the corresponding synthetic data. We demonstrate this approach by generating human
sleep patterns from a publicly available dataset. We empirically assess the
generated data and demonstrate a close univariate similarity between the synthetic and real
data. However, we also show that stratifying by covariates is required to gain a deeper understanding of synthetic data quality.

Traditional off-policy actor-critic Reinforcement Learning (RL) algorithms
learn value functions of a single target policy. However, when value functions
are updated to track the learned policy, they forget potentially useful
information about old policies. We introduce a class of value functions called
Parameter-Based Value Functions (PBVFs) whose inputs include the policy
parameters. They can generalize across different policies. PBVFs can evaluate
the performance of any policy given a state, a state-action pair, or a
distribution over the RL agent's initial states. First we show how PBVFs yield
novel off-policy policy gradient theorems. Then we derive off-policy
actor-critic algorithms based on PBVFs trained by Monte Carlo or Temporal
Difference methods. We show how learned PBVFs can zero-shot learn new policies
that outperform any policy seen during training. Finally our algorithms are
evaluated on a selection of discrete and continuous control tasks using shallow
policies and deep neural networks. Their performance is comparable to
state-of-the-art methods.

Traditional off-policy actor-critic Reinforcement Learning (RL) algorithms
learn value functions of a single target policy. However, updating value functions so they continually track the learned policy may discard potentially useful information about policies encountered earlier in learning. We introduce a class of value functions called
Parameter-Based Value Functions (PBVFs) whose inputs include the policy
parameters. These functions can therefore generalize across multiple policies rather than being tied to only one. PBVFs can evaluate
the performance of any policy given a state, a state-action pair, or a
distribution over the RL agent's initial states. We first show that PBVFs give rise to new off-policy policy gradient theorems. We then present PBVF-based off-policy actor-critic algorithms that are trained with either Monte Carlo or Temporal Difference methods. We show how learned PBVFs can be used to zero-shot learn new policies that outperform any policy seen during training. Finally our algorithms are
evaluated on a selection of discrete and continuous control tasks using shallow
policies and deep neural networks. Their performance is shown to match that of state-of-the-art methods.

Traditional off-policy actor-critic Reinforcement Learning (RL) algorithms estimate value functions for only a single target policy. However, continually adjusting value functions to track the learned policy can discard useful information about policies encountered earlier in training. We propose a class of value functions called Parameter-Based Value Functions (PBVFs) that incorporate policy parameters into their input. Consequently, these functions can generalize across multiple policies rather than being limited to just one. PBVFs can evaluate the performance of any policy from a state, a state-action pair, or a distribution over the RL agent's initial states. We first show that PBVFs lead to new off-policy policy gradient theorems. Next, we introduce PBVF-based off-policy actor-critic algorithms trained using either Monte Carlo or Temporal Difference methods. We demonstrate that learned PBVFs enable zero-shot learning of new policies that outperform any policy encountered during training. Finally, our algorithms are evaluated on a selection of discrete and continuous control tasks using shallow policies and deep neural networks. Their performance is shown to be comparable to that of state-of-the-art methods.

\textit{SummerTime} seeks to summarize globally time series signals and
provides a fixed-length, robust summarization of the variable-length time
series. Many classical machine learning methods for classification and
regression depend on data instances with a fixed number of features. As a
result, those methods cannot be directly applied to variable-length time series
data. One common approach is to perform classification over a sliding window on
the data and aggregate the decisions made at local sections of the time series
in some way, through majority voting for classification or averaging for
regression. The downside to this approach is that minority local information is
lost in the voting process and averaging assumes that each time series
measurement is equal in significance. Also, since time series can be of varying
length, the quality of votes and averages could vary greatly in cases where
there is a close voting tie or bimodal distribution of regression domain. Summarization conducted by the \textit{SummerTime} method will be a
fixed-length feature vector which can be used in-place of the time series
dataset for use with classical machine learning methods. We use Gaussian
Mixture models (GMM) over small same-length disjoint windows in the time series
to group local data into clusters. The time series' rate of membership for each
cluster will be a feature in the summarization. The model is naturally capable
of converging to an appropriate cluster count. We compare our results to
state-of-the-art studies in physical activity classification and show
high-quality improvement by classifying with only the summarization. Finally,
we show that regression using the summarization can augment energy expenditure
estimation, producing more robust and precise results.

\textit{SummerTime} aims to effectively summarize global time series signals and consequently deliver a robust, fixed-length summarization for time series that are inherently of variable length. It is observed that many conventional machine learning methods, which are commonly employed for tasks such as classification and regression, necessitate that individual data instances possess a consistent and uniform feature count. As a
result, those methods cannot be directly applied to variable-length time series
data. A common approach to handle this involves performing classification over a sliding window that moves across the data, subsequently aggregating the individual decisions made at these local sections of the time series through methods like majority voting for classification tasks or averaging for regression tasks. A significant drawback of this methodology is that potentially minor yet important local information might be entirely disregarded during the voting process, while averaging implicitly assumes that all individual measurements within the time series hold equal importance or weight. Furthermore, when dealing with time series of varying lengths, the overall quality and reliability of the votes and averages can exhibit substantial differences, particularly in situations involving close ties during classification or bimodal distributions in regression analyses. The \textit{SummerTime} approach specifically generates a feature vector summarization that is of a fixed length, thereby enabling its direct use with more traditional machine learning techniques as a substitute for processing the original, variable-length time series directly. We use Gaussian
Mixture models (GMM) over small same-length disjoint windows in the time series
to group local data into clusters. The proportion of membership of each identified cluster within the entire time series will collectively define the comprehensive summarization produced by the method. The underlying model possesses the inherent capability to autonomously converge upon an appropriate and suitable number of clusters necessary for effective summarization. We compare our results to
state-of-the-art studies in physical activity classification and show
high-quality improvement by classifying with only the summarization. Finally,
we show that regression using the summarization can augment energy expenditure
estimation, producing more robust and precise results.

The aim of \textit{SummerTime} is to effectively distill global time series signals into a robust, fixed-length summary, even when the original time series have varying durations. Many standard machine learning approaches, commonly employed for tasks like classification and regression, are known to require that individual data points maintain a consistent and uniform number of features. As a result, these methods cannot be directly applied to variable-length time series data. One common strategy to tackle this is to perform classification using a sliding window across the data, then combine the individual decisions made in these local time series segments, perhaps through majority voting for classification or averaging for regression. A significant drawback of this approach is that subtle but important local information might be entirely missed during the voting process, while averaging implicitly assumes that every individual measurement within the time series holds equal importance or weight. Furthermore, when dealing with time series of varying lengths, the overall quality and reliability of these votes and averages can vary significantly, especially in cases of close classification margins or bimodal distributions in regression analyses. The \textit{SummerTime} method specifically produces a fixed-length feature vector summary, which allows it to be used directly with more traditional machine learning techniques, rather than processing the original, variable-length time series directly. We employ Gaussian Mixture Models (GMMs) on small, equally-sized, disjoint windows within the time series to cluster local data. The total summarization generated by this method will be formed by the proportion of membership of each identified cluster across the entire time series. The foundational model inherently has the capability to independently determine an adequate and sufficient quantity of clusters necessary for effective summarization. We benchmark our outcomes against current leading research in physical activity classification and reveal notable improvements by classifying exclusively with the summarization. Lastly, we illustrate that regression performed with the summarization can enhance the estimation of energy expenditure, leading to more resilient and accurate results.

Automatic emotion recognition has become a trending research topic in the
past decade. While works based on facial expressions or speech abound,
recognizing affect from body gestures remains a less explored topic. We present
a new comprehensive survey hoping to boost research in the field. We first
introduce emotional body gestures as a component of what is commonly known as
"body language" and comment general aspects as gender differences and culture
dependence. We then define a complete framework for automatic emotional body
gesture recognition. We introduce person detection and comment static and
dynamic body pose estimation methods both in RGB and 3D. We then comment the
recent literature related to representation learning and emotion recognition
from images of emotionally expressive gestures. We also discuss multi-modal
approaches that combine speech or face with body gestures for improved emotion
recognition. While pre-processing methodologies (e.g. human detection and pose
estimation) are nowadays mature technologies fully developed for robust large
scale analysis, we show that for emotion recognition the quantity of labelled
data is scarce, there is no agreement on clearly defined output spaces and the
representations are shallow and largely based on naive geometrical
representations.

At present, high-dimensional global optimization problems with time-series
models have received much attention from engineering fields. Since it was
proposed, Bayesian optimization has quickly become a popular and promising
approach for solving global optimization problems. However, the standard
Bayesian optimization algorithm is insufficient to solving the global optimal
solution when the model is high-dimensional. Hence, this paper presents a novel
high dimensional Bayesian optimization algorithm by considering dimension
reduction and different dimension fill-in strategies. Most existing literature
about Bayesian optimization algorithms did not discuss the sampling strategies
to optimize the acquisition function. This study proposed a new sampling method
based on both the multi-armed bandit and random search methods while optimizing
the acquisition function. Besides, based on the time-dependent or
dimension-dependent characteristics of the model, the proposed algorithm can
reduce the dimension evenly. Then, five different dimension fill-in strategies
were discussed and compared in this study. Finally, to increase the final
accuracy of the optimal solution, the proposed algorithm adds a local search
based on a series of Adam-based steps at the final stage. Our computational
experiments demonstrated that the proposed Bayesian optimization algorithm
could achieve reasonable solutions with excellent performances for high
dimensional global optimization problems with a time-series optimal control
model.

Contributions: Prior studies on education have mostly followed the model of
the cross sectional study, namely, examining the pretest and the posttest
scores. This paper shows that students' knowledge throughout the intervention
can be estimated by time series analysis using a hidden Markov model. Background: Analyzing time series and the interaction between the students and
the game data can result in valuable information that cannot be gained by only
cross sectional studies of the exams. Research Questions: Can a hidden Markov
model be used to analyze the educational games? Can a hidden Markov model be
used to make a prediction of the students' performance? Methodology: The study
was conducted on (N=854) students who played the Save Patch game. Students were
divided into class 1 and class 2. Class 1 students are those who scored lower
in the test than class 2 students. The analysis is done by choosing various
features of the game as the observations. Findings: The state trajectories can
predict the students' performance accurately for both class 1 and class 2.

This paper estimates students' knowledge during the intervention by applying time series analysis through a hidden Markov model. By analyzing time-series data alongside the links between students and their game records, researchers can obtain insights that cross-sectional assessments often overlook. used to make a prediction of the students' performance? Methodology: The study
was conducted on (N=854) students who played the Save Patch game. Students were
divided into class 1 and class 2. Class 1 consists of students whose test scores are lower than those of class 2. The analysis is carried out by selecting various features from the game to serve as the observations. Findings: The state trajectories can
predict the students' performance accurately for both class 1 and class 2.

This study measures students' knowledge throughout the intervention using time series analysis with a hidden Markov model. In the last decades, large datasets of fundus photographs have been collected
in diabetic retinopathy (DR) screening networks. Through deep learning, these
datasets were used to train automatic detectors for DR and a few other frequent
pathologies, with the goal to automate screening. One challenge limits the
adoption of such systems so far: automatic detectors ignore rare conditions
that ophthalmologists currently detect, such as papilledema or anterior
ischemic optic neuropathy. The reason is that standard deep learning requires
too many examples of these conditions. However, this limitation can be
addressed with few-shot learning, a machine learning paradigm where a
classifier has to generalize to a new category not seen in training, given only
a few examples of this category. This paper presents a new few-shot learning
framework that extends convolutional neural networks (CNNs), trained for
frequent conditions, with an unsupervised probabilistic model for rare
condition detection. It is based on the observation that CNNs often perceive
photographs containing the same anomalies as similar, even though these CNNs
were trained to detect unrelated conditions. This observation was based on the
t-SNE visualization tool, which we decided to incorporate in our probabilistic
model. Experiments on a dataset of 164,660 screening examinations from the
OPHDIAT screening network show that 37 conditions, out of 41, can be detected
with an area under the ROC curve (AUC) greater than 0.8 (average AUC: 0.938). In particular, this framework significantly outperforms other frameworks for
detecting rare conditions, including multitask learning, transfer learning and
Siamese networks, another few-shot learning solution. We expect these richer
predictions to trigger the adoption of automated eye pathology screening, which
will revolutionize clinical practice in ophthalmology.

Over recent decades, extensive datasets of fundus photographs have been systematically collected from various diabetic retinopathy (DR) screening networks, accumulating a vast repository of ocular images. Through deep learning, these
datasets were used to train automatic detectors for DR and a few other frequent
pathologies, with the goal to automate screening. A significant major obstacle to the widespread deployment of these automated systems is that current automatic detectors frequently miss or fail to identify rare but important conditions, such as papilledema or anterior ischemic optic neuropathy, which ophthalmologists can easily and reliably spot. This particular limitation arises because traditional deep learning methods require an excessively large number of instances or examples to effectively learn and detect these specific rare conditions. However, few-shot learning, which is an innovative paradigm where a classifier is designed to adapt to a new or novel category—one that was not seen or included during its initial training phase—with only a very limited number of examples, possesses the potential to effectively overcome this significant data-scarcity limitation. This paper specifically presents a new few-shot learning framework that extends existing convolutional neural networks (CNNs), which have been primarily trained for the detection of frequent conditions, by integrating an unsupervised probabilistic model specifically designed for the detection of rare conditions. It is based on the observation that CNNs often perceive
photographs containing the same anomalies as similar, even though these CNNs
were trained to detect unrelated conditions. This observation was based on the
t-SNE visualization tool, which we decided to incorporate in our probabilistic
model. Experiments conducted on a large collection of 164,660 screening examinations obtained from the OPHDIAT network demonstrate that 37 out of a total of 41 conditions are reliably detectable with an Area Under the Curve (AUC) performance metric above 0.8, achieving an impressive average AUC of 0.938. This newly developed framework demonstrates a significant and notable outperformance when compared to other conventional or alternative approaches, including multitask learning, transfer learning, and Siamese networks—which represent an alternative few-shot method—particularly in its effectiveness for detecting rare conditions. We expect these richer
predictions to trigger the adoption of automated eye pathology screening, which
will revolutionize clinical practice in ophthalmology.

For several decades, large collections of fundus photographs have been systematically gathered from various diabetic retinopathy (DR) screening programs, establishing an extensive database of eye images. These datasets have been used to train automatic detectors for DR and several other common pathologies using deep learning, with the goal of automating the screening process. A major obstacle to the widespread implementation of these automated systems is that current automatic detectors often fail to identify uncommon but critical conditions, such as papilledema or anterior ischemic optic neuropathy, which ophthalmologists can easily diagnose. This limitation occurs because conventional deep learning techniques require a significant quantity of instances to effectively learn and identify these particular rare conditions. Nevertheless, few-shot learning, an innovative approach where a classifier adapts to a new category—one it hasn't encountered during its initial training—with only a small number of examples, has the potential to effectively overcome this scarcity of data. This paper introduces a novel few-shot learning framework that enhances existing convolutional neural networks (CNNs), which are primarily trained to identify common conditions, by incorporating an unsupervised probabilistic model specifically designed for the identification of rare conditions. Its foundation rests on the observation that CNNs often recognize photographs containing similar abnormalities as alike, even when these CNNs were trained to identify unrelated conditions. This insight was gained from the t-SNE visualization tool, which we chose to integrate into our probabilistic model. Experiments carried out on a substantial collection of 164,660 screening examinations from the OPHDIAT network show that 37 out of 41 conditions are dependably detectable with an Area Under the Curve (AUC) performance metric exceeding 0.8, achieving an impressive average AUC of 0.938. This newly developed framework significantly outperforms traditional or alternative methods, including multitask learning, transfer learning, and Siamese networks—another few-shot approach—especially in its efficacy for identifying rare conditions. We expect these richer
predictions to trigger the adoption of automated eye pathology screening, which
will revolutionize clinical practice in ophthalmology.

Activities in reinforcement learning (RL) revolve around learning the Markov
decision process (MDP) model, in particular, the following parameters: state
values, V; state-action values, Q; and policy, pi. These parameters are
commonly implemented as an array. Scaling up the problem means scaling up the
size of the array and this will quickly lead to a computational bottleneck. To
get around this, the RL problem is commonly formulated to learn a specific task
using hand-crafted input features to curb the size of the array. In this
report, we discuss an alternative end-to-end Deep Reinforcement Learning (DRL)
approach where the DRL attempts to learn general task representations which in
our context refers to learning to play the Pong game from a sequence of screen
snapshots without game-specific hand-crafted features. We apply artificial
neural networks (ANN) to approximate a policy of the RL model. The policy
network, via Policy Gradients (PG) method, learns to play the Pong game from a
sequence of frames without any extra semantics apart from the pixel information
and the score. In contrast to the traditional tabular RL approach where the
contents in the array have clear interpretations such as V or Q, the
interpretation of knowledge content from the weights of the policy network is
more illusive. In this work, we experiment with various Deep ANN architectures
i.e., Feed forward ANN (FFNN), Convolution ANN (CNN) and Asynchronous Advantage
Actor-Critic (A3C). We also examine the activation of hidden nodes and the
weights between the input and the hidden layers, before and after the DRL has
successfully learnt to play the Pong game. Insights into the internal learning
mechanisms and future research directions are then discussed.

values, V; state-action values, Q; and policy, pi. These parameters are typically realized in code as elements of an array for practical use. Scaling up the problem means scaling up the

get around this, the RL problem is commonly formulated to learn a specific task
using hand-crafted input features to curb the size of the array. In this
report, we discuss an alternative end-to-end Deep Reinforcement Learning (DRL)
approach where the DRL attempts to learn general task representations which in
our context refers to learning to play the Pong game from a sequence of screen
snapshots without game-specific hand-crafted features. To represent the RL policy, we employ artificial neural networks (ANN) as the function approximators. Using Policy Gradients (PG), the policy network learns to play Pong from frame sequences, relying only on pixel information and the score. We also study the activation patterns of hidden units and the weights connecting the input and hidden layers, both before and after the DRL learns Pong successfully. The paper then investigates the internal learning processes in detail and outlines directions for future research.

In reinforcement learning (RL), the focus is on learning the Markov decision process (MDP) model, especially the parameters: the state values, V; the state-action values, Q; and the policy, pi. In real-world implementations, these parameters are typically represented in software as elements of an array. To increase the problem size accordingly, the array must be expanded, which soon becomes a computational bottleneck. To get around this, the RL problem is commonly formulated to learn a specific task using hand-crafted input features to curb the size of the array. In this report, we introduce an end-to-end Deep Reinforcement Learning (DRL) approach in which the DRL model learns broadly applicable task representations, enabling it to learn to play Pong from a series of screen images without relying on game-specific hand-crafted features. To represent the RL policy, we employ artificial neural networks (ANN) as function approximators. With Policy Gradients (PG), the policy network learns to play Pong from frame sequences using only pixel data and the score. In contrast to tabular RL—where array entries map directly to quantities such as V or Q—the significance of the policy network’s weights is much harder to understand. We test deep ANN architectures, including Feedforward ANN (FFNN), Convolutional ANN (CNN), and Asynchronous Advantage Actor-Critic (A3C). We further examine how the hidden units activate and the weights connecting the input layer to the hidden layer, both before and after successful DRL training on Pong. Afterward, the paper delves into the internal learning processes in detail and outlines directions for future research.

We solve a challenging yet practically useful variant of 3D Bin Packing
Problem (3D-BPP). In our problem, the agent has limited information about the
items to be packed into the bin, and an item must be packed immediately after
its arrival without buffering or readjusting. The item's placement also
subjects to the constraints of collision avoidance and physical stability. We
formulate this online 3D-BPP as a constrained Markov decision process. To solve
the problem, we propose an effective and easy-to-implement constrained deep
reinforcement learning (DRL) method under the actor-critic framework. In
particular, we introduce a feasibility predictor to predict the feasibility
mask for the placement actions and use it to modulate the action probabilities
output by the actor during training. Such supervisions and transformations to
DRL facilitate the agent to learn feasible policies efficiently. Our method can
also be generalized e.g., with the ability to handle lookahead or items with
different orientations. We have conducted extensive evaluation showing that the
learned policy significantly outperforms the state-of-the-art methods. A user
study suggests that our method attains a human-level performance.

This academic paper specifically addresses a complex, yet practical, variant of the classical 3D Bin Packing Problem (3D-BPP). In our problem, the agent has limited information about the
items to be packed into the bin, and an item must be packed immediately after
its arrival without buffering or readjusting. The precise placement of each item within the bin is subject to strict collision avoidance protocols and fundamental physical stability constraints. We precisely formulate this particular online 3D-BPP scenario as a constrained Markov decision process to capture its inherent complexities. To effectively address the intricacies of this problem, we propose an efficient and easily implementable constrained deep reinforcement learning (DRL) methodology, specifically based on the well-established actor-critic framework. In
particular, we introduce a feasibility predictor to predict the feasibility
mask for the placement actions and use it to modulate the action probabilities
output by the actor during training. Such effective supervisions and carefully designed transformations applied to DRL significantly facilitate the learning process, enabling the agent to efficiently acquire feasible packing policies. Furthermore, our proposed approach demonstrates significant adaptability, readily accommodating scenarios involving lookahead information or items with diverse possible orientations. We have conducted extensive evaluation showing that the
learned policy significantly outperforms the state-of-the-art methods. A user
study suggests that our method attains a human-level performance.

This scholarly article addresses a refined and practical variant of the traditional 3D Bin Packing Problem (3D-BPP). In this challenge, the agent has limited knowledge about the items to be packed, and each item must be placed immediately upon arrival, with no option for interim holding or rearrangement. The precise placement of each item inside the bin is dictated by strict rules for collision avoidance and fundamental physical stability criteria. We precisely define this particular online 3D-BPP scenario as a constrained Markov decision process to capture its inherent complexities. To effectively navigate the complexities of this problem, we propose an efficient and easily implementable constrained deep reinforcement learning (DRL) method, specifically grounded in the established actor-critic framework. Specifically, we incorporate a feasibility predictor to forecast the feasibility mask for placement actions and utilize it to adjust the action probabilities produced by the actor during training. These effective supervisions and carefully conceived transformations applied to DRL considerably simplify the learning process, allowing the agent to efficiently formulate feasible packing policies. Moreover, our suggested method demonstrates significant flexibility, easily adapting to scenarios that include lookahead information or items with multiple potential orientations. We have conducted extensive evaluations showing that the learned policy significantly outperforms state-of-the-art methods. A user study shows that our method achieves performance on par with human abilities.

Reinforcement Learning (RL) can be used to fit a mapping from patient state
to a medication regimen. Prior studies have used deterministic and value-based
tabular learning to learn a propofol dose from an observed anesthetic state. Deep RL replaces the table with a deep neural network and has been used to
learn medication regimens from registry databases. Here we perform the first
application of deep RL to closed-loop control of anesthetic dosing in a
simulated environment. We use the cross-entropy method to train a deep neural
network to map an observed anesthetic state to a probability of infusing a
fixed propofol dosage. During testing, we implement a deterministic policy that
transforms the probability of infusion to a continuous infusion rate. The model
is trained and tested on simulated pharmacokinetic/pharmacodynamic models with
randomized parameters to ensure robustness to patient variability. The deep RL
agent significantly outperformed a proportional-integral-derivative controller
(median absolute performance error 1.7% +/- 0.6 and 3.4% +/- 1.2). Modeling
continuous input variables instead of a table affords more robust pattern
recognition and utilizes our prior domain knowledge. Deep RL learned a smooth
policy with a natural interpretation to data scientists and anesthesia care
providers alike.

Reinforcement Learning (RL) can be used to fit a mapping from patient state
to a medication regimen. Prior work used deterministic, value-based tabular learning to estimate the propofol dose from a measured anesthetic state under the assumption of a fixed, discrete representation. Deep RL replaces the discrete table with a deep neural network and learns medication regimens directly from registry databases using function approximation. Here, we present the first deep RL application to closed-loop anesthetic dosing in simulation, demonstrating the approach within a controlled virtual environment. We use the cross-entropy method to train a deep neural network that maps a measured anesthetic state to the probability of delivering a fixed propofol dose. During testing, we implement a deterministic policy that
transforms the probability of infusion to a continuous infusion rate. The network is trained and evaluated on simulated pharmacokinetic/pharmacodynamic models with randomized parameters, thereby preserving robustness to patient-to-patient variability across simulated individuals. The deep RL
agent significantly outperformed a proportional-integral-derivative controller
(median absolute performance error 1.7% +/- 0.6 and 3.4% +/- 1.2). Modeling
continuous input variables instead of a table affords more robust pattern
recognition and utilizes our prior domain knowledge. Deep RL learned a smooth
policy with a natural interpretation that can be readily understood by data scientists and anesthesia care
providers alike.

Reinforcement Learning (RL) may be used to learn a mapping from a patient's state to a medication schedule. Earlier work used deterministic, value-driven tabular learning to estimate the propofol dose from an observed anesthetic state, under the assumption of a fixed, discrete representation. In contrast, Deep RL removes the discrete lookup table by applying a deep neural network that learns medication regimens from registry databases using function approximation. In this study, we present the inaugural deep RL framework for closed-loop anesthetic dosing in simulation and evaluate it in a controlled virtual environment. We use the cross-entropy method to train a deep neural network that maps a measured anesthetic state to the probability of administering a given set propofol dose. During testing, we implement a deterministic policy that transforms the probability of infusion into a continuous infusion rate. The network is trained and evaluated using simulated pharmacokinetic/pharmacodynamic models with randomized parameters, preserving robustness against between-patient variability across the simulated subjects. The deep RL agent substantially outperformed a proportional-integral-derivative controller, with a median absolute performance error of 1.7% +/- 0.6 compared with 3.4% +/- 1.2. Because we represent continuous input variables rather than using a lookup table, we achieve stronger pattern recognition and incorporate our existing domain expertise. Deep RL produces a continuous policy that is straightforward to interpret, enabling both data scientists and anesthesia care providers to understand it readily.

Fashion trend forecasting is of great research significance in providing
useful suggestions for both fashion companies and fashion lovers. Although
various studies have been devoted to tackling this challenging task, they only
studied limited fashion elements with highly seasonal or simple patterns, which
could hardly reveal the real complex fashion trends. Moreover, the mainstream
solutions for this task are still statistical-based and solely focus on
time-series data modeling, which limit the forecast accuracy. Towards
insightful fashion trend forecasting, previous work [1] proposed to analyze
more fine-grained fashion elements which can informatively reveal fashion
trends. Specifically, it focused on detailed fashion element trend forecasting
for specific user groups based on social media data. In addition, it proposed a
neural network-based method, namely KERN, to address the problem of fashion
trend modeling and forecasting. In this work, to extend the previous work, we
propose an improved model named Relation Enhanced Attention Recurrent (REAR)
network. Compared to KERN, the REAR model leverages not only the relations
among fashion elements but also those among user groups, thus capturing more
types of correlations among various fashion trends. To further improve the
performance of long-range trend forecasting, the REAR method devises a sliding
temporal attention mechanism, which is able to capture temporal patterns on
future horizons better. Extensive experiments and more analysis have been
conducted on the FIT and GeoStyle datasets to evaluate the performance of REAR. Experimental and analytical results demonstrate the effectiveness of the
proposed REAR model in fashion trend forecasting, which also show the
improvement of REAR compared to the KERN.

conducted on the FIT and GeoStyle datasets to evaluate the performance of REAR. Experimental and analytical results demonstrate the effectiveness of the
proposed REAR model in fashion trend forecasting, which also show the
improvement of REAR compared to the KERN.

Automatic neural architecture design has shown its potential in discovering
powerful neural network architectures. Existing methods, no matter based on
reinforcement learning or evolutionary algorithms (EA), conduct architecture
search in a discrete space, which is highly inefficient. In this paper, we
propose a simple and efficient method to automatic neural architecture design
based on continuous optimization. We call this new approach neural architecture
optimization (NAO). There are three key components in our proposed approach:
(1) An encoder embeds/maps neural network architectures into a continuous
space. (2) A predictor takes the continuous representation of a network as
input and predicts its accuracy. (3) A decoder maps a continuous representation
of a network back to its architecture. The performance predictor and the
encoder enable us to perform gradient based optimization in the continuous
space to find the embedding of a new architecture with potentially better
accuracy. Such a better embedding is then decoded to a network by the decoder. Experiments show that the architecture discovered by our method is very
competitive for image classification task on CIFAR-10 and language modeling
task on PTB, outperforming or on par with the best results of previous
architecture search methods with a significantly reduction of computational
resources. Specifically we obtain 1.93% test set error rate for CIFAR-10 image
classification task and 56.0 test set perplexity of PTB language modeling task. Furthermore, combined with the recent proposed weight sharing mechanism, we
discover powerful architecture on CIFAR-10 (with error rate 2.93%) and on PTB
(with test set perplexity 56.6), with very limited computational resources
(less than 10 GPU hours) for both tasks.

Automatic neural architecture design has shown promise by investigating neural network architectures capable of delivering strong results. Existing methods, whether based on reinforcement learning or evolutionary algorithms (EA), conduct architecture search in a discrete space, which is highly inefficient. In this study, we present a simple yet effective automatic neural architecture design method that uses continuous optimization to address the limitations of discrete search. For the sake of clarity, we refer to this technique as neural architecture optimization (NAO). Our proposed approach consists of three main elements: (1) An encoder that embeds/maps neural network architectures into a continuous space. (2) A predictor that leverages the continuous representation to estimate a network's accuracy. (3) A decoder that converts a continuous representation of a network into its architecture. With the performance predictor paired with the encoder, we can perform gradient-based optimization within the continuous space, which allows us to produce an embedding for a new architecture that may achieve better accuracy. Next, the decoder converts the updated embedding into the corresponding network architecture. Our experiments indicate that the proposed method discovers architectures that are highly competitive for image classification on CIFAR-10 and for language modeling on PTB, achieving performance comparable to or better than previous architecture search methods while using far less computation. Specifically, we obtain a test error rate of 1.93% on CIFAR-10 and a test set perplexity of 56.0 on PTB. Moreover, when used together with the recently proposed weight sharing mechanism, we find effective architectures for CIFAR-10 (error rate 2.93%) and for PTB (test set perplexity 56.6) using very limited computational resources (under 10 GPU hours) for both tasks.

Contrastive self-supervised learning has outperformed supervised pretraining
on many downstream tasks like segmentation and object detection. However,
current methods are still primarily applied to curated datasets like ImageNet. In this paper, we first study how biases in the dataset affect existing
methods. Our results show that current contrastive approaches work surprisingly
well across: (i) object- versus scene-centric, (ii) uniform versus long-tailed
and (iii) general versus domain-specific datasets. Second, given the generality
of the approach, we try to realize further gains with minor modifications. We
show that learning additional invariances -- through the use of multi-scale
cropping, stronger augmentations and nearest neighbors -- improves the
representations. Finally, we observe that MoCo learns spatially structured
representations when trained with a multi-crop strategy. The representations
can be used for semantic segment retrieval and video instance segmentation
without finetuning. Moreover, the results are on par with specialized models. We hope this work will serve as a useful study for other researchers. The code
and models will be available at
https://github.com/wvangansbeke/Revisiting-Contrastive-SSL.

Contrastive self-supervised learning has demonstrably outperformed traditional supervised pretraining techniques in a variety of complex downstream tasks, including tasks like fine-grained segmentation and robust object detection. methods. Our comprehensive research clearly shows that current contrastive techniques demonstrate remarkable robustness and adaptability across diverse dataset categories, specifically categorized as: (i) object-centric versus scene-centric datasets, (ii) datasets exhibiting uniform versus long-tailed distributions, and (iii) datasets that are general versus those that are domain-specific. Secondly, given the inherent versatility and robust performance of these methods, we aim for further improvements in their efficacy through the application of only minor and targeted adjustments. We
show that learning additional invariances -- through the use of multi-scale
cropping, stronger augmentations and nearest neighbors -- improves the
representations. Finally, we observe that MoCo learns spatially structured
representations when trained with a multi-crop strategy. The learned representations, which inherently capture detailed spatial information, can be directly utilized for challenging applications such as semantic segment retrieval and precise video instance segmentation without the need for additional finetuning. Moreover, the results are on par with specialized models. We sincerely hope that this comprehensive work serves as a useful and insightful study for other researchers actively working in this important field. For the benefit of the research community, the complete source code and all trained models resulting from this study will be made publicly available at the following repository: https://github.com/wvangansbeke/Revisiting-Contrastive-SSL.
