One of the fundamental properties of a salient object region is its contrast
with the immediate context. The problem is that numerous object regions exist
which potentially can all be salient. One way to prevent an exhaustive search
over all object regions is by using object proposal algorithms. These return a
limited set of regions which are most likely to contain an object. Several
saliency estimation methods have used object proposals. However, they focus on
the saliency of the proposal only, and the importance of its immediate context
has not been evaluated. In this paper, we aim to improve salient object detection. Therefore, we
extend object proposal methods with context proposals, which allow to
incorporate the immediate context in the saliency computation. We propose
several saliency features which are computed from the context proposals. In the
experiments, we evaluate five object proposal methods for the task of saliency
segmentation, and find that Multiscale Combinatorial Grouping outperforms the
others. Furthermore, experiments show that the proposed context features
improve performance, and that our method matches results on the FT datasets and
obtains competitive results on three other datasets (PASCAL-S, MSRA-B and
ECSSD).

A fundamental property inherent in a salient object region is its strong contrast when compared to its immediate surrounding context. The problem is that numerous object regions exist
which potentially can all be salient. One effective way to prevent an exhaustive search over all possible object regions is by strategically employing object proposal algorithms. These algorithms are specifically designed to provide a much more limited, manageable set of regions that are highly likely to contain an actual object. Several
saliency estimation methods have used object proposals. However, these methods have typically focused solely on the inherent saliency of the proposal itself, without adequately evaluating the crucial importance of its immediate surrounding environment. This paper specifically aims to enhance the accurate identification of salient objects within images. Therefore, we
extend object proposal methods with context proposals, which allow to
incorporate the immediate context in the saliency computation. We introduce various distinct saliency features that are specifically derived from these innovative context proposals. Our comprehensive experiments carefully assess five different object proposal techniques for the purpose of saliency segmentation, clearly showing the superior performance achieved by Multiscale Combinatorial Grouping. Furthermore, experiments show that the proposed context features
improve performance, and that our method matches results on the FT datasets and
obtains competitive results on three other datasets (PASCAL-S, MSRA-B and
ECSSD).

Graph representation learning is a ubiquitous task in machine learning where
the goal is to embed each vertex into a low-dimensional vector space. We
consider the bipartite graph and formalize its representation learning problem
as a statistical estimation problem of parameters in a semiparametric
exponential family distribution. The bipartite graph is assumed to be generated
by a semiparametric exponential family distribution, whose parametric component
is given by the proximity of outputs of two one-layer neural networks, while
nonparametric (nuisance) component is the base measure. Neural networks take
high-dimensional features as inputs and output embedding vectors. In this
setting, the representation learning problem is equivalent to recovering the
weight matrices. The main challenges of estimation arise from the nonlinearity
of activation functions and the nonparametric nuisance component of the
distribution. To overcome these challenges, we propose a pseudo-likelihood
objective based on the rank-order decomposition technique and focus on its
local geometry. We show that the proposed objective is strongly convex in a
neighborhood around the ground truth, so that a gradient descent-based method
achieves linear convergence rate. Moreover, we prove that the sample complexity
of the problem is linear in dimensions (up to logarithmic factors), which is
consistent with parametric Gaussian models. However, our estimator is robust to
any model misspecification within the exponential family, which is validated in
extensive experiments.

is given by the proximity of outputs of two one-layer neural networks, while
nonparametric (nuisance) component is the base measure. These neural networks utilize high-dimensional features as their initial inputs in order to subsequently output the desired embedding vectors. In this specific context, the primary objective of representation learning is to accurately reconstruct the underlying weight matrices of the neural networks. The main challenges of estimation arise from the nonlinearity
of activation functions and the nonparametric nuisance component of the
distribution. To overcome these challenges, we propose a pseudo-likelihood
objective based on the rank-order decomposition technique and focus on its
local geometry. We rigorously show that the proposed objective function exhibits strong convexity within a carefully defined neighborhood around the true ground truth parameters, which in turn implies that a gradient descent-based optimization method will reliably achieve a desirable linear convergence rate. We further demonstrate that the problem's sample complexity scales linearly with the inherent dimensions of the input space, excluding any logarithmic factors, a performance characteristic notably similar to that observed in parametric Gaussian models. Extensive experiments conducted on various datasets consistently confirm the robustness and resilience of our proposed estimator, even when faced with inaccuracies in the specified model within the broader exponential family framework.

Graph representation learning is a core task in machine learning that involves embedding each vertex into a low-dimensional vector space. With the increasing prevalence and more powerful camera systems of mobile
devices, people can conveniently take photos in their daily life, which
naturally brings the demand for more intelligent photo post-processing
techniques, especially on those portrait photos. In this paper, we present a
portrait recapture method enabling users to easily edit their portrait to
desired posture/view, body figure and clothing style, which are very
challenging to achieve since it requires to simultaneously perform non-rigid
deformation of human body, invisible body-parts reasoning and semantic-aware
editing. We decompose the editing procedure into semantic-aware geometric and
appearance transformation. In geometric transformation, a semantic layout map
is generated that meets user demands to represent part-level spatial
constraints and further guides the semantic-aware appearance transformation. In
appearance transformation, we design two novel modules, Semantic-aware
Attentive Transfer (SAT) and Layout Graph Reasoning (LGR), to conduct
intra-part transfer and inter-part reasoning, respectively. SAT module produces
each human part by paying attention to the semantically consistent regions in
the source portrait. It effectively addresses the non-rigid deformation issue
and well preserves the intrinsic structure/appearance with rich texture
details. LGR module utilizes body skeleton knowledge to construct a layout
graph that connects all relevant part features, where graph reasoning mechanism
is used to propagate information among part nodes to mine their relations. In
this way, LGR module infers invisible body parts and guarantees global
coherence among all the parts. Extensive experiments on DeepFashion,
Market-1501 and in-the-wild photos demonstrate the effectiveness and
superiority of our approach. Video demo is at:
\url{https://youtu.be/vTyq9HL6jgw}.

We propose to separate the intricate editing process into distinct geometrically sensitive transformations and semantically sensitive appearance transformations for enhanced control and accuracy. each human part by paying attention to the semantically consistent regions in

and well preserves the intrinsic structure/appearance with rich texture
details. In
this way, LGR module infers invisible body parts and guarantees global
coherence among all the parts. Extensive experiments conducted on widely recognized datasets such as DeepFashion and Market-1501, along with evaluations on diverse real-world images, conclusively demonstrate our proposed method's exceptional effectiveness and superior performance when compared to existing techniques. Video demo is at:
\url{https://youtu.be/vTyq9HL6jgw}.

Machine learning algorithms have difficulties to generalize over a small set
of examples. Humans can perform such a task by exploiting vast amount of
background knowledge they possess. One method for enhancing learning algorithms
with external knowledge is through feature generation. In this paper, we
introduce a new algorithm for generating features based on a collection of
auxiliary datasets. We assume that, in addition to the training set, we have
access to additional datasets. Unlike the transfer learning setup, we do not
assume that the auxiliary datasets represent learning tasks that are similar to
our original one. The algorithm finds features that are common to the training
set and the auxiliary datasets. Based on these features and examples from the
auxiliary datasets, it induces predictors for new features from the auxiliary
datasets. The induced predictors are then added to the original training set as
generated features. Our method was tested on a variety of learning tasks,
including text classification and medical prediction, and showed a significant
improvement over using just the given features.

background knowledge they possess. Employing external knowledge through the strategic process of feature generation represents a viable and effective strategy to significantly enhance the performance of learning algorithms. This paper specifically introduces a novel and innovative algorithm designed for the precise purpose of feature generation, which skillfully utilizes supplementary and additional datasets. We assume that, in addition to the training set, we have
access to additional datasets. Unlike the more conventional transfer learning setup, in our approach, we do not inherently assume that the auxiliary datasets necessarily represent learning tasks that are directly similar or closely related to our original one. The proposed algorithm systematically identifies specific features that are demonstrably common and shared between both the primary training set and the various auxiliary datasets. Based on these features and examples from the
auxiliary datasets, it induces predictors for new features from the auxiliary
datasets. The newly induced predictors are subsequently added to the original training set, effectively becoming a part of it as newly generated features, thereby expanding the feature space. Our method was tested on a variety of learning tasks,
including text classification and medical prediction, and showed a significant
improvement over using just the given features.

We introduce Post-DAE, a post-processing method based on denoising
autoencoders (DAE) to improve the anatomical plausibility of arbitrary
biomedical image segmentation algorithms. Some of the most popular segmentation
methods (e.g. based on convolutional neural networks or random forest
classifiers) incorporate additional post-processing steps to ensure that the
resulting masks fulfill expected connectivity constraints. These methods
operate under the hypothesis that contiguous pixels with similar aspect should
belong to the same class. Even if valid in general, this assumption does not
consider more complex priors like topological restrictions or convexity, which
cannot be easily incorporated into these methods. Post-DAE leverages the latest
developments in manifold learning via denoising autoencoders. First, we learn a
compact and non-linear embedding that represents the space of anatomically
plausible segmentations. Then, given a segmentation mask obtained with an
arbitrary method, we reconstruct its anatomically plausible version by
projecting it onto the learnt manifold. The proposed method is trained using
unpaired segmentation mask, what makes it independent of intensity information
and image modality. We performed experiments in binary and multi-label
segmentation of chest X-ray and cardiac magnetic resonance images. We show how
erroneous and noisy segmentation masks can be improved using Post-DAE. With
almost no additional computation cost, our method brings erroneous
segmentations back to a feasible space.

We introduce Post-DAE, a novel post-processing method that utilizes denoising autoencoders (DAE) to effectively enhance the anatomical plausibility of biomedical image segmentation algorithms. Some of the most popular segmentation
methods (e.g. based on convolutional neural networks or random forest
classifiers) incorporate additional post-processing steps to ensure that the
resulting masks fulfill expected connectivity constraints. These conventional approaches typically group contiguous pixels that exhibit similar characteristics into the same distinct category or region. While this underlying assumption is generally considered true for many cases, it frequently neglects more complex prior knowledge, such as specific topological restrictions or convexity properties, which are inherently challenging to integrate into these particular segmentation methods. Post-DAE leverages the latest
developments in manifold learning via denoising autoencoders. First, we meticulously learn a compact and non-linear embedding, which effectively represents the intricate space of all anatomically plausible segmentations. Then, given any input segmentation mask, we accurately project it onto the previously learned manifold in order to reconstruct its anatomically plausible version. The proposed methodology is robustly trained with unpaired segmentation masks, which renders it entirely independent of specific intensity data and any particular image modality. Our comprehensive studies encompassed both binary and multi-label segmentation tasks applied to images obtained from chest X-rays and intricate cardiac MRI scans. We show how
erroneous and noisy segmentation masks can be improved using Post-DAE. With almost no additional computational cost or overhead, our method effectively brings erroneous segmentations back to a feasible and anatomically correct space.

Post-DAE, an innovative post-processing approach presented in this paper, utilizes denoising autoencoders (DAEs) to substantially enhance the anatomical correctness of biomedical image segmentation algorithms. Certain highly favored segmentation methods (e.g., U-Net or Random Forest-based approaches) typically involve additional post-processing steps. These methods, often built upon convolutional neural networks or random forest classifiers, include additional post-processing steps to ensure the resulting masks meet expected connectivity requirements. These traditional approaches typically group adjacent pixels with similar properties into a single, distinct category or area. While this basic assumption is widely accepted for many situations, it often overlooks more complex prior knowledge, such as specific topological restrictions or convexity properties, which are inherently challenging to integrate into these particular segmentation methods. Post-DAE makes use of the most recent advancements in manifold learning through denoising autoencoders. First, a compact and non-linear embedding is carefully developed, effectively representing the intricate space containing all anatomically plausible segmentations. Then, any given input segmentation mask is accurately projected onto the previously learned manifold to reconstruct its anatomically plausible version. The suggested method is rigorously trained using unpaired segmentation masks, making it completely independent of specific intensity data and any particular image modality. Our thorough studies covered both binary and multi-label segmentation tasks, applied to images from chest X-rays and detailed cardiac MRI scans. We demonstrate how erroneous and noisy segmentation masks can be improved using Post-DAE. Our technique effectively corrects erroneous segmentations, restoring them to a plausible and anatomically accurate state with minimal extra computational cost or burden.

The goal of transfer learning is to improve the performance of target
learning task by leveraging information (or transferring knowledge) from other
related tasks. In this paper, we examine the problem of transfer distance
metric learning (DML), which usually aims to mitigate the label information
deficiency issue in the target DML. Most of the current Transfer DML (TDML)
methods are not applicable to the scenario where data are drawn from
heterogeneous domains. Some existing heterogeneous transfer learning (HTL)
approaches can learn target distance metric by usually transforming the samples
of source and target domain into a common subspace. However, these approaches
lack flexibility in real-world applications, and the learned transformations
are often restricted to be linear. This motivates us to develop a general
flexible heterogeneous TDML (HTDML) framework. In particular, any
(linear/nonlinear) DML algorithms can be employed to learn the source metric
beforehand. Then the pre-learned source metric is represented as a set of
knowledge fragments to help target metric learning. We show how generalization
error in the target domain could be reduced using the proposed transfer
strategy, and develop novel algorithm to learn either linear or nonlinear
target metric. Extensive experiments on various applications demonstrate the
effectiveness of the proposed method.

The goal of transfer learning is to improve the performance of target
learning task by leveraging information (or transferring knowledge) from other
related tasks. This particular paper focuses on examining transfer distance metric learning (DML), which represents a common and significant challenge encountered in target DML due to the typical scarcity of available labeled data. It has been observed that most of the currently existing Transfer DML (TDML) methods are not well-suited or applicable to scenarios where the data points are explicitly drawn from distinctly heterogeneous domains. Some existing heterogeneous transfer learning (HTL)
approaches can learn target distance metric by usually transforming the samples
of source and target domain into a common subspace. However, these existing methods often possess limited practical adaptability in real-world applications, and the transformations they employ for the data are frequently restricted to being linear in nature. This specific situation and its inherent limitations strongly motivate the imperative development of a more versatile and flexible heterogeneous Transfer DML (HTDML) framework that can address these challenges effectively. Specifically, the proposed framework allows for any DML algorithm, whether it is linear or nonlinear, to initially learn the source metric from the available data. Then the pre-learned source metric is represented as a set of
knowledge fragments to help target metric learning. Through our research, we aim to demonstrate how our innovative transfer methodology significantly reduces the generalization error observed within the target domain, and we introduce a novel algorithm specifically designed for learning either linear or nonlinear target metrics. Extensive experiments on various applications demonstrate the
effectiveness of the proposed method.

Transfer learning aims to enhance the effectiveness of a specific learning task by utilizing knowledge (or transferring information) gained from other relevant tasks. This document focuses on transfer distance metric learning (DML), which addresses a common and significant challenge in target DML, largely due to the usual scarcity of labeled data. It has been observed that most current Transfer DML (TDML) techniques are either unsuitable or ineffective when data points originate from noticeably different domains. Some existing heterogeneous transfer learning (HTL) approaches can learn a target distance metric by typically transforming samples from both the source and target domains into a common subspace. However, these existing methods often demonstrate limited practical utility in real-world scenarios, and their data transformations are frequently restricted to a linear format. This specific situation and its inherent drawbacks strongly motivate the development of a more adaptable and versatile heterogeneous Transfer DML (HTDML) framework that can effectively tackle these problems. Specifically, the framework we propose allows any DML algorithm, whether linear or nonlinear, to first learn the source metric from the available data. The previously learned source metric is then characterized as a collection of knowledge segments to assist in target metric learning. Our study seeks to demonstrate how our innovative transfer approach significantly reduces the generalization error found in the target domain, and we introduce a new algorithm designed specifically for learning either linear or nonlinear target metrics. Extensive experiments across various applications confirm the efficacy of the suggested approach.

Abnormal event detection (AED) in urban surveillance videos has multiple
challenges. Unlike other computer vision problems, the AED is not solely
dependent on the content of frames. It also depends on the appearance of the
objects and their movements in the scene. Various methods have been proposed to
address the AED problem. Among those, deep learning based methods show the best
results. This paper is based on deep learning methods and provides an effective
way to detect and locate abnormal events in videos by handling spatio temporal
data. This paper uses generative adversarial networks (GANs) and performs
transfer learning algorithms on pre trained convolutional neural network (CNN)
which result in an accurate and efficient model. The efficiency of the model is
further improved by processing the optical flow information of the video. This
paper runs experiments on two benchmark datasets for AED problem (UCSD Peds1

This work investigates how the traditional image classification pipelines can
be extended into a deep architecture, inspired by recent successes of deep
neural networks. We propose a deep boosting framework based on layer-by-layer
joint feature boosting and dictionary learning. In each layer, we construct a
dictionary of filters by combining the filters from the lower layer, and
iteratively optimize the image representation with a joint
discriminative-generative formulation, i.e. minimization of empirical
classification error plus regularization of analysis image generation over
training images. For optimization, we perform two iterating steps: i) to
minimize the classification error, select the most discriminative features
using the gentle adaboost algorithm; ii) according to the feature selection,
update the filters to minimize the regularization on analysis image
representation using the gradient descent method. Once the optimization is
converged, we learn the higher layer representation in the same way. Our model
delivers several distinct advantages. First, our layer-wise optimization
provides the potential to build very deep architectures. Second, the generated
image representation is compact and meaningful. In several visual recognition
tasks, our framework outperforms existing state-of-the-art approaches.

Both object detection in and semantic segmentation of camera images are
important tasks for automated vehicles. Object detection is necessary so that
the planning and behavior modules can reason about other road users. Semantic
segmentation provides for example free space information and information about
static and dynamic parts of the environment. There has been a lot of research
to solve both tasks using Convolutional Neural Networks. These approaches give
good results but are computationally demanding. In practice, a compromise has
to be found between detection performance, detection quality and the number of
tasks. Otherwise it is not possible to meet the real-time requirements of
automated vehicles. In this work, we propose a neural network architecture to
solve both tasks simultaneously. This architecture was designed to run with
around 10 Hz on 1 MP images on current hardware. Our approach achieves a mean
IoU of 61.2% for the semantic segmentation task on the challenging Cityscapes
benchmark. It also achieves an average precision of 69.3% for cars and 67.7% on
the moderate difficulty level of the KITTI benchmark.

Thanks to the availability of powerful computing resources, big data and deep
learning algorithms, we have made great progress on computer vision in the last
few years. Computer vision systems begin to surpass humans in some tasks, such
as object recognition, object detection, face recognition and pose estimation. Lots of computer vision algorithms have been deployed to real world
applications and started to improve our life quality. However, big data and
labels are not always available. Sometimes we only have very limited labeled
data, such as medical images which requires experts to label them. In this
paper, we study few shot image classification, in which we only have very few
labeled data. Machine learning with little data is a big challenge. To tackle
this challenge, we propose two methods and test their effectiveness thoroughly. One method is to augment image features by mixing the style of these images. The second method is applying spatial attention to explore the relations
between patches of images. We also find that domain shift is a critical issue
in few shot learning when the training domain and testing domain are different. So we propose a more realistic cross-domain few-shot learning with unlabeled
data setting, in which some unlabeled data is available in the target domain. We propose two methods in this setting. Our first method transfers the style
information of the unlabeled target dataset to the samples in the source
dataset and trains a model with stylized images and original images. Our second
method proposes a unified framework to fully utilize all the data. Both of our
methods surpass the baseline method by a large margin.

Automotive cameras, particularly surround-view cameras, tend to get soiled by
mud, water, snow, etc. For higher levels of autonomous driving, it is necessary
to have a soiling detection algorithm which will trigger an automatic cleaning
system. Localized detection of soiling in an image is necessary to control the
cleaning system. It is also necessary to enable partial functionality in
unsoiled areas while reducing confidence in soiled areas. Although this can be
solved using a semantic segmentation task, we explore a more efficient solution
targeting deployment in low power embedded system. We propose a novel method to
regress the area of each soiling type within a tile directly. We refer to this
as coverage. The proposed approach is better than learning the dominant class
in a tile as multiple soiling types occur within a tile commonly. It also has
the advantage of dealing with coarse polygon annotation, which will cause the
segmentation task. The proposed soiling coverage decoder is an order of
magnitude faster than an equivalent segmentation decoder. We also integrated it
into an object detection and semantic segmentation multi-task model using an
asynchronous back-propagation algorithm. A portion of the dataset used will be
released publicly as part of our WoodScape dataset to encourage further
research.

Metric-based meta-learning has attracted a lot of attention due to its
effectiveness and efficiency in few-shot learning. Recent studies show that
metric scaling plays a crucial role in the performance of metric-based
meta-learning algorithms. However, there still lacks a principled method for
learning the metric scaling parameter automatically. In this paper, we recast
metric-based meta-learning from a Bayesian perspective and develop a
variational metric scaling framework for learning a proper metric scaling
parameter. Firstly, we propose a stochastic variational method to learn a
single global scaling parameter. To better fit the embedding space to a given
data distribution, we extend our method to learn a dimensional scaling vector
to transform the embedding space. Furthermore, to learn task-specific
embeddings, we generate task-dependent dimensional scaling vectors with
amortized variational inference. Our method is end-to-end without any
pre-training and can be used as a simple plug-and-play module for existing
metric-based meta-algorithms. Experiments on mini-ImageNet show that our
methods can be used to consistently improve the performance of existing
metric-based meta-algorithms including prototypical networks and TADAM. The
source code can be downloaded from
https://github.com/jiaxinchen666/variational-scaling.

With the widespread use of mobile phones and scanners to photograph and
upload documents, the need for extracting the information trapped in
unstructured document images such as retail receipts, insurance claim forms and
financial invoices is becoming more acute. A major hurdle to this objective is
that these images often contain information in the form of tables and
extracting data from tabular sub-images presents a unique set of challenges. This includes accurate detection of the tabular region within an image, and
subsequently detecting and extracting information from the rows and columns of
the detected table. While some progress has been made in table detection,
extracting the table contents is still a challenge since this involves more
fine grained table structure(rows & columns) recognition. Prior approaches have
attempted to solve the table detection and structure recognition problems
independently using two separate models. In this paper, we propose TableNet: a
novel end-to-end deep learning model for both table detection and structure
recognition. The model exploits the interdependence between the twin tasks of
table detection and table structure recognition to segment out the table and
column regions. This is followed by semantic rule-based row extraction from the
identified tabular sub-regions. The proposed model and extraction approach was
evaluated on the publicly available ICDAR 2013 and Marmot Table datasets
obtaining state of the art results. Additionally, we demonstrate that feeding
additional semantic features further improves model performance and that the
model exhibits transfer learning across datasets. Another contribution of this
paper is to provide additional table structure annotations for the Marmot data,
which currently only has annotations for table detection.

Supervised learning has proved effective for medical image analysis. However,
it can utilize only the small labeled portion of data; it fails to leverage the
large amounts of unlabeled data that is often available in medical image
datasets. Supervised models are further handicapped by domain shifts, when the
labeled dataset, despite being large enough, fails to cover different protocols
or ethnicities. In this paper, we introduce \emph{extreme consistency}, which
overcomes the above limitations, by maximally leveraging unlabeled data from
the same or a different domain in a teacher-student semi-supervised paradigm. Extreme consistency is the process of sending an extreme transformation of a
given image to the student network and then constraining its prediction to be
consistent with the teacher network's prediction for the untransformed image. The extreme nature of our consistency loss distinguishes our method from
related works that yield suboptimal performance by exercising only mild
prediction consistency. Our method is 1) auto-didactic, as it requires no extra
expert annotations; 2) versatile, as it handles both domain shift and limited
annotation problems; 3) generic, as it is readily applicable to classification,
segmentation, and detection tasks; and 4) simple to implement, as it requires
no adversarial training. We evaluate our method for the tasks of lesion and
retinal vessel segmentation in skin and fundus images. Our experiments
demonstrate a significant performance gain over both modern supervised networks
and recent semi-supervised models. This performance is attributed to the strong
regularization enforced by extreme consistency, which enables the student
network to learn how to handle extreme variants of both labeled and unlabeled
images. This enhances the network's ability to tackle the inevitable same- and
cross-domain data variability during inference.

This thesis introduces a new unsupervised learning framework, called
Alignment-Based Learning, which is based on the alignment of sentences and
Harris's (1951) notion of substitutability. Instances of the framework can be
applied to an untagged, unstructured corpus of natural language sentences,
resulting in a labelled, bracketed version of that corpus. Firstly, the framework aligns all sentences in the corpus in pairs, resulting
in a partition of the sentences consisting of parts of the sentences that are
equal in both sentences and parts that are unequal. Unequal parts of sentences
can be seen as being substitutable for each other, since substituting one
unequal part for the other results in another valid sentence. The unequal parts
of the sentences are thus considered to be possible (possibly overlapping)
constituents, called hypotheses. Secondly, the selection learning phase considers all hypotheses found by the
alignment learning phase and selects the best of these. The hypotheses are
selected based on the order in which they were found, or based on a
probabilistic function. The framework can be extended with a grammar extraction phase. This extended
framework is called parseABL. Instead of returning a structured version of the
unstructured input corpus, like the ABL system, this system also returns a
stochastic context-free or tree substitution grammar. Different instances of the framework have been tested on the English ATIS
corpus, the Dutch OVIS corpus and the Wall Street Journal corpus. One of the
interesting results, apart from the encouraging numerical results, is that all
instances can (and do) learn recursive structures.

This thesis introduces a new unsupervised learning framework, called
Alignment-Based Learning, which is based on the alignment of sentences and

resulting in a labelled, bracketed version of that corpus. To begin, the framework compares every sentence pair, and from this it produces segments that align in both sentences as well as segments that do not align. The non-matching parts are mutually substitutable because swapping one for the other still yields a valid sentence. Accordingly, the differing parts are treated as potential, possibly overlapping, constituents that are collected into hypotheses. The framework can be extended with a grammar extraction phase. The extended framework is called parseABL and builds on the original alignment and selection phases. Unlike ABL, this method additionally produces a stochastic context-free grammar or a tree substitution grammar, depending on how the extracted structures are represented. Different instances of the framework have been tested on the English ATIS
corpus, the Dutch OVIS corpus and the Wall Street Journal corpus. One of the
interesting results, apart from the encouraging numerical results, is that all
instances can (and do) learn recursive structures.

A key problem in location-based modeling and forecasting lies in identifying
suitable spatial and temporal resolutions. In particular, judicious spatial
partitioning can play a significant role in enhancing the performance of
location-based forecasting models. In this work, we investigate two widely used
tessellation strategies for partitioning city space, in the context of
real-time taxi demand forecasting. Our study compares (i) Geohash tessellation,
and (ii) Voronoi tessellation, using two distinct taxi demand datasets, over
multiple time scales. For the purpose of comparison, we employ classical
time-series tools to model the spatio-temporal demand. Our study finds that the
performance of each tessellation strategy is highly dependent on the city
geography, spatial distribution of the data, and the time of the day, and that
neither strategy is found to perform optimally across the forecast horizon. We
propose a hybrid tessellation algorithm that picks the best tessellation
strategy at each instant, based on their performance in the recent past. Our
hybrid algorithm is a non-stationary variant of the well-known HEDGE algorithm
for choosing the best advice from multiple experts. We show that the hybrid
tessellation strategy performs consistently better than either of the two
strategies across the data sets considered, at multiple time scales, and with
different performance metrics. We achieve an average accuracy of above 80% per
km^2 for both data sets considered at 60 minute aggregation levels.

For the purpose of comparison, we employ classical
time-series tools to model the spatio-temporal demand. Our investigation clearly indicates that the efficacy and performance of each tessellation strategy vary considerably based on several critical factors, including the city's unique geographical attributes, the specific spatial distribution of the available data, and the particular time of day, with neither strategy proving consistently optimal throughout the entire forecasting duration. We
propose a hybrid tessellation algorithm that picks the best tessellation
strategy at each instant, based on their performance in the recent past. Our
hybrid algorithm is a non-stationary variant of the well-known HEDGE algorithm
for choosing the best advice from multiple experts. Our comprehensive results clearly indicate that the proposed hybrid tessellation methodology consistently outperforms both individual tessellation strategies across all evaluated datasets, at varying timescales, and when assessed using diverse and rigorous performance metrics. We were able to achieve an impressive average accuracy exceeding 80% per square kilometer for both of the datasets when aggregating demand at 60-minute levels.

The optimal policy of a reinforcement learning problem is often discontinuous
and non-smooth. I.e., for two states with similar representations, their
optimal policies can be significantly different. In this case, representing the
entire policy with a function approximator (FA) with shared parameters for all
states maybe not desirable, as the generalization ability of parameters sharing
makes representing discontinuous, non-smooth policies difficult. A common way
to solve this problem, known as Mixture-of-Experts, is to represent the policy
as the weighted sum of multiple components, where different components perform
well on different parts of the state space. Following this idea and inspired by
a recent work called advantage-weighted information maximization, we propose to
learn for each state weights of these components, so that they entail the
information of the state itself and also the preferred action learned so far
for the state. The action preference is characterized via the advantage
function. In this case, the weight of each component would only be large for
certain groups of states whose representations are similar and preferred action
representations are also similar. Therefore each component is easy to be
represented. We call a policy parameterized in this way an Advantage Weighted
Mixture Policy (AWMP) and apply this idea to improve soft-actor-critic (SAC),
one of the most competitive continuous control algorithm. Experimental results
demonstrate that SAC with AWMP clearly outperforms SAC in four commonly used
continuous control tasks and achieve stable performance across different random
seeds.

The optimal strategy within the domain of reinforcement learning frequently exhibits a notable lack of smoothness and often displays inherent discontinuity, presenting challenges for its direct implementation. Optimal policies designed for states that are seemingly similar in nature can, in fact, diverge quite substantially in their prescribed actions or outcomes. Representing the entire policy using a single function approximator (FA) with shared parameters across all states might therefore prove undesirable, primarily because such widespread parameter sharing inherently hinders the effective representation of policies that are discontinuous and non-smooth in their operational characteristics. A common way
to solve this problem, known as Mixture-of-Experts, is to represent the policy
as the weighted sum of multiple components, where different components perform
well on different parts of the state space. Following this idea and inspired by
a recent work called advantage-weighted information maximization, we propose to
learn for each state weights of these components, so that they entail the
information of the state itself and also the preferred action learned so far
for the state. The action preference is characterized via the advantage
function. In this case, the weight of each component would only be large for
certain groups of states whose representations are similar and preferred action
representations are also similar. This approach consequently simplifies the internal representation required for each individual component within the overall policy structure. We term a policy parameterized in this specific manner an Advantage Weighted Mixture Policy (AWMP) and proceed to apply this innovative idea to significantly improve soft-actor-critic (SAC), which stands as one of the most competitive algorithms currently available for continuous control tasks. Empirical results from our investigations demonstrate that SAC, when integrated with the proposed AWMP framework, significantly outperforms the standard SAC algorithm across four distinct continuous control tasks and moreover consistently maintains stable performance metrics across a range of different random seeds used for initialization.

In reinforcement learning, the optimal strategy often lacks smoothness and frequently exhibits inherent discontinuities, which creates considerable difficulties for direct application. Optimal policies for states that appear similar can actually show substantial differences in their recommended actions or results. Therefore, using a single function approximator (FA) with shared parameters across all states to represent the entire policy might not be ideal, mainly because such broad parameter sharing inherently prevents the accurate representation of discontinuous and non-smooth policies. A common way to address this issue, known as Mixture-of-Experts, involves defining the policy as a weighted sum of several parts, where each part performs best in different areas of the state space. Building on this concept and drawing inspiration from recent work on advantage-weighted information maximization, we suggest learning the weights for these components for each state in such a way that they capture information about the state itself and the preferred action learned for that state thus far. The advantage function defines how actions are preferred. In this case, the weight of each component would only be large for certain groups of states whose representations and preferred action representations are both similar. Consequently, this method streamlines the internal representation needed for each individual component within the comprehensive policy framework. We name a policy structured in this fashion an Advantage Weighted Mixture Policy (AWMP) and then implement this idea to improve soft-actor-critic (SAC), which is considered among the most effective algorithms for continuous control challenges. Our studies show that SAC, when combined with the AWMP framework we introduced, performs significantly better than the regular SAC algorithm across four different continuous control tasks and consistently maintains steady performance across various random seeds.

Intuitive observations show that a baby may inherently possess the capability
of recognizing a new visual concept (e.g., chair, dog) by learning from only
very few positive instances taught by parent(s) or others, and this recognition
capability can be gradually further improved by exploring and/or interacting
with the real instances in the physical world. Inspired by these observations,
we propose a computational model for slightly-supervised object detection,
based on prior knowledge modelling, exemplar learning and learning with video
contexts. The prior knowledge is modeled with a pre-trained Convolutional
Neural Network (CNN). When very few instances of a new concept are given, an
initial concept detector is built by exemplar learning over the deep features
from the pre-trained CNN. Simulating the baby's interaction with physical
world, the well-designed tracking solution is then used to discover more
diverse instances from the massive online unlabeled videos. Once a positive
instance is detected/identified with high score in each video, more variable
instances possibly from different view-angles and/or different distances are
tracked and accumulated. Then the concept detector can be fine-tuned based on
these new instances. This process can be repeated again and again till we
obtain a very mature concept detector. Extensive experiments on Pascal
VOC-07/10/12 object detection datasets well demonstrate the effectiveness of
our framework. It can beat the state-of-the-art full-training based
performances by learning from very few samples for each object category, along
with about 20,000 unlabeled videos.

instance is detected/identified with high score in each video, more variable
instances possibly from different view-angles and/or different distances are
tracked and accumulated. These newly acquired and diverse instances are then critically utilized to further refine and enhance the existing concept detector. This iterative refinement process can be thoughtfully repeated multiple times, allowing for progressive improvements until a very mature and highly accurate concept detector is successfully obtained. Extensive experiments on Pascal
VOC-07/10/12 object detection datasets well demonstrate the effectiveness of
our framework. It can beat the state-of-the-art full-training based
performances by learning from very few samples for each object category, along
with about 20,000 unlabeled videos.

Babies, according to intuitive observations, appear to naturally possess the ability to identify new visual concepts (like a chair or a dog) after seeing just a few positive examples taught by parents or others, and this recognition skill can be progressively refined through exploration and interaction with real-world objects. Inspired by these developmental observations, we present a weakly supervised computational model for robust object detection that seamlessly integrates elements such as prior knowledge, exemplar learning techniques, and contextual video learning. Fundamental to the model's initial understanding, prior knowledge is effectively modeled and utilized through a robust, pre-trained Convolutional Neural Network (CNN). An initial concept detector is carefully built through an exemplar learning process, utilizing the rich deep features extracted from the aforementioned pre-trained CNN, which is particularly beneficial when only a limited number of instances of a novel concept are available. To precisely mimic a baby's adaptive interaction with its surroundings, a sophisticated tracking mechanism is utilized to dependably pinpoint additional instances of the target object within a vast collection of unlabeled online videos. Once a positive instance is detected or identified with a high score in each video, more variable instances, possibly from different view-angles and/or different distances, are tracked and accumulated. These newly acquired and diverse instances are subsequently applied to further improve and fine-tune the existing concept detector. This iterative refinement process can be thoughtfully repeated multiple times, enabling gradual improvements until a highly developed and remarkably accurate concept detector is successfully attained. Thorough experiments carried out on the Pascal VOC-07/10/12 object detection datasets clearly demonstrate the effectiveness of our framework. It outperforms state-of-the-art full-training based methods by learning from a very limited number of samples for each object category, complemented by approximately 20,000 unlabeled videos.

Human activity recognition aims to recognize the activities of daily living
by utilizing the sensors on different body parts. However, when the labeled
data from a certain body position (i.e. target domain) is missing, how to
leverage the data from other positions (i.e. source domain) to help learn the
activity labels of this position? When there are several source domains
available, it is often difficult to select the most similar source domain to
the target domain. With the selected source domain, we need to perform accurate
knowledge transfer between domains. Existing methods only learn the global
distance between domains while ignoring the local property. In this paper, we
propose a \textit{Stratified Transfer Learning} (STL) framework to perform both
source domain selection and knowledge transfer. STL is based on our proposed
\textit{Stratified} distance to capture the local property of domains. STL
consists of two components: Stratified Domain Selection (STL-SDS) can select
the most similar source domain to the target domain; Stratified Activity
Transfer (STL-SAT) is able to perform accurate knowledge transfer. Extensive
experiments on three public activity recognition datasets demonstrate the
superiority of STL. Furthermore, we extensively investigate the performance of
transfer learning across different degrees of similarities and activity levels
between domains. We also discuss the potential applications of STL in other
fields of pervasive computing for future research.

available, it is often difficult to select the most similar source domain to
the target domain. Following the critical phase of source domain selection, precise and effective knowledge transfer between the chosen domains becomes absolutely essential for successful activity recognition. Existing methods only learn the global
distance between domains while ignoring the local property. In this paper, we
propose a novel \textit{Stratified Transfer Learning} (STL) framework specifically designed to perform both the crucial task of source domain selection and the subsequent process of knowledge transfer efficiently. STL is based on our proposed

consists of two components: Stratified Domain Selection (STL-SDS) can select
the most similar source domain to the target domain; Stratified Activity
Transfer (STL-SAT) is able to perform accurate knowledge transfer. Extensive experiments conducted on three widely recognized public activity recognition datasets comprehensively demonstrate the overall effectiveness of the proposed STL framework. Furthermore, we conduct a thorough investigation into the performance of transfer learning when applied across various domains that exhibit differing levels of similarity and activity levels. We also explore the significant potential for STL's future applications in several other related pervasive computing areas.

Video super-resolution (SR) aims at generating a sequence of high-resolution
(HR) frames with plausible and temporally consistent details from their
low-resolution (LR) counterparts. The key challenge for video SR lies in the
effective exploitation of temporal dependency between consecutive frames. Existing deep learning based methods commonly estimate optical flows between LR
frames to provide temporal dependency. However, the resolution conflict between
LR optical flows and HR outputs hinders the recovery of fine details. In this
paper, we propose an end-to-end video SR network to super-resolve both optical
flows and images. Optical flow SR from LR frames provides accurate temporal
dependency and ultimately improves video SR performance. Specifically, we first
propose an optical flow reconstruction network (OFRnet) to infer HR optical
flows in a coarse-to-fine manner. Then, motion compensation is performed using
HR optical flows to encode temporal dependency. Finally, compensated LR inputs
are fed to a super-resolution network (SRnet) to generate SR results. Extensive
experiments have been conducted to demonstrate the effectiveness of HR optical
flows for SR performance improvement. Comparative results on the Vid4 and
DAVIS-10 datasets show that our network achieves the state-of-the-art
performance.

Most deep learning approaches model temporal dependency by predicting optical flow from LR frames and then using it to relate neighboring frames. However, the resolution conflict between
LR optical flows and HR outputs hinders the recovery of fine details. In this paper, we introduce an end-to-end video SR model that jointly super-resolves optical
flows and images, learning both components together. Optical flow SR from LR frames provides accurate temporal
dependency, which in turn ultimately improves video SR performance. Specifically, we first design an optical flow reconstruction network (OFRnet) to estimate HR optical
flows in a coarse-to-fine manner, progressively refining motion details. Next, we use the HR optical flows for motion compensation so that temporal dependency can be captured more accurately. Finally, compensated LR inputs
are fed to a super-resolution network (SRnet) to generate SR results. Extensive
experiments have been conducted to demonstrate the effectiveness of HR optical
flows for SR performance improvement. Comparative results on the Vid4 and
DAVIS-10 datasets show that our network achieves the state-of-the-art
performance.

Video super-resolution (SR) generates high-resolution (HR) frames with realistic, temporally consistent details by transforming low-resolution (LR) inputs into sharper sequences. A central challenge in video SR is using temporal relationships across successive frames in a practical and effective manner. In most deep learning approaches, temporal dependency is modeled by predicting optical flow from LR frames and using it to link adjacent frames. Even so, the resolution disparity between LR optical flows and HR results hinders the recovery of subtle, fine details. Here, we present an end-to-end video SR framework that simultaneously super-resolves optical flows and images, so both components are learned together. In particular, optical flow SR estimated from LR frames provides reliable temporal dependency, which in turn improves overall video SR performance. To achieve this, we first design an optical flow reconstruction network (OFRnet) that predicts HR optical flows in a coarse-to-fine manner, steadily refining motion details. Then, motion compensation is applied based on the HR optical flows, allowing temporal dependency to be represented more accurately. Finally, the compensated LR inputs are fed into a super-resolution network (SRnet) to generate the SR outputs. Extensive experiments were conducted to confirm the effectiveness of HR optical flows in improving SR performance. Comparative results on the Vid4 and DAVIS-10 datasets show that our network achieves state-of-the-art performance.

We consider the problem of referring image segmentation. Given an input image
and a natural language expression, the goal is to segment the object referred
by the language expression in the image. Existing works in this area treat the
language expression and the input image separately in their representations. They do not sufficiently capture long-range correlations between these two
modalities. In this paper, we propose a cross-modal self-attention (CMSA)
module that effectively captures the long-range dependencies between linguistic
and visual features. Our model can adaptively focus on informative words in the
referring expression and important regions in the input image. In addition, we
propose a gated multi-level fusion module to selectively integrate
self-attentive cross-modal features corresponding to different levels in the
image. This module controls the information flow of features at different
levels. We validate the proposed approach on four evaluation datasets. Our
proposed approach consistently outperforms existing state-of-the-art methods.

module that effectively captures the long-range dependencies between linguistic
and visual features. Additionally, we present a novel gated multi-level fusion module, which has been specifically engineered to selectively merge self-attentive cross-modal features derived from diverse image levels. Crucially, this particular module effectively controls the feature information flow at these various, distinct levels. We validate the proposed approach on four evaluation datasets. Our
proposed approach consistently outperforms existing state-of-the-art methods.

Convolutional neural networks (CNNs) achieve translational invariance by
using pooling operations. However, the operations do not preserve the spatial
relationships in the learned representations. Hence, CNNs cannot extrapolate to
various geometric transformations of inputs. Recently, Capsule Networks
(CapsNets) have been proposed to tackle this problem. In CapsNets, each entity
is represented by a vector and routed to high-level entity representations by a
dynamic routing algorithm. CapsNets have been shown to be more robust than CNNs
to affine transformations of inputs. However, there is still a huge gap between
their performance on transformed inputs compared to untransformed versions. In
this work, we first revisit the routing procedure by (un)rolling its forward
and backward passes. Our investigation reveals that the routing procedure
contributes neither to the generalization ability nor to the affine robustness
of the CapsNets. Furthermore, we explore the limitations of capsule
transformations and propose affine CapsNets (Aff-CapsNets), which are more
robust to affine transformations. On our benchmark task, where models are
trained on the MNIST dataset and tested on the AffNIST dataset, our
Aff-CapsNets improve the benchmark performance by a large margin (from 79% to
93.21%), without using any routing mechanism.

However, a noticeable and significant performance gap persists between inputs that have undergone transformation and those that remain untransformed. In
this work, we first revisit the routing procedure by (un)rolling its forward
and backward passes. Our findings from this investigation indicate that the routing mechanism does not contribute to improving CapsNets' overall generalization or their robustness to affine transformations. We also thoroughly explore the inherent limitations within capsule transformations and subsequently propose affine CapsNets (Aff-CapsNets), which exhibit greater resilience when dealing with affine transformations. On our benchmark task, where models are
trained on the MNIST dataset and tested on the AffNIST dataset, our

However, these operations cannot preserve the spatial connections within the learned features. Consequently, CNNs struggle to generalize effectively to diverse geometric alterations of their input. To address this shortcoming, Capsule Networks (CapsNets) were recently developed. CapsNets effectively represent each entity using a specific vector, which is then dynamically routed to higher-level representations through a specialized algorithm. CapsNets have demonstrated greater resilience compared to traditional CNNs, especially when dealing with affine transformations of their input data. Despite this, a noticeable and considerable performance difference persists between transformed and untransformed inputs. In this study, we first re-evaluate the routing process by analyzing its forward and backward operations. Our analysis indicates that the routing mechanism does not improve CapsNets' generalization ability or their resistance to affine transformations. We also thoroughly examine the inherent constraints within capsule transformations and subsequently introduce Affine CapsNets (Aff-CapsNets), which exhibit enhanced robustness to affine transformations. Representation learning and unsupervised learning are two central topics of
machine learning and signal processing. Deep learning is one of the most
effective unsupervised representation learning approach. The main contributions
of this paper to the topics are as follows. (i) We propose to view the
representative deep learning approaches as special cases of the knowledge reuse
framework of clustering ensemble. (ii) We propose to view sparse coding when
used as a feature encoder as the consensus function of clustering ensemble, and
view dictionary learning as the training process of the base clusterings of
clustering ensemble. (ii) Based on the above two views, we propose a very
simple deep learning algorithm, named deep random model ensemble (DRME). It is
a stack of random model ensembles. Each random model ensemble is a special
k-means ensemble that discards the expectation-maximization optimization of
each base k-means but only preserves the default initialization method of the
base k-means. (iv) We propose to select the most powerful representation among
the layers by applying DRME to clustering where the single-linkage is used as
the clustering algorithm. Moreover, the DRME based clustering can also detect
the number of the natural clusters accurately. Extensive experimental
comparisons with 5 representation learning methods on 19 benchmark data sets
demonstrate the effectiveness of DRME.

Representation learning and unsupervised learning constitute fundamental and central topics within the fields of machine learning and signal processing research. Deep learning has emerged as a particularly effective and powerful approach for achieving unsupervised representation learning tasks. This particular paper contributes several significant advancements to the understanding and application of these important topics. (i) We propose to view the
representative deep learning approaches as special cases of the knowledge reuse
framework of clustering ensemble. (ii) We conceptualize sparse coding, when functioning as a feature encoder, as the consensus function for a clustering ensemble, and correspondingly, we consider dictionary learning as the process of training its constituent base clusterings. (ii) Based on the above two views, we propose a very
simple deep learning algorithm, named deep random model ensemble (DRME). Specifically, it is structured as a hierarchical stack composed of multiple random model ensembles. Each random model ensemble is a special
k-means ensemble that discards the expectation-maximization optimization of
each base k-means but only preserves the default initialization method of the
base k-means. (iv) Furthermore, we introduce an innovative method designed to select the most robust representation across different layers by applying the DRME framework to the task of clustering, specifically utilizing single-linkage. The DRME-based clustering approach also possesses the capability to accurately determine the true number of intrinsic clusters present within a dataset. Extensive experimental
comparisons with 5 representation learning methods on 19 benchmark data sets
demonstrate the effectiveness of DRME.

Representation learning and unsupervised learning are essential and fundamental disciplines at the heart of machine learning and signal processing research. Deep learning has emerged as a particularly powerful approach for performing unsupervised representation learning operations. This document makes several valuable contributions to understanding and implementing these crucial domains. (i) We propose viewing representative deep learning approaches as special cases of the clustering ensemble's knowledge reuse framework. (ii) When utilized as a feature encoder, sparse coding is conceived as the consensus function for a clustering ensemble, while dictionary learning is considered the training procedure for its foundational base clusterings. (ii) Building upon these two insights, we present a simple deep learning algorithm known as deep random model ensemble (DRME). Specifically, it is constructed as a hierarchical arrangement composed of multiple random model ensembles. Each random model ensemble operates as a specialized k-means ensemble that bypasses the expectation-maximization optimization of individual base k-means, preserving solely the default initialization technique of the base k-means. (iv) Furthermore, we introduce an innovative technique for choosing the most stable representation across different layers by applying the DRME framework to clustering, specifically using single-linkage. The clustering method based on DRME can also precisely determine the actual number of intrinsic clusters in a dataset. Comprehensive experimental comparisons with 5 representation learning methods on 19 benchmark datasets illustrate DRME's efficacy.

As a vital topic in media content interpretation, video anomaly detection
(VAD) has made fruitful progress via deep neural network (DNN). However,
existing methods usually follow a reconstruction or frame prediction routine. They suffer from two gaps: (1) They cannot localize video activities in a both
precise and comprehensive manner. (2) They lack sufficient abilities to utilize
high-level semantics and temporal context information. Inspired by
frequently-used cloze test in language study, we propose a brand-new VAD
solution named Video Event Completion (VEC) to bridge gaps above: First, we
propose a novel pipeline to achieve both precise and comprehensive enclosure of
video activities. Appearance and motion are exploited as mutually complimentary
cues to localize regions of interest (RoIs). A normalized spatio-temporal cube
(STC) is built from each RoI as a video event, which lays the foundation of VEC
and serves as a basic processing unit. Second, we encourage DNN to capture
high-level semantics by solving a visual cloze test. To build such a visual
cloze test, a certain patch of STC is erased to yield an incomplete event (IE). The DNN learns to restore the original video event from the IE by inferring the
missing patch. Third, to incorporate richer motion dynamics, another DNN is
trained to infer erased patches' optical flow. Finally, two ensemble strategies
using different types of IE and modalities are proposed to boost VAD
performance, so as to fully exploit the temporal context and modality
information for VAD. VEC can consistently outperform state-of-the-art methods
by a notable margin (typically 1.5%-5% AUROC) on commonly-used VAD benchmarks. Our codes and results can be verified at github.com/yuguangnudt/VEC_VAD.

cues to localize regions of interest (RoIs). A normalized spatio-temporal cube
(STC) is built from each RoI as a video event, which lays the foundation of VEC

To build the visual cloze task, we sample a patch from the STC to form an incomplete event (IE) that intentionally omits part of the original event. VEC consistently achieves a large improvement over the current state of the art (typically 1.5%-5% AUROC) on standard VAD benchmarks. The proposed code and experimental results are released at github.com/yuguangnudt/VEC_VAD for public access.

Video anomaly detection (VAD), an important topic for interpreting media content, has made significant strides with deep neural networks (DNNs). However, despite recent improvements, most existing methods still rely heavily on reconstruction- or frame-prediction-based frameworks. They have two shortcomings: (1) they cannot localize video activities in a way that is both sufficiently precise and fully comprehensive. (2) They also fail to effectively incorporate high-level semantics together with temporal context. Inspired by the widely applied cloze test in language studies, we propose a new VAD method named Video Event Completion (VEC) that directly addresses the above gaps through our specific design. We use appearance and motion as mutually complementary cues to identify regions of interest (RoIs). A normalized spatio-temporal cube (STC) is built from each RoI as a video event, which lays the foundation of VEC and serves as a basic processing unit. Second, we instruct the DNN to capture high-level semantics using a visual cloze test. For the visual cloze task, we extract a patch from the STC to form an incomplete event (IE) by intentionally removing part of the original event. Then, the DNN reconstructs the initial video event from the IE by predicting the missing patch region. Third, we further train an independent DNN to predict the optical flow corresponding to the excised patch. Finally, we present two ensemble strategies that use different IE types and modalities, improving VAD by leveraging temporal context and modality cues. Across common VAD benchmarks, VEC reliably achieves a notable improvement over the current state of the art (usually 1.5%-5% AUROC). The proposed code and experimental outcomes are publicly released at github.com/yuguangnudt/VEC_VAD.

Gynaecologists and obstetricians visually interpret cardiotocography (CTG)
traces using the International Federation of Gynaecology and Obstetrics (FIGO)
guidelines to assess the wellbeing of the foetus during antenatal care. This
approach has raised concerns among professionals with regards to inter- and
intra-variability where clinical diagnosis only has a 30\% positive predictive
value when classifying pathological outcomes. Machine learning models, trained
with FIGO and other user derived features extracted from CTG traces, have been
shown to increase positive predictive capacity and minimise variability. This
is only possible however when class distributions are equal which is rarely the
case in clinical trials where case-control observations are heavily skewed in
favour of normal outcomes. Classes can be balanced using either synthetic data
derived from resampled case training data or by decreasing the number of
control instances. However, this either introduces bias or removes valuable
information. Concerns have also been raised regarding machine learning studies
and their reliance on manually handcrafted features. While this has led to some
interesting results, deriving an optimal set of features is considered to be an
art as well as a science and is often an empirical and time consuming process. In this paper, we address both of these issues and propose a novel CTG analysis
methodology that a) splits CTG time-series signals into n-size windows with
equal class distributions, and b) automatically extracts features from
time-series windows using a one dimensional convolutional neural network
(1DCNN) and multilayer perceptron (MLP) ensemble. Collectively, the proposed
approach normally distributes classes and removes the need to handcrafted
features from CTG traces.

Within the field of antenatal care, gynaecologists and obstetricians rely on the established International Federation of Gynaecology and Obstetrics (FIGO) guidelines to visually interpret cardiotocography (CTG) traces in order to assess foetal wellbeing. However, this traditional method of interpretation has generated significant professional concerns regarding the potential for both inter-observer and intra-observer variability, particularly given that the clinical diagnosis derived from it possesses only a 30% positive predictive value for actual pathological outcomes. Machine learning models, trained
with FIGO and other user derived features extracted from CTG traces, have been
shown to increase positive predictive capacity and minimise variability. This enhanced performance, however, is only achievable when class distributions are precisely equal, which is a condition rarely met in typical clinical trials where case-control observations are often heavily skewed, predominantly favoring normal outcomes. Classes can be balanced using either synthetic data
derived from resampled case training data or by decreasing the number of
control instances. However, this either introduces bias or removes valuable
information. Concerns have also been raised regarding machine learning studies
and their reliance on manually handcrafted features. Although this particular approach of using handcrafted features has indeed produced convincing results in various studies, the process of defining the optimal feature set for a given problem is frequently regarded as a blend of both art and science, often proving to be experimental in nature and consuming considerable time. This current paper aims to address both of these identified challenges by introducing a novel CTG analysis method that simultaneously performs two key functions: (a) it segments CTG time-series signals into specific n-size windows, ensuring balanced class distributions within them, and (b) it automatically extracts relevant features from these segmented windows through the use of a combined one-dimensional convolutional neural network (1DCNN) and multilayer perceptron (MLP) ensemble. Therefore, our proposed methodology effectively ensures that classes are normally distributed and completely eliminates the aforementioned necessity for manual feature engineering from the complex CTG traces.

This paper aims to tackle both these identified issues by proposing a new CTG analysis method that simultaneously performs two main functions: (a) it divides CTG time-series signals into specific n-size windows, thereby ensuring balanced class distributions within them, and (b) it automatically extracts relevant features from these segmented windows using a combined one-dimensional convolutional neural network (1DCNN) and multilayer perceptron (MLP) ensemble. In the wake of the highly electrified future ahead of us, the role of energy
storage is crucial wherever distributed generation is abundant, such as in
microgrid settings. Given the variety of storage options that are becoming more
and more economical, determining which type of storage technology to invest in,
along with the appropriate timing and capacity becomes a critical research
question. It is inevitable that these problems will continue to become
increasingly relevant in the future and require strategic planning and holistic
and modern frameworks in order to be solved. Reinforcement Learning algorithms
have already proven to be successful in problems where sequential
decision-making is inherent. In the operations planning area, these algorithms
are already used but mostly in short-term problems with well-defined
constraints. On the contrary, we expand and tailor these techniques to
long-term planning by utilizing model-free algorithms combined with
simulation-based models. A model and expansion plan have been developed to
optimally determine microgrid designs as they evolve to dynamically react to
changing conditions and to exploit energy storage capabilities. We show that it
is possible to derive better engineering solutions that would point to the
types of energy storage units which could be at the core of future microgrid
applications. Another key finding is that the optimal storage capacity
threshold for a system depends heavily on the price movements of the available
storage units. By utilizing the proposed approaches, it is possible to model
inherent problem uncertainties and optimize the whole streamline of sequential
investment decision-making.
