As electrification continues to expand, energy storage becomes crucial in settings with widespread distributed generation, such as microgrids, and is key to their efficient operation. Given the variety of storage options that are becoming increasingly economical, determining which type of storage technology to invest in, along with the appropriate timing and capacity, becomes a critical research question. These issues are likely to grow in importance over time and will require strategic planning based on comprehensive, contemporary frameworks. Reinforcement learning algorithms have already shown strong results in problems where sequential decision-making is a fundamental and defining feature. In operations planning, these algorithms are already used, but mainly for short-term problems with clearly defined constraints and explicit decision contexts. By contrast, we modify and apply these methods to long-term planning by using model-free algorithms together with simulation-based models. A model and expansion plan have been created to optimally identify evolving microgrid designs, adapt to changing conditions, and effectively leverage the capabilities provided by energy storage. We show that better engineering solutions can be achieved to determine the types of energy storage units likely to be central in future microgrid applications. Another important finding is that the optimal storage capacity threshold for a system is strongly influenced by the price dynamics of the available storage units. Through the proposed approaches, inherent problem uncertainties can be represented, and the full sequence of investment decisions over time can be optimized.

Learning descriptive spatio-temporal object models from data is paramount for
the task of semi-supervised video object segmentation. Most existing approaches
mainly rely on models that estimate the segmentation mask based on a reference
mask at the first frame (aided sometimes by optical flow or the previous mask). These models, however, are prone to fail under rapid appearance changes or
occlusions due to their limitations in modelling the temporal component. On the
other hand, very recently, other approaches learned long-term features using a
convolutional LSTM to leverage the information from all previous video frames. Even though these models achieve better temporal representations, they still
have to be fine-tuned for every new video sequence. In this paper, we present
an intermediate solution and devise a novel GAN architecture, FaSTGAN, to learn
spatio-temporal object models over finite temporal windows. To achieve this, we
concentrate all the heavy computational load to the training phase with two
critics that enforce spatial and temporal mask consistency over the last K
frames. Then at test time, we only use a relatively light regressor, which
reduces the inference time considerably. As a result, our approach combines a
high resiliency to sudden geometric and photometric object changes with
efficiency at test time (no need for fine-tuning nor post-processing). We
demonstrate that the accuracy of our method is on par with state-of-the-art
techniques on the challenging YouTube-VOS and DAVIS datasets, while running at
32 fps, about 4x faster than the closest competitor.

Learning descriptive spatio-temporal object models from data is paramount for
the task of semi-supervised video object segmentation. Most current methods rely on models that infer the segmentation mask from a reference mask in the first frame, and they may further improve this prediction by incorporating optical flow information or the preceding mask. However, they often break when sudden appearance changes occur or when objects become occluded, since they fail to model the temporal dimension adequately. More recently, some techniques use a convolutional LSTM to learn long-range features by exploiting information from all preceding frames. Even though these models achieve better temporal representations, they still
have to be fine-tuned for every new video sequence. In this paper, we present a compromise and propose the novel GAN architecture FaSTGAN, designed for learning spatio-temporal object models over finite temporal windows. To achieve this, we
concentrate all the heavy computational load to the training phase by using two
critics that enforce both spatial and temporal mask consistency across the last K
frames. Then at test time, we only use a relatively light regressor, which
reduces the inference time considerably. As a result, our approach combines a
high resiliency to sudden geometric and photometric object changes with
efficiency at test time (no need for fine-tuning nor post-processing). We
show that our method matches state-of-the-art accuracy on YouTube-VOS and DAVIS while running at 32 fps, which is about 4x faster than the closest competitor.

Learning data-driven spatio-temporal object models is crucial for semi-supervised video object segmentation. Many current methods rely on models that infer the segmentation mask from a reference mask in the first frame, and can improve the estimate by incorporating optical flow information or the earlier mask. However, they often break down when objects suddenly change appearance or become occluded, since they do not model the temporal dimension well enough. More recently, some approaches use a convolutional LSTM to learn long-range dependencies by exploiting information from all preceding frames. Even though these models achieve better temporal representations, they still have to be fine-tuned for every new video sequence. In this work, we propose a middle-ground solution with the new GAN architecture FaSTGAN, designed to learn spatio-temporal object models in limited temporal windows. For this purpose, we move the most compute-heavy parts to the training stage alone, using two critics to enforce both spatial and temporal mask consistency across the final K frames. At test time, we then rely only on a much lighter regressor, which greatly reduces inference latency. As a result, our approach is highly robust to sudden geometric and photometric changes in objects and remains efficient during testing, without requiring fine-tuning or post-processing. We also show that our method achieves state-of-the-art performance on YouTube-VOS and DAVIS at 32 fps, about 4x faster than the closest rival.

Computer vision relies on labeled datasets for training and evaluation in
detecting and recognizing objects. The popular computer vision program, YOLO
("You Only Look Once"), has been shown to accurately detect objects in many
major image datasets. However, the images found in those datasets, are
independent of one another and cannot be used to test YOLO's consistency at
detecting the same object as its environment (e.g. ambient lighting) changes. This paper describes a novel effort to evaluate YOLO's consistency for
large-scale applications. It does so by working (a) at large scale and (b) by
using consecutive images from a curated network of public video cameras
deployed in a variety of real-world situations, including traffic
intersections, national parks, shopping malls, university campuses, etc. We
specifically examine YOLO's ability to detect objects in different scenarios
(e.g., daytime vs. night), leveraging the cameras' ability to rapidly retrieve
many successive images for evaluating detection consistency. Using our camera
network and advanced computing resources (supercomputers), we analyzed more
than 5 million images captured by 140 network cameras in 24 hours. Compared
with labels marked by humans (considered as "ground truth"), YOLO struggles to
consistently detect the same humans and cars as their positions change from one
frame to the next; it also struggles to detect objects at night time. Our
findings suggest that state-of-the art vision solutions should be trained by
data from network camera with contextual information before they can be
deployed in applications that demand high consistency on object detection.

For the purposes of training and evaluating object detection and recognition algorithms, computer vision systems frequently rely on the utilization of carefully labeled datasets. YOLO, an acronym for "You Only Look Once," stands out as a prominent and highly effective computer vision model, particularly renowned for its capability to accurately identify various objects across numerous important image datasets. Despite its strengths, these conventional datasets are composed of individual, self-contained images, which fundamentally limits their suitability for thoroughly assessing YOLO's robustness and reliability when encountering the same object across different contextual environments, such as variations in ambient lighting conditions. For example, varying factors like ambient lighting conditions can significantly impact object appearance. This paper describes a novel effort to evaluate YOLO's consistency for
large-scale applications. It does so by working (a) at large scale and (b) by
using consecutive images from a curated network of public video cameras
deployed in a variety of real-world situations, including traffic
intersections, national parks, shopping malls, university campuses, etc. By leveraging the rapid consecutive image capture capability of these cameras, we are able to thoroughly assess YOLO's object identification efficacy and detection consistency under a range of varying conditions, such as the distinct differences between day and night observations. Using our camera
network and advanced computing resources (supercomputers), we analyzed more
than 5 million images captured by 140 network cameras in 24 hours. Compared
with labels marked by humans (considered as "ground truth"), YOLO struggles to
consistently detect the same humans and cars as their positions change from one
frame to the next; it also struggles to detect objects at night time. Our comprehensive findings suggest that current state-of-the-art computer vision solutions would significantly benefit from incorporating training with contextual network camera data, especially for real-world applications that demand exceptionally high consistency in object detection performance.

The training and assessment of object detection and recognition algorithms in computer vision systems frequently rely on carefully labeled datasets. YOLO, which stands for "You Only Look Once," is a prominent and highly effective computer vision model, particularly noted for its skill in accurately identifying a wide range of objects within numerous important image datasets. Nevertheless, these conventional datasets, composed of individual, standalone images, inherently limit their usefulness for thoroughly assessing YOLO's robustness and reliability when encountering identical objects in different situational contexts, such as varying ambient illumination. For example, changeable factors such as ambient lighting can significantly alter an object's appearance. This paper details a new initiative to assess YOLO's consistency for large-scale applications. It does so by working (a) at large scale and (b) by using consecutive images from a curated network of public video cameras deployed in a variety of real-world situations, including traffic intersections, national parks, shopping malls, and university campuses. By leveraging the fast, sequential image capture capability of these cameras, we can thoroughly assess YOLO's performance in object identification and the reliability of its detection across various conditions, including notable differences between day and night observations. Using our camera network and powerful computing resources (supercomputers), we analyzed more than 5 million images collected by 140 network cameras over a 24-hour span. Compared to human-labeled ground truth, YOLO struggles with consistently identifying the same people and vehicles as they move between frames; it also faces difficulties detecting objects at night. Our comprehensive results suggest that incorporating training with contextual network camera data would significantly improve current cutting-edge computer vision solutions, especially for real-world scenarios demanding exceptionally high consistency in object detection performance.

Multi-level feature fusion is a fundamental topic in computer vision. It has
been exploited to detect, segment and classify objects at various scales. When
multi-level features meet multi-modal cues, the optimal feature aggregation and
multi-modal learning strategy become a hot potato. In this paper, we leverage
the inherent multi-modal and multi-level nature of RGB-D salient object
detection to devise a novel cascaded refinement network. In particular, first,
we propose to regroup the multi-level features into teacher and student
features using a bifurcated backbone strategy (BBS). Second, we introduce a
depth-enhanced module (DEM) to excavate informative depth cues from the channel
and spatial views. Then, RGB and depth modalities are fused in a complementary
way. Our architecture, named Bifurcated Backbone Strategy Network (BBS-Net), is
simple, efficient, and backbone-independent. Extensive experiments show that
BBS-Net significantly outperforms eighteen SOTA models on eight challenging
datasets under five evaluation measures, demonstrating the superiority of our
approach ($\sim 4 \%$ improvement in S-measure $vs.$ the top-ranked model:
DMRA-iccv2019). In addition, we provide a comprehensive analysis on the
generalization ability of different RGB-D datasets and provide a powerful
training set for future research.

Multi-level feature fusion is a fundamental topic in computer vision. It has
been exploited to detect, segment and classify objects at various scales. The processes of achieving optimal feature aggregation and effective multi-modal learning become particularly challenging when multi-level features are merged with diverse multi-modal cues. This paper, therefore, proposes a novel cascaded refinement network specifically designed to address and effectively manage the complex multi-modal and multi-level properties inherent in RGB-D salient object detection tasks. In particular, as a first step, we propose a method to regroup the extracted multi-level features into distinct teacher and student feature sets, which is accomplished through the implementation of a bifurcated backbone strategy (BBS). Second, we introduce a
depth-enhanced module (DEM) to excavate informative depth cues from the channel
and spatial views. Subsequently, the rich RGB information and the valuable depth information are then integrated together in a complementary manner, enhancing overall feature representation. Our architecture, named Bifurcated Backbone Strategy Network (BBS-Net), is
simple, efficient, and backbone-independent. Extensive experimentation and rigorous evaluation demonstrate that BBS-Net substantially outperforms eighteen current state-of-the-art models across eight challenging datasets and five robust evaluation metrics, impressively achieving an approximate 4% increase in S-measure over the DMRA-iccv2019 model. Additionally, we conduct a thorough analysis of the generalization ability observed across different RGB-D datasets and, based on our findings, provide a powerful and well-curated training set that can significantly benefit future research endeavors in this field.

A fundamental concept in computer vision involves incorporating features from various levels. This method has been utilized for identifying, segmenting, and categorizing objects across different scales. Significant challenges emerge in effectively combining features and achieving successful multimodal learning, especially when merging multilevel features with diverse multimodal data. Therefore, this paper proposes a novel cascaded refinement network specifically designed to handle the intricate multimodal and multilevel properties inherent in RGB-D salient object detection. First, we introduce a method for arranging the extracted multilevel features into distinct teacher and student groups using a bifurcated backbone strategy (BBS). Second, we present a depth-enhanced module (DEM) to extract useful depth information from both channel and spatial perspectives. Subsequently, the extensive RGB data and essential depth insights are fused complementarily, thereby augmenting the overall feature representation. Our architecture, named Bifurcated Backbone Strategy Network (BBS-Net), is simple, efficient, and backbone-independent. Extensive experiments and rigorous evaluations have shown that BBS-Net achieves significant improvement, outperforming eighteen current state-of-the-art models on eight challenging datasets using five robust evaluation metrics, including an approximately 4% increase in S-measure over the DMRA-ICCV2019 model. Additionally, a comprehensive examination of its generalization abilities across diverse RGB-D datasets was conducted, resulting in a strong and carefully compiled training set intended to significantly advance future research in this area.

Convolutional Neural Networks (CNNs) have a major impact on our society
because of the numerous services they provide. On the other hand, they require
considerable computing power. To satisfy these requirements, it is possible to
use graphic processing units (GPUs). However, high power consumption and
limited external IOs constrain their usability and suitability in industrial
and mission-critical scenarios. Recently, the number of researches that utilize
FPGAs to implement CNNs are increasing rapidly. This is due to the lower power
consumption and easy reconfigurability offered by these platforms. Because of
the research efforts put into topics such as architecture, synthesis and
optimization, some new challenges are arising to integrate such hardware
solutions to high-level machine learning software libraries. This paper
introduces an integrated framework (CNN2Gate) that supports compilation of a
CNN model for an FPGA target. CNN2Gate exploits the OpenCL synthesis workflow
for FPGAs offered by commercial vendors. CNN2Gate is capable of parsing CNN
models from several popular high-level machine learning libraries such as
Keras, Pytorch, Caffe2 etc. CNN2Gate extracts computation flow of layers, in
addition to weights and biases and applies a "given" fixed-point quantization. Furthermore, it writes this information in the proper format for OpenCL
synthesis tools that are then used to build and run the project on FPGA. CNN2Gate performs design-space exploration using a reinforcement learning agent
and fits the design on different FPGAs with limited logic resources
automatically. This paper reports results of automatic synthesis and
design-space exploration of AlexNet and VGG-16 on various Intel FPGA platforms. CNN2Gate achieves a latency of 205 ms for VGG-16 and 18 ms for AlexNet on the
FPGA.

Nonetheless, high power consumption and limited external IO availability reduce their effectiveness in practice and make them less suitable for industrial and mission-critical use cases. consumption and easy reconfigurability offered by these platforms. As research progresses on architecture, synthesis, and optimization, merging these hardware-oriented methods with high-level machine learning software libraries is creating new challenges for practical toolchains. This paper
introduces an integrated framework (CNN2Gate) that supports compilation of a

CNN2Gate performs design-space exploration using a reinforcement learning agent and automatically maps the design onto different FPGAs with limited logic resources while considering the constraints. design-space exploration of AlexNet and VGG-16 on various Intel FPGA platforms. CNN2Gate attains 205 ms latency for VGG-16 and 18 ms for AlexNet on the FPGA, reflecting the performance achieved by the generated designs.

Convolutional Neural Networks (CNNs) have a major impact on contemporary life, largely because the many services they enable and the broad range of real-world applications they support are so extensive. On the other hand, they require
considerable computing power. To meet these requirements, graphics processing units (GPUs) may be utilized. requirements and the straightforward reconfiguration provided by these platforms. presents an integrated framework (CNN2Gate) that enables compiling a

It determines the computation route for each layer, including its weights and biases, and then applies a preselected fixed-point quantization approach to the derived representation. It also stores this data in the correct format for OpenCL synthesis tools, enabling those tools to build and run the project on the FPGA. CNN2Gate performs design-space exploration using a reinforcement learning agent, and then automatically assigns the designs to various FPGAs with limited logic resources while taking the applicable constraints into account. The paper reports results for automated synthesis and
design-space exploration of AlexNet and VGG-16 across a range of Intel FPGA platforms. CNN2Gate achieves a latency of 205 ms for VGG-16 and 18 ms for AlexNet on the FPGA, highlighting the performance of the generated designs.

\textit{Graph Neural Network} (GNN) is a promising approach for analyzing
graph-structured data that tactfully captures their dependency information via
node-level message passing. It has achieved state-of-the-art performances in
many tasks, such as node classification, graph matching, clustering, and graph
generation. As GNNs operate on non-Euclidean data, their irregular data access
patterns cause considerable computational costs and overhead on conventional
architectures, such as GPU and CPU. Our analysis shows that GNN adopts a hybrid
computing model. The \textit{Aggregation} (or \textit{Message Passing}) phase
performs vector additions where vectors are fetched with irregular strides. The
\textit{Transformation} (or \textit{Node Embedding}) phase can be either dense
or sparse-dense matrix multiplication. In this work, We propose
\textit{VersaGNN}, an ultra-efficient, systolic-array-based versatile hardware
accelerator that unifies dense and sparse matrix multiplication. By applying
this single optimized systolic array to both aggregation and transformation
phases, we have significantly reduced chip sizes and energy consumption. We
then divide the computing engine into blocked systolic arrays to support the
\textit{Strassen}'s algorithm for dense matrix multiplication, dramatically
scaling down the number of multiplications and enabling high-throughput
computation of GNNs. To balance the workload of sparse-dense matrix
multiplication, we also introduced a greedy algorithm to combine sparse
sub-matrices of compressed format into condensed ones to reduce computational
cycles. Compared with current state-of-the-art GNN software frameworks,
\textit{VersaGNN} achieves on average 3712$\times$ speedup with 1301.25$\times$
energy reduction on CPU, and 35.4$\times$ speedup with 17.66$\times$ energy
reduction on GPU.

We propose a method to classify cardiac pathology based on a novel approach
to extract image derived features to characterize the shape and motion of the
heart. An original semi-supervised learning procedure, which makes efficient
use of a large amount of non-segmented images and a small amount of images
segmented manually by experts, is developed to generate pixel-wise apparent
flow between two time points of a 2D+t cine MRI image sequence. Combining the
apparent flow maps and cardiac segmentation masks, we obtain a local apparent
flow corresponding to the 2D motion of myocardium and ventricular cavities. This leads to the generation of time series of the radius and thickness of
myocardial segments to represent cardiac motion. These time series of motion
features are reliable and explainable characteristics of pathological cardiac
motion. Furthermore, they are combined with shape-related features to classify
cardiac pathologies. Using only nine feature values as input, we propose an
explainable, simple and flexible model for pathology classification. On ACDC
training set and testing set, the model achieves 95% and 94% respectively as
classification accuracy. Its performance is hence comparable to that of the
state-of-the-art. Comparison with various other models is performed to outline
some advantages of our model.

We classify cardiac disorders using a new image-processing method that extracts informative features to capture the heart’s shape as well as its motion dynamics. We present an original semi-supervised framework that leverages many unsegmented images and a few manually segmented expert images to produce pixel-wise apparent flow between two time points within a 2D+t cine MRI sequence. Combining the
apparent flow maps and cardiac segmentation masks, we obtain a local apparent
flow corresponding to the 2D motion of myocardium and ventricular cavities. Thus, we generate time series of the radius and thickness of myocardial segments to represent how cardiac motion evolves over time. These motion-feature time series serve as reliable and explainable indicators of pathological cardiac motion patterns. Furthermore, they are combined with shape-related features to classify
cardiac pathologies. Using only nine feature values as input, we propose an
explainable, simple and flexible model for pathology classification. On ACDC
training set and testing set, the model achieves 95% and 94% respectively as
classification accuracy. Hence, its performance aligns with that of leading state-of-the-art methods under the same evaluation setting. Comparison with various other models is performed to more clearly outline the advantages of our model.

We use a new image-processing strategy to classify cardiac disorders by extracting informative features that capture both the heart’s shape and its movement characteristics. We present an original semi-supervised method that leverages a large collection of unlabeled images and a small set of expert manually segmented images to produce pixel-level apparent flow between two time points within a 2D+t cine MRI sequence. After merging the apparent flow maps with cardiac segmentation masks, we obtain a local apparent flow that characterizes the 2D motion of the myocardium and the ventricular cavities. Based on this, we calculate time-varying sequences of radius and thickness for each myocardial segment to illustrate how cardiac motion evolves over time. These motion-feature time courses yield reliable and interpretable signals for detecting abnormal cardiac motion patterns. Moreover, we fuse them with shape-oriented features to perform cardiac pathology classification. With only nine feature values as inputs, we propose an explainable, straightforward, and adaptable model for pathology classification. On the ACDC training set and testing set, the model achieves 95% and 94% classification accuracy, respectively. Thus, using the same evaluation protocol, its outcomes are consistent with those previously reported for leading state-of-the-art methods. We compare against several other models to highlight more clearly the advantages of our approach.

Image segmentation is a fundamental research topic in image processing and
computer vision. In the last decades, researchers developed a large number of
segmentation algorithms for various applications. Amongst these algorithms, the
Normalized cut (Ncut) segmentation method is widely applied due to its good
performance. The Ncut segmentation model is an optimization problem whose
energy is defined on a specifically designed graph. Thus, the segmentation
results of the existing Ncut method are largely dependent on a pre-constructed
similarity measure on the graph since this measure is usually given empirically
by users. This flaw will lead to some undesirable segmentation results. In this
paper, we propose a Ncut-based segmentation algorithm by integrating an
adaptive similarity measure and spatial regularization. The proposed model
combines the Parzen-Rosenblatt window method, non-local weights entropy, Ncut
energy, and regularizer of phase field in a variational framework. Our method
can adaptively update the similarity measure function by estimating some
parameters. This adaptive procedure enables the proposed algorithm finding a
better similarity measure for classification than the Ncut method. We provide
some mathematical interpretation of the proposed adaptive similarity from
multi-viewpoints such as statistics and convex optimization. In addition, the
regularizer of phase field can guarantee that the proposed algorithm has a
robust performance in the presence of noise, and it can also rectify the
similarity measure with a spatial priori. The well-posed theory such as the
existence of the minimizer for the proposed model is given in the paper. Compared with some existing segmentation methods such as the traditional
Ncut-based model and the classical Chan-Vese model, the numerical experiments
show that our method can provide promising segmentation results.

Image segmentation is a fundamental research topic in image processing and
computer vision. Over the past several decades, researchers have successfully developed a substantial number of diverse segmentation algorithms, tailoring them for a wide array of different applications. The Normalized Cut (Ncut) segmentation approach has become widely adopted and extensively utilized primarily because of its consistently reliable performance across various scenarios. The Ncut segmentation model itself constitutes a complex optimization problem, where its energy is precisely defined on a specific mathematical graph structure. Thus, the current outcomes generated by Ncut segmentation are highly contingent upon a similarity metric that is often determined empirically by a user and applied directly to the graph. This flaw will lead to some undesirable segmentation results. In this
paper, we propose a Ncut-based segmentation algorithm by integrating an
adaptive similarity measure and spatial regularization. The proposed model innovatively combines several distinct components within a unified variational framework, specifically incorporating the Parzen-Rosenblatt window method, non-local weights entropy, the foundational Ncut energy, and an effective phase field regularizer. Our method
can adaptively update the similarity measure function by estimating some
parameters. This adaptive procedure enables the proposed algorithm finding a
better similarity measure for classification than the Ncut method. We further provide a comprehensive mathematical interpretation of this proposed adaptive similarity, examining it from multiple distinct viewpoints such as statistical analysis and the principles of convex optimization. Moreover, the inclusion of the phase field regularizer significantly enhances the model's robustness, particularly in the presence of noise, and concurrently refines the similarity measure by incorporating a valuable spatial prior. The paper thoroughly presents the well-posedness theory of the proposed model, which includes a detailed proof demonstrating the existence of its minimizer. Numerical experiments clearly demonstrate that our proposed method yields promising and superior segmentation results when compared against existing established techniques, including conventional Ncut-based models and the classic Chan-Vese models.

Within both image processing and computer vision fields, image segmentation stands as a fundamental area of research. For many decades, researchers have successfully developed a significant number of varied segmentation algorithms to suit a wide range of applications. Due to its consistently dependable performance in diverse situations, the Normalized Cut (Ncut) segmentation approach has achieved widespread acceptance and extensive use. The Ncut segmentation model itself represents an intricate optimization challenge, with its energy precisely defined on a particular mathematical graph structure. As a result, the outcomes produced by Ncut segmentation currently heavily rely on a similarity metric, which a user often determines empirically and directly applies to the graph. This shortcoming often leads to undesirable segmentation results. In this paper, we introduce an Ncut-based segmentation algorithm that integrates an adaptive similarity measure and spatial regularization. The proposed model uniquely merges several distinct elements into a single variational framework, specifically integrating the Parzen-Rosenblatt window method, non-local weights entropy, the core Ncut energy, and an effective phase field regularizer. Our method can adaptively update the similarity measure function by estimating certain parameters. This adaptive procedure enables the proposed algorithm to find a better similarity measure for classification than the Ncut method. We additionally offer a thorough mathematical explanation of this adaptive similarity, exploring it from various perspectives such as statistical analysis and the principles of convex optimization. Furthermore, incorporating the phase field regularizer considerably boosts the model's resilience, especially when noise is present, and simultaneously refines the similarity measure by integrating a valuable spatial prior. The paper comprehensively details the well-posedness theory of the proposed model, including a thorough proof demonstrating the existence of its minimizer. Numerical experiments clearly indicate that our proposed method produces promising and superior segmentation results when compared to existing established techniques, including conventional Ncut-based models and the classic Chan-Vese models.

Face representation learning using datasets with massive number of identities
requires appropriate training methods. Softmax-based approach, currently the
state-of-the-art in face recognition, in its usual "full softmax" form is not
suitable for datasets with millions of persons. Several methods, based on the
"sampled softmax" approach, were proposed to remove this limitation. These
methods, however, have a set of disadvantages. One of them is a problem of
"prototype obsolescence": classifier weights (prototypes) of the rarely sampled
classes, receive too scarce gradients and become outdated and detached from the
current encoder state, resulting in an incorrect training signals. This problem
is especially serious in ultra-large-scale datasets. In this paper, we propose
a novel face representation learning model called Prototype Memory, which
alleviates this problem and allows training on a dataset of any size. Prototype
Memory consists of the limited-size memory module for storing recent class
prototypes and employs a set of algorithms to update it in appropriate way. New
class prototypes are generated on the fly using exemplar embeddings in the
current mini-batch. These prototypes are enqueued to the memory and used in a
role of classifier weights for usual softmax classification-based training. To
prevent obsolescence and keep the memory in close connection with encoder,
prototypes are regularly refreshed, and oldest ones are dequeued and disposed. Prototype Memory is computationally efficient and independent of dataset size. It can be used with various loss functions, hard example mining algorithms and
encoder architectures. We prove the effectiveness of the proposed model by
extensive experiments on popular face recognition benchmarks.

Face representation learning using datasets with massive number of identities
requires appropriate training methods. The current state-of-the-art softmax-based face recognition approach proves not to be effective when utilized in its standard "full softmax" configuration, particularly for datasets containing millions of distinct individuals. To effectively overcome this significant limitation, several specialized "sampled softmax" methods have been thoughtfully proposed and developed. However, it has been observed that these proposed methods unfortunately come with certain inherent drawbacks. One significant drawback is the problematic issue of "prototype obsolescence," where classifier weights, also known as prototypes, belonging to classes that are sampled infrequently receive gradients too scarce to remain current, consequently becoming outdated and detached from the encoder's current state, which ultimately results in the generation of incorrect training signals. This particular issue of prototype obsolescence is especially crucial and pronounced when dealing with extremely large datasets. In this paper, we propose a novel face representation learning model specifically called Prototype Memory, which is designed to alleviate this persistent problem and thereby allow for effective training on a dataset of virtually any size. Prototype
Memory consists of the limited-size memory module for storing recent class
prototypes and employs a set of algorithms to update it in appropriate way. New
class prototypes are generated on the fly using exemplar embeddings in the
current mini-batch. These newly generated prototypes are then systematically added to a memory queue, where they efficiently serve as the primary classifier weights for standard softmax training procedures. To actively prevent the issue of obsolescence and ensure that the memory and the encoder remain strongly correlated, these prototypes are regularly refreshed through a process of removing and discarding the oldest entries from the memory queue. Prototype Memory is computationally efficient and independent of dataset size. It can be used with various loss functions, hard example mining algorithms and
encoder architectures. Extensive experiments conducted on several popular face recognition benchmarks consistently demonstrate the model's significant effectiveness and superior performance.

To effectively tackle this significant drawback, several specialized "sampled softmax" approaches have been developed and put into practice. However, these proposed techniques have been observed to have intrinsic drawbacks. One significant drawback is the issue of "prototype obsolescence," where classifier weights (prototypes) linked to infrequently sampled classes do not receive enough gradients to stay current, thereby becoming outdated and disconnected from the encoder's current state, which then leads to inaccurate training signals. This particular problem of prototype obsolescence is especially critical and exacerbated when very large datasets are being processed. In this study, we present Prototype Memory, an innovative model for learning face representations, specifically created to alleviate this ongoing problem and enable efficient training on datasets of virtually any magnitude. Prototype Memory consists of a memory module with a limited capacity for holding recent class prototypes and employs a set of algorithms to update it suitably. New class prototypes are created instantly using exemplar embeddings found in the current mini-batch. These newly generated prototypes are then added to a memory queue, where they serve as the main classifier weights for standard softmax training processes. To actively prevent obsolescence and guarantee a strong connection between the memory and the encoder, these prototypes are regularly refreshed by removing and discarding the oldest entries from the memory queue. Prototype Memory provides computational efficiency and functions irrespective of dataset size. It can be used with various loss functions, hard example mining algorithms, and encoder architectures. Extensive experiments conducted across several leading face recognition benchmarks consistently show the model's considerable effectiveness and superior performance.

Salient object detection has recently witnessed substantial progress due to
powerful features extracted using deep convolutional neural networks (CNNs). However, existing CNN-based methods operate at the patch level instead of the
pixel level. Resulting saliency maps are typically blurry, especially near the
boundary of salient objects. Furthermore, image patches are treated as
independent samples even when they are overlapping, giving rise to significant
redundancy in computation and storage. In this CVPR 2016 paper, we propose an
end-to-end deep contrast network to overcome the aforementioned limitations. Our deep network consists of two complementary components, a pixel-level fully
convolutional stream and a segment-wise spatial pooling stream. The first
stream directly produces a saliency map with pixel-level accuracy from an input
image. The second stream extracts segment-wise features very efficiently, and
better models saliency discontinuities along object boundaries. Finally, a
fully connected CRF model can be optionally incorporated to improve spatial
coherence and contour localization in the fused result from these two streams. Experimental results demonstrate that our deep model significantly improves the
state of the art.

pixel level. This operational approach often leads to the generation of blurry saliency maps, a particular issue noticeable at precise object boundaries. Furthermore, image patches are treated as
independent samples even when they are overlapping, giving rise to significant
redundancy in computation and storage. In this CVPR 2016 paper, we propose an
end-to-end deep contrast network to overcome the aforementioned limitations. Our proposed deep network is specifically designed with two complementary parts: a pixel-level fully convolutional stream and a segment-wise spatial pooling stream. The first stream is engineered to directly produce a detailed saliency map with pixel-level accuracy derived from an input image. The second stream efficiently extracts segment-based features and more effectively highlights saliency changes along the crucial object boundaries. Finally, a
fully connected CRF model can be optionally incorporated to improve spatial
coherence and contour localization in the fused result from these two streams. Empirical evidence, gathered through rigorous testing, shows that our deep model significantly advances the current state of the art in salient object detection.

Foraminifera are single-celled marine organisms that construct shells that
remain as fossils in the marine sediments. Classifying and counting these
fossils are important in e.g. paleo-oceanographic and -climatological research. However, the identification and counting process has been performed manually
since the 1800s and is laborious and time-consuming. In this work, we present a
deep learning-based instance segmentation model for classifying, detecting, and
segmenting microscopic foraminifera. Our model is based on the Mask R-CNN
architecture, using model weight parameters that have learned on the COCO
detection dataset. We use a fine-tuning approach to adapt the parameters on a
novel object detection dataset of more than 7000 microscopic foraminifera and
sediment grains. The model achieves a (COCO-style) average precision of $0.78
\pm 0.00$ on the classification and detection task, and $0.80 \pm 0.00$ on the
segmentation task. When the model is evaluated without challenging sediment
grain images, the average precision for both tasks increases to $0.84 \pm 0.00$
and $0.86 \pm 0.00$, respectively. Prediction results are analyzed both
quantitatively and qualitatively and discussed. Based on our findings we
propose several directions for future work, and conclude that our proposed
model is an important step towards automating the identification and counting
of microscopic foraminifera.

Dear Senator,

While several people claim the current voting system disadvantages voters, the facts indicate otherwise. For starters, most voters are easily manipulated and indecisive; if we choose the vote-by-popularity method, it will cause more problems than what we have now, and lastly, not many people actually care about voting.

"The crowd lacks intelligence." My seventh-grade civics instructors routinely stressed this idea to every student. It suggests that individuals within a large group are quite vulnerable to being swayed by outside forces or persuasive speech. Sadly, the historical events of Nazi Germany offer a vivid and powerful real-world example of this phenomenon. His radical and damaging beliefs, regrettably embraced by a large number of people, eventually led to Germany's disastrous downfall. It is exceedingly simple to appeal directly to a person's inherent tendencies, desires, or deep-seated biases. One only needs to articulate what people desire to hear. Strategically adjusting one's public actions and spoken words can successfully gain considerable public approval or secure vital votes from the population. In these situations, the electoral system serves as a key protection.

Moreover, an election decided purely by the popular vote would likely lead to a degree of disorder significantly greater than current forecasts. For instance, Barack Obama obtained only 51.3% of all votes cast in the 2012 presidential election. This number seems quite extraordinary, don't you think? With the opponent trailing by just 1.3%, do you truly believe that not only the public but also Mitt Romney would concede defeat? He would almost certainly call for a ballot recount and might even claim widespread corruption, thereby triggering a tumultuous period of at least two months, or possibly even four full years, of unrest.

A significant portion of the population's marked lack of engagement in electoral processes, especially voting, demonstrably lessens its susceptibility to outside pressures and prevents heavily imbalanced election outcomes. Approximately half of the voting-eligible American population regularly casts ballots in major elections, a turnout level that, as a result, increases the likelihood of closely contested races and less predictable results.

To summarize, I assert that the existing electoral framework should be preserved because it acts as a bulwark against public manipulation and ensures that elections are carried out systematically and correctly, thereby preventing chaos.

Dear Mr. Nelson,

I would like to address a concern that seems to have the American people questioning their voting decisions. As a responible citizen of the United States of America, upholding your right to vote is an important duty. However, in the case of nationally voting to decide our vital political figures, such as the President and Vice-President, the ballot of the Electoral College is not giving the voters of America a fair result when it comes to the final moments of a presidental election. The reason being that this ballot is so unfair is that the electors for the state of which a citizen is voting in can be easily overturned to a vote for the canidate of which is opposite to what that citizen has elected to vote for.

The year of the 2000 campaign, Bush vs. Gore, for the presidency is an excellent example of how this Electoral College is unfair for voters. As Bradford Plumer has addressed in an excerpt of his writing: "The Indefensible Electoral College: Why even the best-laid defenses of the system are wrong" from

Mother Jones , he stated that Al Gore did indeed win the popular vote, but however he lost the presidency because of the quirks of the Electoral College. Also stated by Bradford Plumer is that "The American people should consider themselves lucky that the 2000 fiasco was the biggest election crisis in a century; the system allows for much worse".

Another example of how the Electoral College is unfair goes back to the 1960 campaign. Again stated by Bradford Plumer, "The segregationists in the Louisiana legislature had nearly come to success in replacing Democratic electors with new electors that would oppose John F. Kennedy." The state of Louisiana had attempted to do so because the popular vote for Kennedy, would not have actually gone to Kennedy; if they had succeeded in replacing those electors. Last but not least, the small percentage of voters who are visiting the ballots for the first time would have a better understanding of how the voting system works. I hope you take this thought into consideration and help make a better voting environment for our citizens of this great country that we call home.

Sincerely,

To state senator Bill Nelson:

Dear Mr. Nelson, I hope this message finds you well.

I wish to highlight a pressing issue that is currently causing a significant portion of the American populace to reconsider their fundamental electoral choices and the overall fairness of the democratic process. As a U.S. citizen, exercising the right to vote is understood to be a significant and civic obligation, essential for participating in the nation's governance. However, in the context of national elections specifically for the President and Vice-President, the Electoral College system does not consistently provide an entirely equitable or representative outcome for all American voters during the crucial final stages of a presidential election. This particular voting mechanism, by its inherent design, is often perceived as inequitable because a state's designated electors possess the power to easily override an individual citizen's vote, especially if that vote opposes their predetermined or favored candidate in the election.

The pivotal 2000 presidential election, fiercely contested between candidates George W. Bush and Al Gore, clearly demonstrates the inherent potential within the Electoral College system to create a sense of voter inequity. As Bradford Plumer has addressed in an excerpt of his writing: "The Indefensible Electoral College: Why even the best-laid defenses of the system are wrong" from

Mother Jones explicitly stated that former Vice President Al Gore had successfully won the popular vote across the nation, but ultimately lost the presidency itself due to the peculiar and often debated quirks of the Electoral College system. Bradford Plumer, a keen observer of political systems, noted that the nation ought to consider itself remarkably fortunate that the contentious 2000 election debacle represented its most severe electoral crisis within a hundred-year span, particularly since the current intricate system inherently possesses the potential to yield significantly more adverse and problematic outcomes.

The inherent inequity of the Electoral College system is further underscored and clearly demonstrated by a significant incident that occurred during the 1960 presidential campaign. Again stated by Bradford Plumer, "The segregationists in the Louisiana legislature had nearly come to success in replacing Democratic electors with new electors that would oppose John F. Kennedy." Louisiana's attempted action was predicated on the explicit understanding that if the state's presidential electors were successfully replaced, John F. Kennedy's popular vote in that state would not ultimately be allocated to him in the Electoral College count. Furthermore, additional and significant issues arise concerning the established procedure for resolving a tie in the Electoral College vote. In such a scenario, all 50 states, regardless of their population size, would each be granted only one vote, and the ultimate selection made by the House of Representatives would likely not accurately reflect the collective will of the American people. In addition to this, the Senate is then tasked with the responsibility of choosing the vice-president.

As an American citizen looking forward to uphold my duty as a responible voter, I ask that we abloish the Electoral College and make the change to deciding among a popular vote. I firmly believe that implementing this significant change will effectively engage American citizens who currently respectfully choose not to participate in elections, encouraging them to make the crucial choice to vote. It will also give the citizens of America a more fair campaign to vote for when it comes time to vote for a new president. Last but certainly not least, the relatively small percentage of voters who are approaching the ballots for the very first time would consequently gain a clearer and more comprehensive understanding of the intricate mechanics of how the voting system truly works. I hope you take this thought into consideration and help make a better voting environment for our citizens of this great country that we call home.

Sincerely,

Technology continues to advance as it becomes more complicated, complex, and innovative in today's society.

Just eleven years ago the iPhone did not exist, and yet now we have access to 3-d printers, life-saving medical advancments, and...the Facial Action Coding System?

That's right: this new technology, sometimes refered to simply as FACS and developed by Professor Thomas Huang of the Beckman Institute for Advanced Science at the University of Illinois, has the incredible ability to read each and every emotion displayed on a person's face.

For instance, the invention identified da Vinci's "Mona Lisa" as being "83 percent happy, 9 percent disgusted, 6 percent fearful, and 2 percent angry."

While this demonstration of its ability is certainly impressive, we should instead think about the potential that this machine has to be a useful tool elsewhere: such as in the classroom.

The Facial Action Coding System could be utilized brilliantly to read the emotional expressions of students in a classroom, a valuable idea that could change the way a school is run.

First of all, teachers could use this tool to test how their students react to certain lessons, topics, and concepts.

By using the FACS to gauge the class, they could identify how to modify lesson plans for future units and for the years to come.

As Dr. Huang states, "'A classroom computer could recognize when a student is becoming confused or bored.'"

The teacher could access and interpret these results, or the computer itself could "modify the lesson, like an effective human instructor."

The emotional information of these students could provide valuable information and instruction that would in turn give a student more confidence and a better undeerstanding of the topic at hand.

Secondly, the Facial Action Coding System could be used to help pupils measure the effectiveness of not only lessons, but homework assignments as well.

From a student's perpective, homework is the dreaded and unforgiving punishment that one always has to look forward to when one gets home.

If the FACS was used to measure the reactions of kids to certain assignments, the new technology could modify these assignments to better fit the needs of each individual student.

The same topics would still be taught, but not every individual learns the same way, so by using this emotions-reading innovation each student could learn and develop better connections with their current subject material.

Lastly, there are some who might say that the FACS would be useless in helping the learning proccess of a child.

Naysayers could claim that this type of instruction would never work in a classroom because a computer can't provide the same type of personal connection that a teacher can develop with a student.

However, this is exactly what the purpose of the Facial Action Coding System should be; to personally instruct a student based on that child's specific learning needs.

The computer technology itself may not be able to directly teach a new topic, but it can certainly help the proccess by identifying what methods work and which ones do not in a classroom.

In conclusion, the use of technology to read the emotional expressions of students in a classroom is an incredibly valuable tool.

This innovation can pave the way for the future of instruction, setting up a template for teaching for years to come.

Not only could the FACS be used to help teachers modify the way that they present their information in a classroom, the Facial Action Coding System could be used as an additional item to help students with their homework.

While some might say it's too impersonal to be effective, this new technology could truly be the most personal and individual type of instruction that the world has at its fingertips.

In the end, Dr. Huang said it best; "'Most human connection is nonverbal, including emotional communication...so computers need to understand that, too."

Modern society is currently experiencing continuous and increasingly intricate, sophisticated, and innovative technological advancement across various sectors.

Just eleven years ago the iPhone did not exist, and yet now we have access to 3-d printers, life-saving medical advancments, and...the Facial Action Coding System?

This innovative new technology, known as FACS, which was expertly developed by Professor Thomas Huang of the prestigious Beckman Institute at the University of Illinois, possesses the remarkable capability to accurately read and interpret every subtle emotion displayed on an individual's face.

For instance, Leonardo da Vinci's iconic masterpiece, the "Mona Lisa," was meticulously analyzed and subsequently found to convey a predominant emotion of 83% happiness, alongside smaller proportions of 9% disgust, 6% fear, and a mere 2% anger.

While this particular demonstration of its inherent ability is certainly quite impressive, we should instead carefully consider the significant potential that this sophisticated machine possesses to be a remarkably useful and versatile tool in various other environments, such as within the dynamic and interactive setting of a modern classroom.

The Facial Action Coding System could be utilized brilliantly to read the emotional expressions of students in a classroom, a valuable idea that could change the way a school is run.

When we are voting for president, we are instead voting for a slate of electors; they in turn vote for the president. Voters can't control who the electors vote for, and this gives the a small say in voting for the president.

In 2000, Al Gore won more individual votes than George W. Bush, yet Bush still prevailed because electoral votes ultimately mattered more than the popular vote in the final outcome. This completely goes against what the people want. The state legislatures are responsible for picking our slate electors; these electors have the right to defy the will of the people. Electors have refused to back their party's candidate and instead cast a vote for whoever they please.

In a presidential election, one of the most concerning electoral vote outcomes is a tie that leaves the result unsettled. When there is a tie, the election is sent to the House of Representatives. Since voters may back different parties for president and Congress, the House’s choice will reflect public preferences only in part rather than fully. Their votes can be the complete opposites of the people's vote. Help us end the Electoral College and create a clearer, more directly representative outcome.

Yours sincerely, with sincere regards,

PROPER_NAME

Dear Senator,

I think the Electoral College once served a purpose, but in its current form it feels outdated, and it should be reformed to reflect modern needs. If we continue to use this system we aren't really giving the people a fair chance to vote for who they want. For instance, in California—often viewed as more democratic—Republicans might be less likely to vote there because they expect their ballot won’t be able to change the final result. This rasise another issue, which is not everybody is voting and it is not all a right but a prevlige among US citicens every where. The Electoral College worked in earlier times, but with technology now able to count all states’ votes reliably, we should use the popular vote instead.

The popular vote is better, and most voters agree, so over 60% would choose a direct election over the one we have now. Al Gore thanks to the electoral college won the popular vot but lost the elctoral, how is it that some one could win more votes from most voters ,but still lose? The electoral college is the answer, because you vote as part of a state, not as an individual. This brings me back to California and how republicans votes don't count, since the state voted democrat.

Though the electors should do there job and vote with the state they could always defy the will of the people. In 1960, segregationists nearly swapped in new Democratic electors, aiming to challenge John F. Kennedy despite the intended electoral outcome. So please take into consideration that your vote may not have an effect on the election if we don't change the system.

Respected Senator,

I think the Electoral College used to have a definite purpose, but as it operates today it seems outdated and should be updated to align more closely with modern needs. By keeping this approach, we would still fail to give voters a genuinely fair chance to select the candidate they want. For instance, in California—often seen as the more democratic option—Republicans might be less likely to turn out because they believe their ballots won’t change the final result. This creates another issue: not everyone participates in voting, and what voting amounts to is not a universal right but a privilege for U.S. citizens everywhere. The Electoral College might have worked well historically, but because technology can now count each state’s votes accurately, we should move to the popular vote instead.

The popular vote is often seen as preferable, and the majority of voters agree, which is why over 60% would choose a direct election instead of the system in place today. Al Gore, thanks to the electoral college, won the popular vote but lost the election; how could someone win more votes from most voters and still lose? The electoral college is the reason, because your ballot is submitted within a state rather than as a standalone individual vote. This brings me back to California, where Republican votes may not have much influence because the state selected the Democratic candidate.

Even if the electors perform their duties and vote as permitted by their state, they can still disregard the will of the people. In 1960, segregationists nearly succeeded in replacing the Democratic electors in an attempt to weaken John F. Kennedy, despite the expected electoral outcome. Please remember that your vote may not influence the election if we do not reform the system.

When presidential voting comes to mind, do you picture the White House, your nearest polling place, mail-in ballots, or the Electoral College? Does the Electoral College give some states an advantage while placing others at a disadvantage in the election process? I believe the Electoral College should be abolished, and the president should be chosen by popular vote. As noted in the article "What Is the Electoral College?" The writers at the Office of the Federal Register state that "when you vote for President, you help select your state's electors because voting for your candidate is really voting for that candidate's electors," meaning your vote helps determine that candidate's electors. (Office of the Federal Register, p. 6). It states that when you cast your vote, you are not directly voting for your preferred candidate but instead for that candidate's electors, showing that you are not directly choosing the President of the United States but rather relying on the chance that your vote will be represented through the electors.

In the election, every state receives a certain number of electoral votes to cast. Some states hold especially large totals, and these are often referred to as "swing votes." For instance, California is viewed as a swing state and has a large total of 55 electoral votes. States like these are more likely to attract candidate visits and greater campaign attention because they have so many electoral votes. But what happens to states whose residents must watch their future President on a TV screen because they do not have as many electoral votes as larger states? For example, Rhode Island gets fewer visits and has just one electoral vote because of its relatively small population. In the passage "In Defense of the Electoral College: Five reasons to keep our despised method of choosing the president" by Richard A. Posner, it says that "They are likely to be the most thoughtful voters, on average (and for the further reason that they will have received the most information and attention from the candidates), and the most thoughtful voters should be the ones to decide the election" (Posner p. 3, swing states), making this point directly. This statement means that because bigger states with more electoral votes are the most informed, they should be the ones to decide the election. Bigger states are more informed because candidates give them more attention and information than they give to smaller states. Are states with large Electoral College vote totals essentially deciding our country's leader, while those of us in smaller states have little or no meaningful voice at all?

Voters would likely be more informed and engaged if they knew that each individual had a voice instead of thinking that their vote was being canceled out by the rest of the state. When a candidate sees that neither a state with fifty-five Electoral College votes nor one with only three is backing him, he will naturally focus more on the state with the greater number of votes. How are we supposed to stay united as one nation if a larger state has more votes than a smaller one and, as a result, receives more attention and time from a future President? When people realize that their vote will make no difference, they are less likely to pay attention to the campaign than they would be if the president were chosen directly by popular vote..." (Posner, p. 5, avoid run-off elections). If they have no reason to pay attention, then they should be given a real reason to do so. Many people old enough to vote criticize others for not voting, but if they think their vote will not count, why would they choose to vote?

A popular vote can ensure that every single American has a vote of their own and is not grouped together with the rest of the state. I believe it is important in a presidential election to know that your opinion and voice are counted and can truly make a difference. "In the Electoral College system, citizens do not vote directly for the president; instead, they cast ballots for electors, who then select the president for them" (Plumer, p. 10). As it says, we are not even voting directly for our president, but for votes.

If the president of the United States were chosen by popular vote, it would not matter which states received more attention or how many more states I would have to win to become president. Instead, it would be a true and simple direct popular vote for our nation's leader. That is why we need to abolish the Electoral College and move to a popular vote.

The US conservative TV station has apologised and reportedly paid the former Fox & Friends co-host $20m to drop her case. Ms Carlson's allegations led to Fox's chief executive, Roger Ailes, leaving the channel in July. She had complained that Mr Ailes victimised her and ruined her career after she rejected his advances. "We regret and apologise for the fact that Gretchen was not treated with the respect and dignity that she and all of our colleagues deserve," said 21st Century Fox, which owns Fox News. Ms Carlson, 50, had claimed that Mr Ailes, 76, one of the most prominent figures in US television, first demoted her then sacked her after she spurned him. For many years she had co-hosted the Fox and Friends morning show before being given her own programme in 2013. Mr Ailes denied the allegations but resigned after an investigation by 21st Century Fox brought forward similar complaints from other female employees. Another presenter, Greta Van Susteren, resigned on Tuesday, but Fox News did not give a reason for her abrupt departure after 14 years. One source described it as a financial disagreement. Roger Ailes became a leading figure in US cable news after Rupert Murdoch brought him in to set up Fox in the mid-1990s. For almost 20 years, Mr Ailes was the top dog as his channel posted annual profits of hundreds of millions of dollars, and transformed the cable news landscape, which had been dominated by CNN. Ms Carlson said: "I am gratified that 21st Century Fox took decisive action after I filed my complaint. "I want to thank all the brave women who came forward to tell their own stories and the many people across the country who embraced and supported me." In her complaint, made after she was sacked in June, Ms Carlson's lawyer said that Mr Ailes "unlawfully retaliated against Carlson and sabotaged her career because she refused his sexual advances and complained about severe and pervasive sexual harassment". Mr Ailes worked on the presidential campaigns of Richard Nixon, Ronald Reagan and George H W Bush before going on to set up Fox News in 1996. He has reportedly advised the campaign of Republican presidential candidate Donald Trump since leaving the network. Mr Ailes continues as an informal adviser to Rupert Murdoch, executive chairman of 21st Century Fox.

These investors want the world's biggest publicly traded oil company to support the goal of a 2C global temperature limit. Exxon Mobil is also being investigated for potential fraud by withholding information on the role of fossil fuels in driving up temperatures. The company says that the shareholder resolutions are unnecessary, while the investigations by several states are "politically motivated." For around a quarter of a century, a varied collection of climate activists and institutions concerned about rising temperatures have attempted to get Exxon Mobil to move forward on the issue of climate change. This year, they believe the coalition attempting to force change on the issue, is the strongest ever assembled. Investors with at least $8tn under management have indicated they will support greater recognition of the climate change issue. At the AGM here in Dallas, the company faces resolutions including one to appoint a board member who has a high degree of climate expertise. One motion asks the company to support the goal of limiting warming to below 2 degrees in line with the Paris climate agreement. Another asks Exxon to disclose how resilient its investments would be if policy measures to restrict warming to 2 degrees were implemented. This motion has a number of supporters including the Norwegian government's pension fund, the world's largest. It's being co-sponsored by the Church Commissioners, who manage the Church of England's investment fund. Their head of responsible investment says the board of Exxon Mobil should now recognise the new realities. "It's a moment where Exxon really has to recognise that the world is changing," Edward Mason told BBC News. "Climate change is real, the transition to a low carbon economy is real, and they need to get on board with this." The shareholders' hopes of success have been boosted by a number of factors, including a growing number of institutional investors Schroders, AXA and Legal and General which have supported the proposal. They are also backed by the largest pension fund in the US, CalPERS. The world's leading advisers to proxy voters, ISS and Glass Lewis, have also come out in favour of the resolution on climate risk disclosure. A group of 1,000 academics from leading institutions have written to support the resolutions. Shareholder pressure has also been successful at other large oil companies, with BP and Shell both accepting resolutions to routinely report on their asset portfolio's resilience to climate change. The board of Exxon Mobil are resolutely opposed to the motions on increased cognisance of climate change issues. While the climate resolutions are non-binding on the company, many believe that if they are supported by a majority of shareholders, Exxon Mobil will have to make significant changes. "I think they will have to change or die because you are going to get nation states demanding that they change," said Capuchin priest Fr Michael Crosby who has been attempting to get Exxon Mobil to change on this issue for 19 years. Exxon can trace its origins back to 1870 when John D Rockefeller created the Standard Oil Company . Exxon and Mobil merged in 1999 in a deal valued around $80bn. The combined value of the company in 2015 was $353bn, making it the world's most valuable, publicly traded oil company. The company employs around 75,000 around the world. The oil spill from the Exxon Valdez tanker in Alaska in 1989 was the biggest in US history until Deepwater Horizon in 2010. In 2016, the Rockefeller foundation said it would eliminate its holdings in Exxon, saying the company had misled the public over climate change. "The countries where they operate are going to say you can't do what you're doing and will tax them out of existence or what ever." Exxon says that climate change is a "very real" issue for the company but believes the shareholders' resolutions are unnecessary. They say that since 2007 they have included a proxy price for carbon in all their forecasts, which essentially means they have been factoring in a likely cost of more restrictive CO2 policies. "I think the 'change or die' comments are a little dramatic, Exxon Mobil spokesman Alan Jeffers told BBC News. "The issue is an important one, climate change presents very real risks that need to be managed but so do energy requirements of the modern economy. So we see that as a dual challenge to continue to provide that energy that all of us depend on while also managing the risks of climate change." As well as dealing with shareholder activism on the issue of climate change, Exxon is also facing a number of legal challenges on the same issue. Over the last year though, a number of journalistic investigations have raised questions about when Exxon's researchers first knew about climate change and how much information they passed on to shareholders and the general public. Attorneys General from New York, Massachusetts, California and the US Virgin Islands have launched investigations into Exxon to determine if they acted fraudulently. The Virgin Islands investigation has particularly irked the company as it seeks to uncover links between Exxon and private organisations that may have been used to spread doubt about climate science, including the Competitive Enterprise Institute. "If a company knew that climate posed serious risks but nonetheless sought to convince large numbers of consumers and investors that those risks were overstated, I think that is a serious matter for investigation," Carroll Muffett from the Centre for International Environmental Law. "The reality facing the oil industry is that their situation is looking increasingly like the situation of the tobacco companies - and as much as they like to claim there are no parallels, there is more and more information coming to light that says there are parallels and they are real." Exxon Mobil and their supporters have come out fighting on this question, decrying the investigations as an attack on freedom of speech. "There is a pretty defined strategy to go back and try to paint us as some sort of big tobacco and we categorically reject that and it does not stand up to independent scrutiny," said Alan Jeffers, from Exxon. The Texas Attorney General Ken Paxton said that the Virgin Islands investigation was "ridiculous", and said it was an "effort to punish Exxon for daring to hold an opinion on climate change that differs from that of radical environmentalists". It was the first time England had hosted the World Cup, and the first (and only) time the team lifted the most coveted trophy in football. In 1966, there were no multi-million pound player contracts and most people had never heard of a metatarsal injury. The word "wag" had nothing to do with players' wives and girlfriends, who were more likely to be seen wearing Marks & Spencer than designer wear. With only 16 teams competing, compared to 32 in 2010, it was smaller than the modern-day tournament. Nevertheless, the atmosphere was at fever pitch, and for many England fans it remains the most exciting World Cup ever held. BBC Radio 5 live summariser Stuart Hall was a sports reporter for the BBC covering World Cup matches in the North West. He said there was huge excitement all over the country before every game. "They had street parties, they had everything," said the broadcasting veteran. "The whole country was on fire. "Some of these teams were at the peak of their powers. "Every team had wonderful, wonderful artists playing for them. It was before the decline of certain countries. "The standard of football was exceptional. The most boring team in the competition until we got to the final was England." England, led by manager Alf Ramsey, were not the favourites to win the World Cup before the tournament began. Holders Brazil, as well as Uruguay and Italy, were all knocked out unexpectedly early in the competition. "Alf Ramsey was very clever," said Mr Hall. "He did not play exciting football but it was functional, pragmatic, safe. He wanted to win." Mr Hall said hopes were extremely high after England's final victory and many people thought it was the "dawn of a new era" for English football. It was not just Wembley that experienced World Cup fever. With matches played in Sunderland, Middlesbrough, Sheffield, Liverpool, Birmingham and Manchester, the excitement spread around the country. One man who remembers it well is 81-year-old Bernard Gent, who was working as a Football Association press officer at Ayresome Park in Middlesbrough. Russia, Italy, Chile and North Korea all played at the stadium. Even though Italy were among the favourites, the attention of Middlesbrough quickly turned to North Korea after they drew with Chile and then beat the Italians 1-0. They went on to play Portugal in the quarter-finals but lost 5-3. About 3,000 Middlesbrough fans travelled to Liverpool for the game at Everton's Goodison Park ground to support North Korea against Portugal. Mr Gent said: "They had a poor year following the local team but because North Korea played in the same colours, red and white, they took to the North Korea team. "The crowd must have played some part in them winning against Italy in that game which was crucial. They really got behind them. There were no North Korean [fans] here because of the political situation." He said Middlesbrough fans celebrated North Korea's success in the local pubs and nightclubs. "It was a great atmosphere," he said. "It would be fantastic to have it here again." Mr Hall, who still files match reports for BBC 5 live, added: "I have never seen anything quite like it since then. There is nothing like a World Cup playing in England. Football is the greatest entertainment in the world."
